Start with cold-air drainage. Cold air is denser than warm air, so on a clear, calm night it flows downhill like water and pools in valley bottoms, hollows, and any depression. This katabatic drainage produces a genuine temperature inversion, and the difference between a valley floor and a bench thirty metres above it is commonly 5 to 10°C, occasionally more. A site partway up a gentle slope can therefore be dramatically warmer than the flat, inviting hollow just below it. The trade-off runs the other way at the top: exposed ridgelines and summits escape the cold sink but take the full wind, which usually costs more than the inversion gains. The sweet spot is a bench or terrace on the hillside, out of both the pool and the worst of the wind. In the northern hemisphere a south or south-east-facing aspect also catches morning sun, which matters more than it sounds when you are cold at dawn.

Always look up before committing. Dead branches hanging in the canopy and dead or leaning trees, known as widow-makers, fall without warning, and they fall most readily in wind or after rain loosens root systems. People have been killed sleeping under one. Scan the full circle of trees whose height could reach your site, not just the one directly overhead.

Water is a real trade-off rather than a simple positive. Being near a stream means easy access for drinking and washing, and it also means more insects, colder and damper air overnight in the immediate channel, and background noise that masks approaching weather or people. In arid terrain it becomes an outright hazard: dry washes and canyon bottoms flash flood from rain falling many miles upstream that you never see or hear, and a flat, clear, gravel-floored wash is one of the most dangerous places to sleep in that country precisely because it looks like the best campsite available. A working compromise is to camp roughly sixty metres back from and above the water.

Finish with three quick checks. Note the prevailing wind and orient the entrance away from it, using the lean of trees and the shape of drifted snow or debris as evidence rather than relying on the moment's breeze. Look at the ground itself for game trails, since animals will walk their route through your camp at night, and for ant nests, wasp holes, and standing deadwood. And in winter mountains, check what is above you on the slope: never build beneath an avalanche path, a cornice, or a gully that funnels snow, however sheltered the spot appears.

sections.heading: Snow Shelters: The Quinzhee and the Trench
sections.body:
Snow feels like the enemy of warmth, and a well-built snow shelter is among the best-insulated structures buildable by hand. The reason is that snow is mostly trapped air. Low-density snow conducts heat at roughly 0.05 to 0.15 watts per metre per kelvin, comparable to commercial building insulation and a fraction of the figure for ice or wet ground, so a wall of it is an excellent blanket rather than a block of cold.

A quinzhee is built by piling loose snow into a mound roughly seven to eight feet across and letting it sit undisturbed for at least an hour or two before hollowing it out. That waiting period is not optional. It allows sintering, in which the contact points between snow crystals partly melt under the mound's own weight and then refreeze, bonding the pile into a self-supporting dome. Mixing snow of different temperatures and grain sizes as you shovel accelerates it. Before digging, push a couple of dozen sticks about a foot long through the outer surface, aimed radially toward the centre. When you meet the inner tip of a stick while hollowing, stop digging at that point, which leaves a wall roughly twelve inches thick without the risk of breaking through. Raise a sleeping platform above the entrance level so cold air drains down and out, which is the same trick that makes a proper snow cave warm.

A snow trench is the low-effort alternative and needs perhaps thirty minutes: dig body-width and as deep as the pack allows, roof it with branches, skis, a tarp, or cut snow blocks, and shovel loose snow over the roof for extra insulation. Either shelter's interior tends to stabilise close to 32°F (0°C) regardless of how much colder it gets outside, which in a −20°F night is a fifty-degree improvement bought with a shovel.

That same airtight insulating quality carries two genuine hazards, and both are worth treating as hard rules rather than judgment calls. Carbon dioxide from your own breathing accumulates in a sealed space, so a snow shelter needs a ventilation hole of at least fist size poked through the roof, checked periodically, since drifting snow and refreezing meltwater can seal it over during the night. Keep a shovel or a ski pole inside for exactly that reason, and for digging out if the entrance drifts shut. Running any flame or stove inside a poorly ventilated snow shelter risks lethal carbon monoxide accumulation, and it also melts the ceiling into a dripping glaze that then refreezes into ice, destroying the insulation.

The honest caveat is effort. Building a quinzhee is hard physical work, and soaking your layers in sweat while doing it can leave you worse off than before. Strip a layer, work slowly, and keep a dry set sealed in the pack for the moment you stop.

sections.heading: Recognizing Hypothermia Before It's an Emergency
sections.body:
Hypothermia, a fall in core body temperature below about 95°F (35°C), rarely announces itself clearly, and the person developing it is usually the last to notice, because impaired judgment is one of its earliest symptoms. That single fact reorganises the whole problem: recognition is a group responsibility, and the useful question is not how you feel but how the person next to you is behaving.

Wilderness medicine teaches a mnemonic for the mild stage, the umbles. Mumbles is slurred or slowed speech. Fumbles is clumsy hands, dropped items, and trouble with zippers, buckles, or knots, which appears early because manual dexterity degrades badly once hand temperature falls below roughly 60°F. Stumbles is unsteady walking and poor coordination. Grumbles is irritability, withdrawal, apathy, or an uncharacteristic refusal to keep taking sensible precautions. Anyone showing several of these in cold, wet, or windy conditions should be treated as hypothermic and warmed and dried immediately rather than watched for another hour. Intense shivering at this stage is a good sign, since it means the body is still generating heat.

As core temperature falls into the moderate range, roughly 90 to 82°F (32 to 28°C), confusion deepens and, counterintuitively, shivering can stop altogether as thermoregulation begins to fail. The absence of shivering in someone who is clearly cold is a serious deterioration, not a sign of recovery. Paradoxical undressing, in which a severely hypothermic person removes clothing because constricted surface vessels suddenly dilate and produce a rush of warmth, appears in this range and is a well-documented finding at cold-weather death scenes. Below about 82°F (28°C) the risks become cardiac arrhythmia and unconsciousness, and a severely hypothermic person can appear dead, with no detectable pulse or breathing, while remaining viable. The working axiom is that nobody is dead until they are warm and dead, and resuscitation should not be abandoned on a cold patient simply because vital signs are hard to find; check breathing and pulse for a full sixty seconds before concluding anything.

Field priority is to stop further heat loss before attempting active rewarming. Get the person out of wind and wet, remove wet clothing, insulate thoroughly from the ground, and wrap them in dry layers with a vapour barrier and a windproof outer shell, the arrangement often called a hypothermia wrap or burrito. Do not rub limbs, do not apply direct high heat to arms and legs, and do not give alcohol; all three drive cold, acidotic blood from the extremities back to the core. Heat packs belong against the chest, armpits, and groin, never directly on skin.

Handle a severely hypothermic person gently. Rough movement can trigger a fatal arrhythmia in a cold heart, a real phenomenon sometimes called rescue collapse, so a cold casualty is moved carefully rather than quickly, and kept horizontal. Warm sweet drinks help only if the person is fully alert and able to swallow reliably.

sections.heading: Gear Worth Carrying for Shelter & Warmth
sections.body:
Most of a good shelter kit is small, cheap, and multi-purpose, bought once and left permanently in a pack. What justifies each item is which of the four heat-loss pathways it addresses, and buying several things that all block the same one is the common mistake.

A metallised emergency blanket is a radiation barrier. Its aluminised surface reflects most of the infrared a body emits, which is genuinely useful for something weighing under two ounces, and it blocks wind. It gives almost no conductive insulation, so it must never be the only thing between you and the ground, and because it is vapour-impermeable, sweat condenses inside it; expect to be damp by morning and treat that as a fair trade. A tarp addresses rain and radiative loss to the sky at once, and unlike a tent it can be pitched a dozen ways to suit the wind. Cordage is what turns a tarp into a shelter.

A closed-cell foam pad is the item most often left behind and most often regretted. It attacks conduction, the largest loss in most improvised shelters, and unlike an inflatable pad it cannot fail from a puncture. A sleeping bag's ratings deserve careful reading: under the ISO standard the comfort rating is what a typical cold sleeper actually needs, while the extreme rating is a six-hour survival figure at which a person is expected to be badly hypothermic rather than asleep. Buy on comfort.

A saw generally beats a hatchet for ridgepoles and ribbing: it cuts faster for the energy spent and is far less likely to open a leg wound in cold, clumsy hands. A wool or synthetic hat and gloves matter out of proportion to their weight, because the head and hands have high surface area, little insulating fat, and, in the hands, the dexterity every other task depends on. A cheap thermometer is the only way to turn a belief that a shelter works into evidence.
ingredients: An emergency space blanket (Mylar), from a camping/outdoor store or pharmacy — reflects radiated body heat back at you; genuinely effective for its size and weight
A lightweight tarp (roughly 8x10 ft, polyester or silnylon, with reinforced corner grommets), from a camping/outdoor or hardware store
50 feet of paracord or similar nylon cordage, from an outdoor/hardware store
A bivy sack, or large heavy-duty contractor-grade trash bags as an improvised rain/wind layer, from an outdoor store or hardware store
A folding saw or small hatchet, from a hardware/outdoor store — for cutting ridge poles and ribbing without exhausting yourself
A closed-cell foam sleeping pad, from a camping store — insulates against ground conduction, which matters more in cold weather than most people expect
A sleeping bag rated comfortably below the coldest temperature you realistically expect, from an outdoor store
A wool or synthetic-fill hat and gloves, from a clothing/outdoor store — the head and extremities lose heat out of proportion to their size
A basic outdoor thermometer, from a hardware or general store — useful for actually testing and proving out shelter insulation, as below

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Sleep-Test a Debris Shelter This Weekend
sections.body: Reading about insulation is not the same as feeling it work, and the gap between the two is where most improvised shelters fail. This exercise turns the physics into a measured result, in conditions where being wrong costs nothing but a cold evening. Two things reliably surprise people on a first attempt: how much debris a roof needs once it compresses, and how much of the night's heat loss went into the ground rather than out through the walls. Both are far easier to learn near a parked car than during an emergency.
steps: In full daylight, pick a site using the terrain criteria above: a bench partway up a slope, not a valley bottom or exposed ridge, checked overhead for dead branches, oriented so the opening faces away from the prevailing wind.
Find or cut a ridgepole a couple of feet longer than your own height, and prop one end on a sturdy forked branch or low tree fork at roughly waist height, with the other end resting on the ground.
Lean ribbing sticks against both sides of the ridgepole at a steep angle, spaced a hand's width apart, to form the shelter's skeleton.
Add a lattice of smaller sticks and twigs crosswise over the ribbing — this is what keeps your insulating debris from sliding straight through the gaps.

Pile debris (dry leaves, pine needles, dry grass, small brush) over the entire structure to a genuine depth of at least 2–3 feet once compressed — this is the single most common failure point of a first attempt: debris that looks thick when loosely piled compresses down to a few insulating inches, so build it far thicker than feels necessary.
Stuff a thick layer of the same dry debris inside the shelter as a sleeping "nest" you'll actually lie on and pull around yourself, since insulation below and around you matters as much as the roof.

Run the test: on a mild-but-cool, dry evening (not your first attempt at genuinely dangerous cold), place one thermometer inside the shelter and a second control thermometer in the open air nearby at the same height, both shielded from direct wind, and compare readings after 30–60 minutes — a well-built shelter typically shows a meaningfully warmer reading, which is your proof the design is working rather than just a guess.

If conditions and preparation allow, sleep-test it for real on a mild night with a backup plan (a car or heated space nearby, someone aware of where you are, and a phone), and use the experience to find and patch drafts, gaps, or thin spots in the debris layer — every real shelter benefits from a second pass once you can feel where the cold is getting in.

Never treat an unverified shelter as your only line of defense in genuinely hazardous cold — build and test in safe, forgiving conditions first, well before you'd ever need to rely on the skill for real.

guides.title: Choosing a Safe Shelter Site
guides.summary: How to pick the ground you sleep on: the hazards that kill people in otherwise good shelters, the microclimate and drainage that decide whether you stay warm and dry, and a systematic survey you can run in fifteen minutes before you build anything.

sections.heading: Why the Ground You Choose Matters More Than the Shelter
sections.body:
Most people learning wilderness or emergency shelter spend their attention on construction — how to lay a debris hut, how to pitch a tarp, how to cut snow blocks. That is the wrong emphasis. A mediocre shelter on a well-chosen site will keep you alive. An excellent shelter on a bad site can kill you, and does, with some regularity. The site determines the hazards you are exposed to while you sleep, the rate at which your body loses heat, whether water runs through your bed at two in the morning, and whether anyone can find you.

The reason is that shelter is fundamentally about controlling four heat-loss pathways and one class of external threat. Heat leaves the body by conduction into whatever you are lying on, by convection into moving air, by radiation to the cold sky, and by evaporation from wet skin and wet clothing. A shelter addresses convection, radiation and rain. It does almost nothing about conduction, which is governed entirely by what is underneath you — and conduction into cold wet ground is typically the largest single loss for a person lying down, because ground conducts heat roughly twenty times faster than still air and, unlike air, does not warm up and stay warm around you. Choosing a site with dry, deep, dead organic material is worth more than an hour of roof-building.

The external threats are almost all site-determined and almost all act while you are asleep and least able to respond. Falling limbs, flash floods, rockfall, avalanche, rising tide, lightning, cold air pooling in a hollow, carbon monoxide accumulating in a sealed space, and animals following the trail you camped across are hazards of place, not of construction.

There is also a hard practical constraint: energy and daylight. In a genuine emergency you will typically have a few hours and a body that is already stressed, dehydrated and possibly injured. Building a shelter is heavy work and generates sweat, which then chills you. A well-chosen site cuts the work dramatically — a natural windbreak, a fallen tree to build against, a rock overhang, a dense stand of conifers with dry needles beneath — and the time saved is the difference between finishing before dark and working in the dark while cooling.

Finally, site choice is reversible in a way that construction is not. Spending fifteen minutes assessing three candidate locations before committing costs you very little. Discovering at midnight that you are in a drainage channel, after two hours of building, costs you the shelter, the daylight and possibly the night. Experienced parties treat the survey as a non-negotiable step in the same way a pilot treats a pre-flight check: it is boring, it is done every time, and its value is entirely in the rare occasion when it catches something.

sections.heading: The Priority Order: Hazards First, Comfort Last
sections.body:
Site selection goes wrong when people evaluate candidates in the order the features present themselves — a flat spot, a nice view, a stream close by — rather than in order of what can actually harm them. The disciplined approach is to run a fixed sequence and to treat the early stages as veto conditions: a site that fails a hazard check is eliminated outright, regardless of how good it looks otherwise.

The first pass is lethal hazards. These are the ones that can kill you outright while you sleep: water that can rise, ground that can move, objects that can fall, and exposure that can freeze you. Anything overhead that could come down, any channel that water could run through, any slope steep enough to slide, any ground below a high-water mark or tide line, and any position that makes you the tallest object during a thunderstorm is disqualifying. This pass is fast, it is done by looking up, looking down and looking uphill, and it should be finished within a few minutes at each candidate.

The second pass is thermal. Where does cold air go at night, where does wind come from, what is the ground made of, and what is the sky exposure? This determines whether the night is survivable and how much fuel or insulation you will need. It is not a comfort question in cold conditions; hypothermia is a lethal hazard operating on a slower timescale.

The third pass is water and resources. How far is drinkable water, how far is fuel and shelter material, and is the terrain between you and them navigable in the dark? A site 400 metres from water is usually better than one 10 metres from it, for reasons of flooding, insects, cold air and animal traffic, but a site two kilometres from water in a hot climate is a serious problem.

The fourth pass is rescue. Can you be seen from the air or from a likely search route, is there an open area nearby for signalling, and does staying put make sense at all?

Only then comes comfort: flatness, softness, view, privacy, morning sun.

A useful mnemonic used in several military and outdoor curricula is to check that a site is safe, secluded from hazard, has a source of water, has suitable materials, and is level enough to lie on — but the ordering is the substance, not the acronym. The commonest fatal error is inverting it: choosing the flat, soft, pretty spot by the river, which is flat and soft precisely because a river periodically floods it and deposits silt there. Ground that is unusually convenient is often convenient because a natural process maintains it, and identifying which process is the whole skill.

sections.heading: Reading the Ground for Water: Drainage and Flood
sections.body:
Water is the hazard most often underestimated, because the danger is invisible in dry weather and arrives at speed. The essential skill is reading terrain for where water goes when it rains, which is a matter of shape and evidence rather than guesswork.

Start with shape. Water flows to and along the lowest continuous line. Any depression, gully, dry wash, ditch, dip in a trail, or flat area at the base of a slope is a drainage path, whether or not there is water in it now. Alluvial fans — the gentle aprons of loose material where a steep channel meets a flat valley — are exactly where debris flows spread out, and they are seductive campsites: flat, well-drained, open. Canyon floors and slot canyons are the most dangerous of all, because they concentrate a large catchment into a narrow channel and offer nowhere to climb.

Then look for evidence, because past floods leave records. Look for a debris line of twigs, grass and litter caught against upstream sides of trees and rocks; that marks a previous high-water level, and you want to be well above it. Look for scour — bare soil, undercut banks, exposed roots, rocks with a clean upstream face. Look at vegetation: a band of young, uniform-aged trees or willows in a strip usually means periodic scouring, while old, large, undisturbed trees with deep litter beneath them suggest ground that has not been flooded in decades. Silt or sand deposits on flat ground, or fine sediment lodged in grass, are deposition from flooding. Smooth, rounded, sorted cobbles in a dry channel mean that channel carries water with force.

The critical point about flash flooding is that the rain need not fall on you. A thunderstorm 20 kilometres upstream in a catchment can send a surge down a dry wash under a clear sky, and in steep terrain that surge can arrive as a wall rather than a rise. Desert washes are notorious for this. If you can hear a river rising or see it turn brown and start carrying debris, move immediately and upward, not along the channel.

The margins to work with are modest but real. As little as 15 centimetres of moving water can knock an adult off their feet, and 60 centimetres will float most cars. In practical terms, camp at least a few metres in elevation above any watercourse — more in a narrow steep catchment — and never in the bottom of a gully, however sheltered it feels. If heavy rain begins, the correct response is to move before conditions make moving difficult, not to wait and assess.

Coastal and tidal sites need the same analysis with a predictable clock. The strandline of dried seaweed, shells and litter marks recent high water, but the highest spring tides — around new and full moon — can run a metre or more above an average high tide, and a storm surge higher still. Camp above the highest debris line you can find, not the nearest one, and check that your exit from a beach or cove is not cut off at high water.

sections.heading: Cold Air Drainage and the Thermal Belt
sections.body:
One of the most useful and least known facts in site selection is that cold air behaves like water. It is denser than warm air, so on a clear calm night it flows downhill, pools in hollows and fills valley bottoms. The result is that the coldest place in a landscape at dawn is very often the flat, sheltered, convenient valley floor, and the warmest is partway up the adjacent slope.

The mechanism is radiative cooling followed by gravity drainage. After sunset, ground with a clear view of the sky radiates infrared energy to space and cools rapidly; the air immediately above it cools by contact, becomes denser, and slides downslope. Over a few hours this produces a cold pool in any depression, capped by a temperature inversion in which air actually gets warmer with height for the first tens of metres. The band above the cold pool but below the exposed ridge is called the thermal belt, and it is where fruit growers plant orchards to avoid frost.

The magnitude is not trivial. Differences of 5 to 10 degrees Celsius between a valley floor and a slope 30 to 50 metres above it are common on clear still nights, and in enclosed basins with good radiative conditions the difference can exceed 15 degrees. Frost hollows and karst dolines regularly record the lowest temperatures in an entire region. If you are marginal on insulation, choosing the slope over the hollow can be the difference between an uncomfortable night and hypothermia.

The practical rule is to camp above the valley floor and below the crest — roughly a third to two-thirds of the way up a slope, on a bench or shoulder if one exists. You are then out of the cold pool and out of the ridge-top wind. Avoid closed depressions of any size, including small hollows a few metres across, which will hold their own miniature cold pool; if you must use one for wind shelter, expect it to be markedly colder and insulate accordingly.

Two qualifications matter. First, this effect requires clear skies and light winds; on an overcast, windy night, mixing destroys the inversion and the valley may be the warmer place because it is out of the wind. Second, cold air drainage can also carry other things: in some volcanic terrain, dense carbon dioxide accumulates in hollows and has killed campers and livestock, and in cave country, air draining from a cave mouth can be persistently cold and damp.

Vegetation gives the pattern away. A band of frost-sensitive species on a mid-slope with hardier species above and below, or a treeline that dips downward in a valley bottom, both indicate a cold pool that forms reliably.

sections.heading: Wind: Exposure, Shelter and the Lee-Side Trap
sections.body:
Wind is the second great thermal hazard, and it acts far faster than air temperature alone suggests. Moving air strips away the thin boundary layer of warmed air clinging to skin and clothing, so convective heat loss rises steeply with wind speed. In still air at 0 degrees Celsius an insulated person is comfortable; at 0 degrees with a 40 kilometre per hour wind, exposed flesh feels closer to minus 10 and freezes far faster. Wind also drives rain and spindrift through gaps, flattens fires, prevents you from hearing danger, and destroys shelters overnight.

The obvious response is to seek the lee — the downwind side of a ridge, boulder, bank, dense thicket or fallen log. This is correct in principle and has two traps.

The first trap is that the immediate lee of a sharp obstacle is not calm; it is a zone of turbulent recirculation, where air rolls back on itself and gusts arrive from unpredictable directions. Tucking directly behind a large boulder often gives worse conditions than sitting three or four obstacle-heights downwind, where the flow has begun to reattach. Dense vegetation is generally a better windbreak than a solid object precisely because it is porous: a permeable barrier of about 50 percent density reduces wind speed over a longer distance downwind, roughly ten to twenty times its own height, without generating a violent eddy immediately behind it.

The second trap is snow and debris accumulation. Anything that slows the wind causes it to drop what it is carrying, so the lee of an obstacle is exactly where drifts form. A shelter dug into a comfortable hollow behind a ridge can be buried by morning, and in some conditions the accumulating snow will collapse the roof or seal the entrance. On snow, look at existing drift shapes to read the prevailing wind, and site so that drifting builds up beside rather than over your entrance.

Prevailing wind direction is readable from the landscape. Flagged trees, with branches growing on only one side, indicate a persistent wind from the bare side. Krummholz — stunted, ground-hugging conifers — marks severely exposed ground. Sand and snow ripples, eroded soil on one side of tussocks, and lichen distribution all help.

Local diurnal winds add a complication: valleys typically exhale downslope at night as cold air drains, and inhale upslope during the day as the surface heats. Coastal sites reverse similarly, with an onshore sea breeze by day and a weaker offshore land breeze at night. So the shelter you site at four in the afternoon with the wind on your back may face into it by midnight. Orient the entrance perpendicular to or away from the expected night wind, not the afternoon one.

sections.heading: Look Up: Widowmakers, Trees and Lightning
sections.body:
The hazard people fail to check most reliably is the one directly above their heads. In forestry and firefighting the term for a dead or hanging limb is a widowmaker, and it earned the name. A branch of only 10 kilograms falling 15 metres arrives with enough energy to kill, it gives no warning, and it typically comes down in wind or overnight when temperature changes and moisture loosen it.

Before choosing any wooded site, stand on the spot and look straight up, then walk a slow circle scanning the canopy. You are looking for dead branches still attached, broken limbs lodged in the crown, dead trees standing among live ones, trees with a pronounced lean, trees with fungal brackets on the trunk or a hollow sound when struck, root plates lifting on one side, and evidence of recent fall on the ground beneath. A conservative rule is to place your shelter outside the drip line of any tree with visible dead wood, and outside a radius equal to at least the height of any standing dead tree.

Certain species and conditions deserve extra caution. Eucalypts are notorious for dropping large healthy limbs without warning, especially in hot still weather. Beech, poplar and willow shed readily. Burned stands are extremely dangerous for years after a fire, as fire-killed trees fall unpredictably; wildland firefighters avoid camping in them at all. Ice-loaded or heavily snow-laden branches will release without warning as they warm.

Trees are simultaneously the best available shelter material and a lightning hazard. Lightning strikes the tallest object in an area preferentially and can also injure through side flash, jumping from a struck tree to a nearby person, and through ground current spreading outward through the soil, which is what kills livestock sheltering under trees in groups. The practical guidance is to avoid ridgelines, summits, isolated tall trees, open water and open ground during a storm; if in forest, choose a stand of uniform shorter trees rather than the tallest, and keep several metres from any trunk. The commonly taught 30-30 rule is that if thunder follows a flash within 30 seconds, the storm is within about 10 kilometres and you should already be under cover, and you should wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before moving out.

In treeless country the equivalent overhead check is for cliffs, overhangs and cornices. Rock shelters and overhangs are attractive and often already contain a floor of fallen debris, which tells you what the roof does over time. Check for fresh spalls, loose blocks and dripping seams, and never shelter beneath a snow cornice on a ridge crest. A floor of angular fresh rock fragments beneath an overhang is a warning, not a convenience: it is the roof, arriving in instalments.

sections.heading: Slope Hazards: Avalanche, Rockfall and Landslide
sections.body:
Any site with ground above it inherits whatever that ground may do. Assessing this is a matter of identifying the path something would take if it let go, and standing outside it.

Snow avalanche is the best-quantified of these hazards. The overwhelming majority of slab avalanches release on slopes between about 30 and 45 degrees, with the peak frequency near 38 degrees; below roughly 25 degrees slabs rarely release, and above 50 degrees snow tends to shed continuously in small amounts rather than accumulating into slabs. But a safe camping slope is not enough, because avalanches run out onto flat ground below. The runout can extend a long way past the base of the slope — as a rough field approximation, a large path's debris may reach a point from which the line of sight back to the starting zone is depressed by only about 18 to 25 degrees. Camping at the foot of a steep gully, on the flat below an open bowl, or on a bench beneath a cornice puts you in a runout zone even though your own ground is flat. Terrain traps — gullies, creek beds, depressions, the uphill side of dense trees — are especially bad, because a modest slide that would be survivable on open ground buries deeply when funnelled.

Rockfall follows similar logic without the seasonal variability. A slope of loose angular fragments, a talus or scree cone, is by definition an active rockfall deposit; it exists because rock arrives regularly. Look at the size sorting: larger blocks roll further, so the biggest boulders sit at the outer edge of the cone, and that outer edge marks the reach. Camp outside it. Fresh, unweathered, lichen-free rock faces on fallen blocks indicate recent activity. Freeze-thaw cycles at dawn and dusk, and heavy rain, are the peak triggers.

Landslide and debris flow require saturated ground and are usually preceded by rain. Warning signs include cracks or scarps in the soil upslope, tilted or bowed trees, hummocky ground, seepage emerging at a slope base, and fresh bare scars. Steep slopes with shallow soil over bedrock, recently burned catchments, and undercut banks are the usual settings. After a wildfire, the loss of vegetation and the formation of a water-repellent soil layer can raise debris flow risk for several years, and canyon mouths below burned catchments become genuinely dangerous in the first heavy rains.

In earthquake country, add the possibility that a stable slope becomes unstable in seconds, which argues for keeping shelters away from the base of steep ground even where nothing is currently moving. Volcanic terrain adds lahars, which follow drainages for tens of kilometres and can arrive hours after an eruption with no local warning; on any volcano, valley floors are the hazard and low ridges between them are the refuge.

sections.heading: Water: Near Enough to Use, Far Enough to Be Safe
sections.body:
Water is the resource that most strongly attracts campsites and one of the better reasons to keep some distance. The right answer is almost always to camp a few hundred metres away and walk to it.

The reasons are cumulative. Flooding is the first, and it applies to small streams as much as large rivers; a modest creek in a steep catchment can rise a metre in twenty minutes. Cold air pools along watercourses, so the ground beside a stream is typically several degrees colder and considerably damper than ground fifty metres up the bank; damp air means condensation inside a shelter and wet insulation, which is the fastest way to lose the thermal value of everything you are carrying.

Insects are the second. Mosquitoes, midges and blackflies breed in still or slow water and disperse only limited distances, so moving away from the water, and onto slightly higher ground catching a breeze, substantially reduces exposure. In malarial or dengue regions this stops being an irritation and becomes a health decision.

The third reason is animal traffic. Every animal in the area comes to water, usually at dawn and dusk, along established trails. Camping across a game trail or beside a drinking spot puts you in the path of everything from deer to bears to hippopotamus, which kill more people in Africa than most predators. Identify game trails — narrow, compacted, often tunnelling through vegetation at animal height, with tracks and droppings — and site away from them.

The fourth is contamination and courtesy. Human waste, washing water and food scraps close to a watercourse pollute it for you and everyone downstream. The widely used Leave No Trace standard is to camp, wash and bury waste at least 60 metres, about 200 feet or seventy adult paces, from any water. In an emergency this remains sound hygiene, because contaminating your own supply is a real risk.

Against all this sits the cost of carrying water. In hot or arid conditions, a person may need 4 to 6 litres a day, weighing 4 to 6 kilograms, and a long haul over rough ground is significant work. The practical compromise is to camp within a few hundred metres, on the first substantially higher ground, with a clear route you could follow in the dark.

Finally, judge the water itself. Flowing water above human habitation and grazing is safer than standing water; water emerging from a spring is generally cleaner than surface flow. But assume all untreated water requires boiling or filtration regardless of appearance, because clarity says nothing about pathogens. A brisk rolling boil is sufficient at any altitude a person is likely to be at; the often-quoted requirement for several minutes is a safety margin rather than a biological necessity.

sections.heading: The Ground Itself: Insulation, Slope and Surface
sections.body:
What you lie on matters more than what you lie under, because conduction into the ground is usually the dominant heat loss for a sleeping person. Earth, rock and especially wet ground are effective heat sinks with essentially unlimited capacity: they will draw warmth out of you all night without ever warming to a comfortable temperature.

The remedy is trapped air, and the requirement is loft under compression. Dry leaf litter, conifer needles, dry grass, bracken, moss, cattail fluff, or spruce boughs laid in overlapping shingles all work. The critical point is that bedding compresses drastically under body weight: a pile that looks generous at 30 centimetres may squash to three or four, which is nearly useless. Aim for at least 20 centimetres of compressed thickness beneath your torso and hips, which usually means piling 45 to 60 centimetres loose. Anything you carry — a pack, a rope, spare clothing, a foam pad — goes under the torso, not under the legs, because the torso is where core heat is lost fastest.

Site selection largely determines whether this material exists at all. A mature conifer stand with deep needle duff, a hardwood forest floor in autumn, or dry grassland gives you bedding within arm's reach. Bare rock, gravel, wet meadow and sand give you almost none, and sand is particularly deceptive: it feels soft and conducts heat readily. Snow is a better base than wet ground because it can be compacted and insulates well once you have a barrier between you and it, but it demands more insulation beneath, not less.

Choose a gentle slope, not dead flat ground. A grade of roughly two to five degrees drains rainwater away instead of ponding under you, and you sleep with your head at the uphill end. Steeper than about seven or eight degrees and you slide downhill all night. Cross-slope sleeping is uncomfortable and causes you to roll.

Clear and inspect the actual footprint. Remove stones, sticks and roots, which will find your hip bones within an hour. Check for anthills and ant trails, termite mounds, buried wasp or ground-hornet nests — the entrance is a small hole with steady insect traffic — and thorny or irritant plants. Poison ivy, oak and sumac, stinging nettle and various nettle-family shrubs are worth learning to recognise regionally. In the Caribbean, the manchineel tree is dangerous to shelter under at all, as rain dripping off its leaves blisters skin.

Finally, test the ground for water retention: dig a few centimetres and feel it. Damp subsoil under a dry surface means the site will be wet by morning, and a site where you can smell wet peat or see rushes, sedges or sphagnum is holding a water table just below the surface whatever the top looks like.

sections.heading: Aspect, Sun and Seasonal Judgement
sections.body:
The direction a slope faces — its aspect — changes the amount of solar energy it receives by a factor that is easily two or three, and this shows up in temperature, snow persistence, ground dryness, vegetation and even the material available to build with.

In the northern hemisphere, south-facing slopes receive sun for most of the day at a steeper incidence angle and are warmer, drier and clear of snow earlier; north-facing slopes are colder, hold snow and moisture, and often carry denser conifer cover and deeper duff. The pattern reverses in the southern hemisphere. East-facing ground gets early morning sun, which matters enormously in cold conditions because it warms you and dries condensation at the moment you are coldest and least motivated. West-facing ground stays warm into the evening but is often exposed to prevailing weather in mid-latitudes.

Deciding what you want from aspect depends on the problem you are solving. In cold or wet conditions, prioritise morning sun and afternoon warmth: an east-to-south-facing bench, out of the cold pool, is close to ideal. Position the shelter opening toward the sunrise and toward any fire. In hot or desert conditions, invert everything: seek shade, prefer north-facing ground in the northern hemisphere, and site so that the shelter is shaded through the hottest hours, roughly 11:00 to 16:00. In genuine desert heat, the difference between full sun and shade can exceed 15 degrees Celsius in air temperature and far more in radiant load, and a shaded, ventilated, double-layered shade structure raised off the ground beats an enclosed shelter.

Sky exposure is a separate variable from sun. On a clear night, a site with a wide open view of the sky radiates heat efficiently and can drop several degrees below air temperature, which is why frost forms on car roofs and open lawns but not under trees. A partial canopy overhead acts as a radiation shield and measurably reduces overnight cooling. This is one of the few cases where a slightly less open site is thermally better.

Seasonal judgement means asking what the site will be in twelve hours and in three days, not what it is now. A dry gully in a dry season is fine until the rains; a snow bridge over a creek fails as it warms; a sun-warmed south slope in spring is exactly where wet-snow avalanches release in the afternoon; a tidal flat is dry ground twice a day. Look at the site and ask what changes, on what clock, and whether you would be able to leave when it does.

Vegetation reads aspect for you, and reading it saves a compass. In mid-latitudes, the shaded slope usually carries mosses, ferns, thicker lichen on tree trunks and a deeper, damper litter layer; the sunny slope carries drier grasses, more open canopy and shallower soil. Snow lingering in patches on one aspect long after another has cleared is the clearest single indicator of where the sun does and does not reach.

sections.heading: Wildlife, Insects and Living Hazards
sections.body:
Animals are less often a lethal threat than people expect and more often a serious nuisance that costs sleep, food and equipment. Site selection handles most of it.

The core principle is not to camp on infrastructure that animals already use. Avoid game trails, water access points, berry patches and fruiting trees in season, carcasses, and obvious feeding or wallowing areas. Look for tracks, scat, rubbed bark, claw marks, flattened vegetation, matted beds and heavily browsed plants. In bear country the standard practice is a triangle layout: sleep in one place, cook and eat at least 100 metres downwind, and store food and anything scented — toothpaste, sunscreen, rubbish, cooked clothing — a further 100 metres away and suspended or in a canister. Never store food in a shelter.

Insects are the more consistent problem. Mosquito activity peaks at dusk and dawn and falls sharply in wind above roughly 8 to 15 kilometres per hour, so a breezy knoll beats a sheltered hollow near still water. Blackflies favour running water and daylight. Ticks concentrate in long grass, bracken and leaf litter at the edges of paths and clearings, and questing ticks wait on vegetation at knee height, so a cleared, short-vegetation site with a bare margin around it substantially reduces contact. In regions with tick-borne disease, this is a real health decision, not a comfort one.

Ants deserve specific mention because they ruin sites quietly. Before committing, watch the ground for two minutes for trails, and look for small crater-shaped mounds and cleared runways. Fire ants, army ants and bull ants can make a site untenable in minutes. Termite mounds indicate an active colony that may extend under your ground.

Snakes and scorpions shelter where you would: under rocks, logs, in leaf litter, in crevices, and in anything that offers a warm cavity. Do not put your hands or feet where you cannot see, lift logs toward you so they shield you, shake out boots and clothing before wearing them, and avoid rock crevice systems for sleeping. Most bites happen to hands and feet during careless handling.

Plants complete the list. Learn the local irritants — poison ivy, oak and sumac in North America, giant hogweed whose sap causes phototoxic burns, stinging trees in Australian rainforest, manchineel in the Caribbean. Avoid clearing or burning unknown vegetation, because smoke from urushiol-bearing plants can cause severe airway irritation. Also avoid dense, dry, resinous scrub as a shelter setting if you intend to have a fire; eucalypt, pine, gorse, chaparral and dry grass carry fire fast and can trap you against terrain.

One further consideration applies in livestock country. Cattle, horses and sheep are curious, heavy and clumsy, and a herd moving through a camp at night will flatten a shelter and can injure someone inside it. Look for fresh dung, hoofprints, trampled ground, water troughs and gates, and camp away from the routes between grazing and water. Guard dogs protecting flocks in mountain regions are a genuine hazard and are best avoided by distance rather than confrontation.

sections.heading: Materials, Fuel and the Work Budget
sections.body:
A site is also a supply of the things you need to build and stay warm, and this is where a slightly worse-looking location can beat a better one. Building a shelter and gathering a night's firewood is several hours of work, and every hundred metres you must carry material multiplies that cost. Assess resources before committing, not after.

The thermal argument is blunt. A person in cold conditions burns roughly 8 to 12 megajoules a day at rest and considerably more working; you cannot afford to spend that energy walking for fuel. If you plan to maintain a fire through a cold night, you will need far more wood than intuition suggests — commonly an armful an hour, and for a long winter night a stack roughly the size of the shelter itself. Sites without that much dead standing wood within easy reach are not viable for a fire-warmed shelter, and a site that forces you to choose between fire and sleep has effectively chosen for you.

The material inventory below is what a natural shelter actually consumes. Take stock of it by walking a fifty-metre radius before you commit, not by hoping. Dead wood still standing off the ground is dramatically drier than anything lying on the forest floor, which wicks moisture continuously; in sustained rain, standing dead wood and the sheltered inner heartwood of a split log may be the only dry fuel available at all. Where you have a choice, prefer a site whose materials are uphill or level from the shelter rather than downhill, because dragging poles up a slope while tired is disproportionately expensive.
ingredients: Dead standing wood, still attached and off the ground: the driest fuel available even in wet weather, in thumb to wrist thickness for a working fire.
Dry tinder that stays dry in rain: birch bark, resinous pine knots and fatwood, the dead lower twigs of conifers, dry grass heads, cattail down, or shredded inner bark.
Bulk bedding: deep leaf litter, conifer needles, dry bracken, grass or moss, in sufficient quantity to give 20 centimetres compressed under your torso.
Roofing and cladding: slabs of bark, evergreen boughs, large leaves such as palm or banana, dead grass thatch, or an existing tarp or sheet if you carry one.
Framing: fallen poles and saplings two to four metres long, plus a natural ridge support such as a fallen trunk, forked tree, rock ledge or bank.
Cordage if lashing is needed: inner bark of willow, lime, elm or cedar, spruce roots, or split grass and vine.
Insulating ground cover on snow: spruce boughs laid in overlapping shingles, curved side up, at least two layers deep.

sections.heading: Being Found: Access, Visibility and Rescue
sections.body:
If you expect rescue, the shelter site is also a signalling site, and the two requirements pull in opposite directions. Shelter wants concealment from wind, canopy overhead, low ground, and small scale. Being found wants exposure, open sky, contrast and size. The resolution is usually to sleep in a sheltered spot and to prepare a signalling area nearby, within a minute's walk, that you keep ready.

Search aircraft and helicopters look down through a narrow effective cone and are scanning quickly. A person under tree canopy is essentially invisible. What is visible from the air is contrast and geometry: straight lines, right angles, and shapes that nature does not make. A clearing, a beach, a sandbar, a frozen lake, a ridge top or a burn scar all serve. Lay out ground-to-air symbols at least three metres per stroke, larger if you can, using anything that contrasts with the background — logs on snow, stamped tracks in snow, seaweed on sand, rocks on grass. The internationally recognised marks include a large V meaning assistance required and an X meaning medical assistance required. Three of anything — three fires in a triangle, three whistle blasts, three flashes — is the standard distress signal.

The single most effective daylight device is a signal mirror, which can be visible for tens of kilometres, followed by high-visibility fabric and smoke. Smoke should contrast with the background: green vegetation and damp material make white smoke against dark forest, while rubber, plastic or oil make black smoke against snow. At night, fire and torchlight carry well, and a headtorch flashed rhythmically is far better than a steady beam.

Access matters too. If you are with a vehicle or aircraft, stay with it: it is vastly more visible than you are and provides shelter and materials. Do not move a casualty from an obvious search location to a comfortable but hidden one without leaving clear, durable indication of the direction and distance moved, marked at the point rescuers will reach first.

Finally, weigh the decision to stay or move honestly. Staying put is correct when someone knows your route and expected return, when you have water and shelter, or when moving is dangerous or your party includes injured people. Moving is correct when nobody will miss you, when the site cannot sustain you, or when a known road, river or coastline lies within reliable reach. Whichever you choose, choose it deliberately and once; oscillating between the two wastes the daylight and energy that both strategies depend on.

Prepare the signal before you need it, because the aircraft will not circle while you gather wood. Build the signal fire fully, lay the green boughs or damp material beside it ready to throw on, and keep the mirror, whistle and torch on your body rather than in a pack. Search flights are often brief and may pass once; the difference between a fire that lights in ten seconds and one that takes five minutes is frequently the whole outcome.

sections.heading: A Systematic Site Survey You Can Run in Fifteen Minutes
sections.body:
The value of a checklist is that it works when you are tired, cold and frightened, which is exactly when judgement degrades and people commit to the first flat spot they find. Run the same sequence every time, out loud if you are with others, and give any party member the authority to veto on a hazard finding.

Time it deliberately. Allow roughly fifteen minutes for the survey and aim to have it finished with at least two hours of usable daylight remaining, because building, gathering bedding and collecting fuel will take longer than you expect and doing any of it in the dark roughly doubles the cost. If light is already short, accept a merely adequate site now rather than a good one later; a mediocre shelter finished before dark beats a good one abandoned half-built.

Assess at least two candidates if terrain allows. Comparison is far more reliable than absolute judgement, because it forces you to articulate why one is better and surfaces the factors you would otherwise skip.
steps: Stop and orient. Note the time, remaining daylight, current weather, wind direction and the forecast trend if you know it. Decide how long you have.

Stand on the candidate spot and look straight up, then turn a slow full circle scanning the canopy and any cliff above for dead limbs, leaning or dead trees, loose rock and cornices. Any finding is an immediate veto.
Look uphill and trace the path anything falling or sliding would take. Identify avalanche runouts, talus edges, gully mouths and alluvial fans. Step outside them.

Look downhill and along the contour for drainage. Find the low line water would follow, look for debris lines, scour, silt and uniform-aged vegetation, and establish how far above any watercourse or tide mark you are.
Judge the thermal position. Are you in a hollow or valley bottom where cold air will pool, or on a bench above it? Are you exposed on a crest? Aim for the middle third of a slope.
Check the wind. Identify the prevailing direction from flagged trees, drifts and ripples, find natural porous shelter, and plan the entrance to face away from the expected night wind.

Inspect the actual sleeping footprint on hands and knees. Clear stones and roots, check slope and drainage, dig a few centimetres to test for damp, and look for ants, nests, thorns and irritant plants.
Confirm resources within easy carrying distance: bedding material, dead standing fuel, framing poles, and water at a workable but safe distance.
Confirm the rescue picture: nearest open ground for signalling, sight lines, and whether the site is findable.
Commit, and mark the site clearly enough that you can find it again in the dark from your water and fuel routes.

sections.heading: Urban, Vehicle and Disaster Sheltering
sections.body:
The same reasoning applies in built environments, but the hazards change and the timescales compress. After an earthquake, storm, flood or conflict, the ordinary assumption that buildings are safe no longer holds.

Structural judgement comes first. Unreinforced masonry — brick or stone without steel reinforcement — is the most lethal common building type in earthquakes, and older buildings with heavy tile or slate roofs, parapets, chimneys and decorative cornices shed those elements onto the pavement below. Soft-storey buildings, with a large open ground floor such as a shopfront or parking area beneath heavier storeys, collapse in a characteristic pancake. Look for new cracks, particularly diagonal cracks in walls or X-shaped cracks in concrete columns, doors and windows out of square, floors visibly out of level, and exposed reinforcement. Any of these mean do not enter. Modern steel or reinforced concrete frames, low-rise timber-framed houses, and single-storey structures are generally safer.

Utilities are the second hazard. Smell for gas and do not create sparks or flames if you detect it. Assume downed power lines are live and stay at least ten metres away, further in wet conditions, because current spreads through wet ground. Avoid standing floodwater entirely: it hides open drains and debris, may be electrically live, and is typically contaminated with sewage and fuel.

Within a chosen building, the safe positions are lower floors but above flood level, interior rooms away from windows and exterior walls, and spaces without heavy objects overhead. Avoid basements in flood or where gas may accumulate. Glass curtain walls are a serious hazard in wind and after blast.

Vehicle sheltering is often the best available option and is systematically underrated. A car is windproof and waterproof, visible from the air, and contains useful materials, but it is a poor insulator and becomes as cold as the outside air within an hour. Insulate beneath yourself with floor mats, seat covers and clothing, block windows to reduce radiative loss, and clear snow from the exhaust before running the engine — carbon monoxide from a blocked tailpipe kills people in stranded vehicles every winter. Run the engine only intermittently, roughly ten minutes an hour, with a downwind window cracked.

The universal rule across all enclosed shelters, urban or wild, is that no fuel-burning device — charcoal, camping stove, generator, patio heater — may be used in an enclosed space. Carbon monoxide has no smell, produces confusion before collapse, and has killed whole families sheltering after storms. If you must cook, do it outdoors or in a space open to the sky on at least one full side, and never sleep in the same space as a burning appliance.

One social point is routinely omitted from technical advice: official shelters, however unappealing, generally offer water, sanitation, medical care and information that improvised sites cannot, and the correct default after a large disaster is to find out where they are rather than to shelter alone by preference.

sections.heading: When You Get It Wrong: Warning Signs and Moving
sections.body:
No survey catches everything, and a competent shelter user is defined partly by willingness to abandon a bad decision. The failure mode that kills is commitment: having spent two hours building, people talk themselves into staying on ground they would never have chosen fresh.

Certain signs mean move now, without further deliberation. Rising water, a change in the sound of a nearby stream, or water turning brown and carrying debris. A creaking or cracking sound overhead in wind. Whumpfing sounds or shooting cracks in a snowpack, which indicate a collapsing weak layer and are among the clearest avalanche warnings there are. Fresh rockfall arriving nearby. A sudden smell of gas, or a headache and nausea shared by more than one person in an enclosed space, which should be treated as carbon monoxide until proven otherwise: get everyone outside into fresh air immediately and do not go back in.

Other signs mean reassess but not necessarily flee. Condensation soaking your insulation, which usually means poor ventilation or a site too close to water. Waking cold in the small hours despite adequate cover, which usually means insufficient ground insulation rather than an inadequate roof. Persistent damp underneath. Wind that has swung and is now driving into the entrance. Insect pressure that prevents sleep.

Moving at night is genuinely dangerous, and the decision should weigh that honestly. If the hazard is acute — water, gas, structural, avalanche — move regardless, but move deliberately: gather everything, keep the group together, use a light, and go to a specific identified place rather than wandering. If the hazard is thermal or comfort-related, the usual right answer is to improve in place. Adding insulation beneath you, plugging gaps, building a reflector or moving the entrance are all faster than relocating.

There is a broader honesty worth stating. Much shelter advice, including some in wide circulation, is repeated without testing and some of it is wrong or dangerously optimistic. Debris huts genuinely work but require far more material than pictures suggest. Snow caves are warm but demand ventilation and a real risk of collapse or of being sealed in. A fire in front of an open lean-to warms you far less than people expect, because most of its radiant output goes elsewhere. Practise in benign conditions, at night, in the rain, before you need to rely on any of it — the gap between reading a technique and executing it while cold and tired is the largest single source of failure.

It is also worth accepting that most sites are compromises. Perfect ground with no hazard overhead, no drainage, ideal thermal position, abundant material, safe water and clear sight lines for rescue rarely exists, and waiting for it is itself a failure mode. The discipline is to be absolutely rigid on the lethal hazards, which are non-negotiable and usually easy to avoid by moving fifty metres, and to trade freely on everything else. A cold, lumpy, awkward night on safe ground is an inconvenience you will forget; the alternative is not.

guides.safetyNote: Site errors kill more people than shelter-building errors. The three that recur are camping in a drainage that floods at night, sleeping directly on cold ground without insulation underneath, and burning any fuel inside an enclosed shelter. Carbon monoxide is odourless and can be lethal within minutes in a snow cave or sealed tent. If you are ever unsure whether a site floods, move higher; the cost of being wrong is not symmetrical.

guides.title: Reading Overhead Hazards Before You Camp
guides.summary: How to look up and read the canopy, cliff or slope above a campsite before you commit to it: why falling wood and rock are lethal, the field indicators of a dangerous tree, and a repeatable site survey you can run in a few minutes.
guides.safetyNote: Overhead hazard assessment reduces risk but never eliminates it, and no tent or shelter offers meaningful protection from falling wood or rock. When in doubt, camp in the open, well away from any tree, cliff or slope. Never attempt to fell a suspect tree, dislodge a hanging limb, or climb to inspect one; both are jobs for trained people with the right equipment.

sections.heading: The Danger Nobody Looks At
sections.body: When people choose a campsite they look down and around. They look for flat ground, for drainage, for water, for shelter from wind, for a spot clear of ant nests and rocks. Almost nobody looks up, and looking up is the single highest-value thirty seconds in the whole process, because the overhead hazards are the ones that arrive while you are asleep, give no warning, and allow no reaction. Every other camp hazard offers you something. A bear approaching your food can be heard and deterred. Rising water can be watched. Hypothermia announces itself hours in advance through shivering and clumsiness. A failing tent can be repaired at three in the morning by someone who is cold and annoyed but entirely alive. A falling limb is different in kind. It travels the last ten metres in well under a second, it strikes without sound that precedes it, and the person it lands on was horizontal, unconscious, and inside a fabric structure that offers no protection whatsoever. The tent is not a factor in the outcome. Nylon stops nothing. This is why experienced foresters, arborists, wildland firefighters and mountain guides all share a habit that casual campers lack: they scan the canopy before they commit to a position, every single time, including for a lunch stop. In wildland firefighting the hazard is formalised. Snags, meaning standing dead trees, are among the leading causes of fatality and serious injury for United States wildland firefighters outside of burnovers and vehicle accidents, and crews are trained to identify, flag and avoid them as a matter of routine. The same physics applies to a family tent pitched in a pleasant grove. The hazards themselves fall into a small number of families, and once you know the families you can read almost any site quickly. There are dead or dying trees that will eventually come down whole. There are broken limbs lodged in a canopy waiting for the next gust. There are defects in apparently healthy trees that make them fail without warning. There is rock above you on slopes and under cliffs, moving on a cycle driven by freezing and thawing. There is snow and ice in the form of cornices, loaded branches and avalanche paths. And there are human artefacts, principally power lines and decaying structures. It is worth being clear that the risk is real but not enormous in absolute terms. Most people camp under trees for a lifetime without incident, which is precisely why the habit is so easily lost. The hazard is low-probability and maximum-consequence, and that combination is the one human intuition handles worst. You cannot learn it from experience, because the feedback from a bad decision arrives once and is final. None of this requires special equipment or qualifications to assess at a useful level. It requires knowing what the indicators look like, understanding roughly why trees and rock fail, and building the habit of deliberately raising your eyes and turning a full circle before you unpack. That habit is cheap, and the failure it prevents is not survivable.

sections.heading: Why a Modest Branch Is Lethal: The Arithmetic of Falling Objects
sections.body: People routinely underestimate overhead danger because they judge a branch by how heavy it feels in the hand. A dead limb you could lift with one arm seems harmless. The arithmetic says otherwise, and it is worth working through once because the numbers change how you look at a canopy permanently. An object falling freely gains speed according to the acceleration due to gravity, about 9.81 metres per second squared. After falling a height h its speed is the square root of twice that acceleration times the height. From 15 metres, a realistic height for the lower canopy of a mature conifer, that gives roughly 17 metres per second, which is about 62 kilometres per hour. From 25 metres it is 22 metres per second, near 80 kilometres per hour. Air resistance barely matters for a compact dense object over these distances, so these figures are close to reality rather than theoretical ceilings. Energy is what does damage, and energy is mass times gravity times height. A 5 kilogram limb, which is a piece of deadwood perhaps 8 centimetres thick and 2 metres long, falling 15 metres, arrives with about 735 joules. For scale, a 9 millimetre pistol round leaves the muzzle with roughly 500 joules. A 20 kilogram limb from 20 metres carries nearly 3,900 joules, comparable to a rifle round. A whole dead tree of 500 kilograms toppling is in a different category again, of the order of tens of thousands of joules, which is why nothing portable protects against it and why avoidance is the only strategy. What converts energy into injury is stopping distance. Force is roughly energy divided by the distance over which the object decelerates. That 735 joule limb striking a skull and stopping within about 5 centimetres of combined deformation delivers an average force near 15 kilonewtons. Experimental work on cadaver skulls puts the fracture threshold for blunt impact in the region of 4 to 6 kilonewtons, with wide variation by location and by individual. The limb exceeds it by a factor of three, and that is the small limb. Falling onto soft ground or a sleeping bag lengthens the stopping distance and helps somewhat, but not by the factor required. Shape matters too, in a way that works against you. A long straight limb falling butt-first concentrates its entire energy on a few square centimetres, behaving much like a dropped spear, and dead conifer branches routinely orient this way because the thicker end is heavier. A branch that arrives flat across a tent may cause bruising and a broken pole; the same branch arriving end-on goes through the fabric and through whatever is beneath it. Two practical conclusions follow. First, there is no useful threshold below which a piece of overhead deadwood is safe. Anything you would not want dropped on you from a first-floor window is lethal from a canopy. Second, height matters as much as mass, so the tall thin snag at the edge of the clearing deserves the same respect as the massive one directly overhead.

sections.heading: The Vocabulary: Snags, Widowmakers, Hangers, Leaners and Stubs
sections.body: Precise words make hazards easier to see, because naming a category trains the eye to pick it out. The terminology below is standard among foresters and arborists across the English-speaking world, with minor regional variation. A snag is a standing dead tree. It may be freshly killed with bark and fine branches intact, or an old weathered spar with nothing left but the trunk. Snags are ecologically extremely valuable, providing nest cavities for woodpeckers and owls and habitat for a large fraction of forest invertebrates, so the correct response is to camp away from them rather than to fell them. The important insight is that a snag's danger changes over its life. A recently dead tree still has structurally sound wood and roots and is relatively stable, though it sheds fine branches readily. As decay proceeds, first the small branches drop, then large limbs, then the top breaks out, and finally the roots rot enough that the whole stem topples. Depending on species and climate, the whole sequence takes anywhere from about five to fifty years. A widowmaker is any detached or partly detached piece of wood suspended overhead. The word is old logging slang and it is not hyperbole. The classic form is a broken limb that has fallen and been caught in the branches below, sometimes metres away from the tree it came from. A hanger is the specific case of a broken branch still hanging in the canopy, whether caught in another tree or still attached to its own trunk by a strip of bark or a splintered hinge. Hangers are the most common overhead hazard after storms, and they are the most treacherous because they are already broken, are held by nothing reliable, and can be released by a wind far weaker than the one that broke them. A leaner is a tree that has partially fallen and is resting against another. Leaners store elastic energy and can release suddenly, and they can also cause the supporting tree to fail. A leaner that has been stationary for years is not proof of safety; it is proof that the supporting tree has not yet given way. A stub is the remnant of a large branch that has broken off close to the trunk. Stubs matter because they indicate a history of limb failure on that tree, and because the wood behind a stub is almost always decaying, which weakens the trunk locally. Two further terms are worth carrying. A codominant stem is a tree that forks into two roughly equal trunks, a common structural weakness. Included bark is bark trapped inside such a fork, preventing the two stems from knitting together and creating a joint that can split under load.

sections.heading: How Trees Actually Fail: Decay, Wind Loading and Root Loss
sections.body: Trees are remarkably good structures, and understanding why they usually stand up makes the exceptions visible. A living tree is a tapered cantilever that adds material where stress is highest, a process arborists call adaptive growth. Because wood is laid down in response to load, healthy trees tend toward a uniform stress distribution across their surface. This is the origin of the reassuring observation that a tree which has stood through many storms in its current shape is probably adequate for similar storms, and it is also the origin of the dangerous exception: change the loading, and the adaptation no longer matches. A tree that has spent eighty years sheltered inside a dense stand grows a slender trunk and a small root plate, because it never had to resist wind. Fell the trees around it and it becomes a lone spar with a canopy suddenly exposed, and it will often come down in the first serious blow. This is why the edges of recent clearcuts, new clearings, and freshly widened tracks are unusually hazardous places to camp. Failure comes in three modes and each has different indicators. Trunk failure occurs when decay or a defect reduces the effective section so far that bending stress exceeds strength. Wood is a fibre composite and is far stronger in tension along the grain than in compression across it, so trunk failures often begin as a compression buckle on the leeward side. Branch failure occurs at attachments, usually where a branch is poorly joined, oversized relative to its parent stem, or decayed at the union. Root failure, also called windthrow, occurs when the whole plate of roots and soil rotates out of the ground, and it is governed as much by soil and water as by the tree: saturated ground, shallow soils over rock, and recent excavation all reduce anchorage dramatically. Decay is the common thread and it is caused overwhelmingly by fungi, which digest the structural polymers of wood. White rots break down lignin and cellulose and leave a pale, fibrous, spongy residue; brown rots consume the cellulose and leave a dark, crumbly, cubically cracked residue that has lost almost all its strength. Brown rot is the more alarming to find, because strength loss runs well ahead of visible volume loss. Critically, decay travels through a tree long before it becomes visible from outside, and the appearance of a fungal fruiting body, the mushroom or bracket, generally indicates that the decay is already extensive, since the fungus only fruits once it is well established. Wind load rises with roughly the square of wind speed, so a 90 kilometre per hour gust imposes about four times the force of a 45 kilometre per hour gust. That non-linearity explains why forests seem stable for years and then shed an enormous quantity of material in a single event.

sections.heading: Reading a Dead Tree: The Field Indicators of a Snag
sections.body: Identifying a dead tree sounds trivial and is not, particularly in winter when deciduous trees are bare, at night, or in dense stands where a dead stem is screened by living neighbours. The indicators below work in most temperate and boreal forests and take seconds to check. Start with the fine structure of the crown, because it is the most reliable single signal and is visible from a distance. A living broadleaf tree in leaf is obvious, but out of season look at the twigs: living twigs are flexible, have plump buds, and form a dense fine network against the sky. A dead crown has lost its twigs entirely, leaving a coarse, bare, angular silhouette with visible gaps. On conifers, dead trees retain rust-red needles for roughly one season and then drop them, so a red crown means recent death and a bare grey crown means several years. Red-crowned trees are structurally sound but shed fine debris; grey-crowned trees are the ones to take seriously. Next look at the bark. Living bark adheres tightly. As a tree dies the cambium beneath decomposes and the bark loosens, then falls in sheets or plates, exposing smooth pale sapwood. Bark shed accumulating in a ring at the base is a strong indicator, and it is often the first thing you notice on the ground. Extensive woodpecker excavation, particularly the large rectangular holes made by pileated woodpeckers in North America or black woodpeckers in Europe, means the bird found abundant insect larvae, which means the wood is already soft. Small round exit holes in dense patterns mean bark beetle activity. Then look at the top. A broken-out top, sometimes called a spike top, means the upper stem has already failed and the remaining stem is decayed at least to that height. Look for a jagged or hollow-looking break rather than a clean natural taper. Test the base if you can safely reach it. Sound wood struck with a stick or the back of an axe rings; decayed wood gives a dull thud and may dent. Wood you can push a finger into, or that crumbles when picked at, has lost essentially all its strength. Look also for a hollow at the base, for fungal brackets, for charring from an old fire scar, and for carpenter ants or termites, whose presence indicates existing softness rather than causing it. Finally read the ground. A litter of fallen branches, a spray of splintered wood, or a fan of debris on one side of a trunk tells you exactly what this tree has been doing and in which direction. The ground beneath a tree is the tree's own record of its behaviour, and it is the indicator that campers most often walk across without registering.

sections.heading: Defects in Apparently Healthy Trees
sections.body: The most dangerous trees are not always dead ones. A vigorous, fully leafed tree with a serious structural defect gives none of the obvious cues, and it carries the full weight of a live crown, which after rain or snow is enormous. Half a dozen defects are worth learning. Codominant stems are the commonest. Instead of one dominant trunk with subordinate branches, the tree forks into two or more stems of similar diameter. The fork itself is often fine when the two stems have grown together with a raised ridge of bark between them, indicating a proper union. It is dangerous when bark is trapped in the join, a condition called included bark, visible as a tight inward-turned seam rather than a raised ridge. Included bark means the stems are pressing against each other rather than knitted, and such unions split, frequently taking half the tree with them. Any fork with a crack below it is imminent. Fungal fruiting bodies on a living tree are a serious finding. Brackets on the trunk indicate internal decay; those at the base or on surface roots indicate root and butt rot, the more dangerous location because it undermines anchorage. Honey fungus, in the genus Armillaria, produces clumps of honey-coloured mushrooms at the base in autumn and black bootlace-like strands under the bark, and it kills root systems. Ganoderma species form hard shelf-like brackets low on the trunk and are strongly associated with root failure. Cavities and hollows are less predictive than most people assume, because a hollow tube retains most of the bending strength of a solid rod of the same diameter. The often-quoted arboricultural guide is that risk rises sharply once the sound wall thickness falls below about one-third of the stem radius, a rule associated with Claus Mattheck. It is a rough screen, not a calculation, and it performs poorly where the cavity has an open slot, since an open section loses torsional stiffness dramatically. There is also a category of tree that fails without any detectable defect at all, and honesty requires saying so. Sudden limb drop, sometimes called summer branch drop, is a documented phenomenon in which a large healthy horizontal limb detaches on a still, hot afternoon with no wind and no visible decay. It is best known in eucalyptus but is recorded in oak, beech, poplar and elm. The mechanism remains genuinely contested; proposed explanations involve internal moisture changes, heat and shrinkage stresses, and none is firmly established. The implication is that heavy horizontal limbs deserve respect regardless of apparent health, particularly in hot calm weather when campers are most inclined to lie under them. Other defects worth knowing include long vertical cracks that open and close as the tree moves in wind; heavy horizontal limbs extending far from the trunk with little taper; dense masses of thin upright shoots called epicormic growth, signalling earlier stress; and old storm stubs with decay showing. Ivy is not itself a structural threat, but a heavy load adds wind sail and conceals every defect described here, which is reason enough to avoid a smothered tree.

sections.heading: The Ground Tells You About the Top: Roots, Lean and Soil
sections.body: Whole-tree failure is a root and soil event more often than a trunk event, and the evidence is at your feet rather than in the canopy.
