This is convenient, because the base of a tree can be examined closely in poor light while the crown cannot. Begin with lean. A tree that has grown at an angle, leaning toward light at a forest edge or away from prevailing wind, is usually well adapted to that posture and will have laid down reaction wood to compensate. What matters is recent lean, and it has distinctive signatures. Look for a crescent of cracked or heaved soil on the side opposite the lean, where the root plate has begun to lift. Look for exposed roots on the tension side that were previously buried. Look for a gap opening between trunk and soil on the lean side. And look at the trunk's own history: a tree that grew straight and now leans shows a curved base with a straight upper stem, whereas one that has always leaned curves gradually toward vertical at the top as it reached for light. The first is a failing tree; the second is a normal one. Then assess anchorage. Root plates are surprisingly shallow, typically extending only 0.5 to 1 metre deep in most soils while spreading laterally well beyond the crown. Anything that has cut that plate compromises the tree, and the cut may be old and grassed over. Look for trenches, tracks, road cuts, building foundations, eroded stream banks and terraces on the uphill or upwind side. A tree standing on the lip of an eroding bank has lost its anchorage on the side it will fall toward. Trees rooted in thin soil over bedrock, common on ridges and in mountain terrain, have no deep anchorage at all and blow over in groups. Water is the modifier that turns a marginal tree into a falling one. Saturated soil loses much of its shear strength, so windthrow risk after prolonged rain, during a spring thaw, or in seasonally flooded ground is far higher than the same wind on dry ground. This is why storms that combine heavy rain with wind fell many more trees than dry gales of the same speed, and why a site that felt solid in summer may not be in March. Finally, read the neighbours. Several recently uprooted trees lying in the same direction is a record of a specific past wind event and a strong indication that the survivors on that patch are the marginal ones now newly exposed. Camping in a fresh windthrow gap is choosing the least stable ground in the forest, which is unfortunate because such gaps are flat, open, sunlit and superficially inviting. The same applies to the clearing created by a single recently fallen giant: the reason there is space for your tent is that the canopy failed there, and the trees now bordering that space have just lost their mutual shelter.

sections.heading: Hangers and the Aftermath of Storms
sections.body: The period following a windstorm, a heavy wet snowfall, or an ice storm is by a wide margin the most dangerous time to be in a forest, and it is exactly when people go out to see the damage. The reason is that a storm does not simply fell trees; it breaks a much larger number of branches and leaves them lodged in the canopy, held by friction, by a strip of bark, or by a splintered hinge of fibres. These hangers are released later, by a wind far weaker than the one that made them, by thawing, by a bird landing, or by nothing identifiable at all. The hazard persists far longer than most people expect. Fresh hangers come down over weeks, but a limb can remain lodged for a year or more, and it becomes more dangerous over time as the bark strip holding it rots. After a major ice storm the shedding continues through the following season. Forestry organisations routinely close trails and campgrounds for extended periods after such events, and the closures are not bureaucratic caution. Hangers are difficult to see, which is what makes them so effective at killing people. They sit within the visual clutter of the canopy, often at an angle that hides them from directly below, and in leaf they can be invisible. The single most useful technique is to change your viewing angle: walk twenty metres away, turn around, and look back at the crown above your proposed site against the sky, where a detached limb shows as an object crossing branches at the wrong angle. In dim conditions a headlamp or torch shone up into the canopy makes hangers stand out because the broken end is pale and reflects light differently from bark. Distinguish three things when you look. A hanger caught in another tree's branches is unpredictable and can travel sideways when it comes down, so the danger zone is wider than the branch is long. A partly attached branch still hinged to its parent will swing on release, describing an arc that may end well away from directly beneath. And a broken top or a large split at a fork is the worst case, because it can bring down a mass measured in hundreds of kilograms. After a significant storm the safest response is straightforward and should override the desire for a picturesque site. Camp in the open, on short vegetation, on a beach, in a meadow, or among young trees no taller than a few metres. Accept exposure to wind and rain in exchange for having nothing overhead. If the only shelter available is forest, choose the youngest, most uniform stand you can find, since young trees have small limbs and small limbs falling from low heights carry survivable energy. Never camp in an area of partial blowdown where some trees are down and others lean into their neighbours.

sections.heading: Weather as a Multiplier: Wind, Rain, Ice and Snow Load
sections.body: A site that is acceptable in still, dry conditions may be unacceptable the same night under different weather, and understanding the multipliers lets you adjust rather than guess. The forecast, if you have one, is therefore part of your site assessment, and if you do not have one the sky and the barometer are. Wind is the dominant driver and its effect is strongly non-linear, because the force on a tree rises with roughly the square of wind speed. In broad terms, gusts of 40 to 50 kilometres per hour begin dislodging loose deadwood and small hangers; 60 to 80 brings down substantial limbs and the weakest snags; beyond about 90 kilometres per hour whole healthy trees begin to fail, and above 120 the failures become widespread. What matters for camping is that the threshold for a marginal snag is low, well within the range of an ordinary unremarkable night. Gustiness matters more than mean speed, because a tree that has deflected under steady wind can be caught by a sudden increase before it recovers, and this is why squall lines and thunderstorm outflows fell more trees than their average wind speed suggests. Rain contributes in two ways. It saturates soil and reduces its shear strength, raising windthrow risk substantially, and it adds weight to foliage. Wet foliage on a large broadleaf crown can add hundreds of kilograms, and it increases the crown's effective wind area as well. The combination is what makes autumn storms in leaf so much more destructive than winter gales of identical speed on the same bare trees, and it is why prolonged rain preceding a wind event should raise your assessment of every tree on the site by a full grade rather than being treated as a separate inconvenience. Snow and ice are the most dramatic multipliers. Wet snow adheres to branches and accumulates at densities far above dry powder. A large limb can carry many times its own weight in accreted snow, and the load arrives gradually and silently over hours, typically overnight, which is why snow-load failures characteristically happen in the small hours. Freezing rain is worse still, coating every twig in a shell of clear ice; accumulations of 10 to 20 millimetres of radial ice are enough to devastate a mature forest, and major ice storms leave landscapes that look shelled. Two further effects deserve mention. Rapid warming after a snowfall releases loaded snow from conifer branches in heavy falling masses, sometimes called snow bombs, which are dangerous chiefly because they can collapse a tent and bury someone in it. And a rapid thaw after a hard freeze releases both rock and hangers that the ice had been holding in place. If wind rises sharply at night while you are pitched under trees, the correct decision is to get up and move to open ground, uncomfortable as that is.

sections.heading: The Site Survey: A Repeatable Procedure
sections.body: What follows is a survey that takes three to five minutes and should be run on every site before anything comes out of the pack, including for a lunch stop or a rest in bad weather. Doing it in a fixed order matters, because the failure mode is not ignorance but distraction: people who know all of this still pitch under a snag because they arrived tired at dusk and started with the tent. A fixed sequence survives tiredness in a way that good intentions do not, which is the same reason pilots use checklists for tasks they have performed thousands of times. Run it aloud with a companion if you have one, since saying a finding out loud makes it much harder to quietly discount.
steps: Stop at the edge of the candidate site and do not put anything down yet. Dropping the pack commits you psychologically to the spot and makes you rationalise away what you subsequently see.

Look at the ground first, but for evidence rather than comfort. Walk the area and note fallen branches, splintered wood, bark plates, fresh sawdust or frass, and any fan of debris on one side of a trunk. This litter is the site's own record of what falls there and how often.
Turn a slow full circle looking upward, taking at least twenty seconds. In poor light, sweep the canopy with a headlamp; broken pale wood and detached limbs catch the beam differently from bark.

Identify every tree whose height exceeds its distance from your intended sleeping position, since only those can reach you. Assess each one: living or dead, crown intact or broken, bark tight or shedding, forks sound or included, base solid or hollow, roots undisturbed, lean recent or established.

Walk twenty to thirty metres away and look back at the canopy above your site silhouetted against the sky. Hangers and dead limbs that are invisible from directly beneath are usually obvious from this angle.

Check the ground beneath specifically where your head will lie, which is the part of the tent that matters. Move the tent a few metres rather than accepting a marginal limb overhead; a few metres is often enough.

Consider tonight's weather rather than this moment's. Ask whether the site would still be acceptable in a 70 kilometre per hour gust, in heavy rain on already-wet ground, or under 15 centimetres of wet snow.

Make the decision explicitly and out loud if you are with others, naming what you accepted and why. If any tree is dead, has a broken top, holds a hanger, leans recently, or shows a large bracket fungus, move.
Once pitched, re-check after any significant change: a storm passing through, a heavy snowfall, or a thaw. A site that was sound on arrival is not necessarily sound at three in the morning.

sections.heading: Setting the Safe Radius: Estimating Tree Height in the Field
sections.body: The governing rule is simple. A tree can only reach you if its height exceeds its distance from where you are lying, so the minimum separation from any suspect tree is one tree length, and the standard working margin used by fallers and forestry crews is one and a half tree lengths. The extra half accounts for bounce, for limbs thrown clear on impact, and for the fact that a falling stem may strike another tree and redirect. For a 30 metre conifer that means 45 metres, which is a long way and is frequently more space than a forested site offers. When it does not, the answer is not to shave the margin but to choose different ground. Estimating height is therefore a practical skill. The stick method is the most useful because it needs nothing but a straight stick and works alone. Hold a stick vertically at arm's length and slide your grip until the length of stick above your hand equals the distance from your hand to your eye, so that the visible stick subtends 45 degrees. Now walk toward or away from the tree, keeping the stick vertical and your arm straight, until the top of the stick lines up with the top of the tree and your hand lines up with its base. At that point you are standing at a distance equal to the tree's height, because you have formed an isosceles right triangle. Pace out the distance to the trunk and you have the height. On sloping ground the method degrades and should be used only as an approximation. The shadow method is simpler where the sun is out and the ground is level. Measure your own shadow and your own height, then measure the tree's shadow; the tree's height is its shadow length multiplied by the ratio of your height to your shadow length. If your shadow is 1.2 metres, you are 1.8 metres tall, and the tree's shadow is 20 metres, the tree is 20 times 1.8 divided by 1.2, which is 30 metres. A rougher method that suffices for camp decisions is comparison. Learn the typical mature height of the dominant species where you travel, since most stands are fairly uniform: mature lodgepole pine commonly reaches 20 to 30 metres, Douglas fir 40 to 70, European beech 30 to 40, and coast redwood far more. Pacing is the other half of the skill and is worth calibrating once. Count double paces over a measured 100 metres on level ground; most adults take between 60 and 70. Knowing your own figure converts an estimate into a measurement, and it costs nothing to carry. Where the numbers say you cannot achieve one and a half tree lengths, one full tree length away from a tree that is otherwise sound is a reasonable compromise; a snag, a leaner or a hanger deserves the full margin regardless of inconvenience.

sections.heading: Rock Above You: Cliffs, Overhangs and Talus
sections.body: In mountain, canyon and coastal terrain the overhead hazard is stone rather than wood, and it obeys different rules. Rock is heavier and harder than wood, so the energies involved are much larger; a fist-sized stone of 2 kilograms falling 40 metres arrives at about 28 metres per second carrying nearly 800 joules and is comfortably lethal. Helmets help against small debris and are worth wearing when moving beneath cliffs, but they are not a camping strategy. Rockfall is driven mainly by the freeze-thaw cycle. Water enters cracks, freezes, expands by about 9 per cent, and levers the rock apart, so the strongest release occurs when temperatures cross zero degrees Celsius, particularly on sunlit faces in spring and autumn and during the first hours of morning sun on a cold night's accumulation of ice. In glaciated alpine terrain the pattern reverses toward afternoon, when melting ice releases the debris it had cemented. Heavy rain is a strong trigger year-round, as is a rapid thaw, an earthquake, and animals or people above you. The single most useful field skill is reading the talus, the apron of broken rock beneath a cliff. That apron exists because material falls there, and its character tells you the rate. Lichen is the key. Lichens grow slowly, on the order of millimetres per decade for many crustose species, so a block richly covered in lichen has not moved for a long time, while bare, sharp-edged, unweathered rock of a different colour from its surroundings has moved recently. A slope of clean angular blocks with no lichen, no soil between them, and no established vegetation is an active rockfall chute, and you should not camp on it or beneath it. Conversely, mature trees growing undisturbed on a talus slope, with soil developed between the blocks, indicate decades of stability. Look upward too. Fresh light-coloured scars on the face show where rock recently detached. Perched blocks, loose-looking flakes, and overhangs with visible cracks behind them are all warnings. Gullies and couloirs are natural funnels and concentrate everything that falls from a wide catchment into a narrow line, which is why the flat, sheltered, tempting patch at the base of a gully is one of the worst campsites in mountain terrain. Overhangs and shallow caves deserve particular caution. They look like ideal shelter and are frequently used, but an overhang exists precisely because the rock beneath it eroded away, and the roof is under tension. Undercut coastal cliffs and river banks are actively being removed by water and collapse without notice. Camp out from the base of a cliff by at least the cliff's height where the ground allows it, and prefer a site on the outside of the talus apron rather than tucked against the wall.

sections.heading: Snow and Ice Overhead: Cornices, Avalanche Paths and Loaded Trees
sections.body: Winter and alpine camping adds a family of overhead hazards that are invisible to summer habits, and they are the ones most likely to bury rather than strike. Cornices are the wind-built overhanging drifts that form on the lee side of ridges. They are dangerous in two directions. Camping beneath one places you in the fall line of a mass that may weigh many tonnes and which frequently triggers an avalanche on the slope below when it releases. Camping above one risks walking onto it, since from the windward side a cornice looks like continuous ground, and cornices break back much further from the ridge crest than their visible lip suggests. The conventional margin is to stay back from a corniced ridge by at least twice the estimated depth of the cornice, and further where visibility is poor. Release is driven mainly by warming, so afternoons on sunny days and periods of rising temperature are the peak risk, along with the loading period during and just after a storm. Avalanche terrain must be assessed as an overhead hazard even when you are nowhere near a slope you intend to travel on. The relevant question when siting a tent is what is above and what is the runout: a slope of about 30 to 45 degrees anywhere above you is capable of producing a slab avalanche, and the debris travels well beyond the base of the slope onto ground that is itself flat and inviting. Terrain traps such as gullies, benches and the flats immediately below a slope are where debris piles deepest. Avalanche assessment is a substantial discipline in its own right, and anyone camping in snow-covered mountains should treat formal avalanche training as a prerequisite rather than a refinement. Loaded trees are the mundane and frequently underestimated hazard. Conifer branches accumulate large masses of wet snow which release suddenly during a thaw or when the tree is disturbed. A falling mass of dense snow can flatten a tent, break poles, soak everything inside and, in the worst case, bury and asphyxiate a sleeping occupant. Pitching under heavily loaded conifers is a common winter error made for good reasons: the ground beneath them is shallower in snow and sheltered from wind. The compromise is to pitch just outside the drip line of the branches rather than beneath the crown, which keeps most of the wind shelter while moving you out of the fall zone, and to knock accessible loaded branches clear with a pole before pitching where you can reach them safely. Tree wells are the related ground hazard, being the void of loose snow around a trunk beneath the sheltering branches, into which a person can fall head-first and become trapped. Finally, in spring, watch for icicles and ice masses on cliffs and structures, and for glide cracks on steep snow slopes, which indicate the whole snowpack is creeping downhill and can release as a slab.

sections.heading: Power Lines, Structures, and the Lightning Question
sections.body: Human-made overhead hazards are easy to overlook precisely because they are familiar, and two of them kill campers regularly. Overhead electrical conductors are the more insidious, because electricity does not require contact. High voltage can arc across an air gap, and the gap grows with voltage: a distribution line at 11 kilovolts needs only centimetres, while a transmission line at 400 kilovolts can flash over a metre or more, further in damp or dirty air. The practical rule used in most jurisdictions is a minimum approach distance of at least 3 metres for lines up to about 50 kilovolts, increasing substantially above that, and for camping purposes the sensible margin is far greater: do not pitch beneath any conductor at all. The specific dangers are carbon fibre and aluminium tent poles, which are excellent conductors and are raised vertically while you hold them; fishing rods; and the wet guy line, which conducts far better than a dry one. Sagging or fallen lines after a storm should be treated as live regardless of appearance, and the ground around a downed conductor carries a voltage gradient, so the correct movement away from one is a shuffle with feet together rather than normal walking. Decaying structures are the second family. Abandoned barns, bothies, mine headframes, derelict buildings and old shelters attract campers seeking a roof. Untreated timber roofs fail from the top down; corrugated metal sheeting rusts through at the fixings and comes off in the wind as a large flying blade; masonry parapets and chimneys are the first things to fall from an unmaintained building. Old mine workings add the risk of collapse and of accumulated toxic or oxygen-poor air. As a general rule a structure nobody is maintaining is more dangerous than open ground, and camping alongside the wall of a ruin is often worse than camping ten metres away from it. Lightning is the overhead hazard that behaves least like the others because it seeks height rather than falling. The practical guidance is well established. Avoid being the tallest object and avoid being next to the tallest object; a strike on a tree can pass to a person nearby through the ground or by a side flash. Do not shelter under an isolated tall tree, which is the classic fatal choice. In forest, prefer a stand of uniform shorter trees. Avoid ridges, summits, open water and open ground, and avoid metal structures, fences and wire. The 30-30 rule is a useful heuristic: if the interval between flash and thunder is under 30 seconds, the storm is within about 10 kilometres and you should already be sheltering; wait 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming. A tent offers no protection from lightning whatsoever, and its poles make matters marginally worse.

sections.heading: Regional Cases: Beetle Kill, Palms, Deserts and the Tropics
sections.body: General principles need local calibration, because the dominant overhead hazard differs sharply by region and by recent history. Insect-killed forest is the largest-scale example. Bark beetle outbreaks, particularly mountain pine beetle in western North America since around 2000, have killed conifers across tens of millions of hectares, producing landscapes of standing dead lodgepole and ponderosa pine. Such forests pass through a hazardous phase roughly five to fifteen years after death, when root systems have decayed but the stems still stand, and fall rates in that window are extremely high. Land management agencies have closed campgrounds and trails in affected areas for exactly this reason. Similar situations follow large wildfires, where fire-killed trees with burned-out root collars stand for years and fall unpredictably, often without wind. Fire-killed stands are among the most dangerous forests to camp in and remain so for a decade or more. Eucalyptus forest in Australia deserves its own note, since the genus is notorious both for sudden limb drop in calm hot weather and for shedding very large branches generally. Australian bushcraft convention treats camping under large eucalypts, particularly river red gums along watercourses, as something to be avoided, and the trees are known colloquially by names reflecting that reputation. The irony is that the shade and flat ground beside a river gum are exactly what a tired traveller wants. Palms present the coconut question, which is worth handling honestly because it is widely repeated and poorly sourced. The often-quoted figure of 150 deaths per year worldwide from falling coconuts has no solid basis; it appears to derive from loose extrapolation of a 1984 study by Peter Barss reporting a small number of coconut-related hospital admissions in Papua New Guinea. The real number is unknown and probably much lower. That said, the physics is not in doubt: a coconut of 1 to 2 kilograms falling 20 metres carries several hundred joules and has certainly caused serious injuries and deaths. Do not hang a hammock or pitch under a fruiting palm; look up and count the nuts. Desert and canyon country shifts the hazard toward rock and toward the undercut alcove, which offers shade at the price of a roof under tension. In the humid tropics, rapid decay means dead branches are abundant and dead wood is often concealed by dense epiphytes, mosses and vines, so the visual indicators described for temperate forest are much less reliable and the safe default is more conservative. Managed campgrounds are a special case worth naming, because they invert the usual assumption. Many are deliberately sited in mature shade trees, and the mature specimens in them are frequently stressed by soil compaction from decades of foot traffic and vehicles, which damages roots and accelerates decline. A well-run site will have a tree inspection programme and will have removed or pruned the worst offenders, but you cannot see whether that is true, and budget cuts show up in the canopy years later. The presence of other tents is not evidence. Run the same survey you would in wild country.

sections.heading: When You Cannot Move: Failure Modes and Damage Limitation
sections.body: Assessment sometimes fails, and sometimes the assessment is correct but there is nowhere better to go. Both situations deserve honest treatment, because pretending otherwise leads people to make the worst available choice while feeling they have followed the rules. Start with the failure modes, since knowing them is most of the defence. The commonest by far is the late arrival. Camp is made in the dark by people who are tired, cold and past the point of caring, and the survey is skipped entirely. The countermeasure is to decide your camping time in advance and stop while it is still light enough to see a canopy, accepting a worse site earlier rather than a blind site later. The second is the established site fallacy: a fire ring, flattened ground and other people's rubbish feel like evidence of safety, when they only prove that people camped there and left. Popular sites in unmanaged areas often sit under mature trees precisely because that is where the shade is. The third is comfort-driven selection, where shelter from wind, flat ground and shade all correlate with dense mature canopy, so every comfort instinct pulls you toward the hazard. The fourth is habituation, the quiet accumulation of uneventful nights that erodes the habit until it disappears. When there is genuinely no better ground, work the margins you have. Move the tent so that your head is not under the worst limb, since a strike to the legs is survivable and a strike to the head is not. Sleep on the side of the trunk opposite the lean and away from the heaviest overhanging branch. Prefer to be beyond the drip line of a crown rather than under its centre. Choose the smaller, younger, more uniform trees over the grand old one. Orient the tent so that its length runs radially away from the trunk rather than tangentially across the fall line, which reduces the target it presents. And take the weather seriously: if wind is forecast to rise, being wet in the open is a far better outcome than being sheltered under a snag. If something does fall and someone is struck, treat it as a high-energy blunt injury with likely head, spine and chest involvement. Do not move the casualty unless there is continuing danger overhead, in which case moving them is the priority; protect the airway, control bleeding, keep them warm, and get help. Suspect spinal injury in any strike to the head or trunk. Assume more debris may follow, particularly if a limb has just torn free and left others disturbed, and move everyone clear before beginning any prolonged care. The habit this whole subject asks for is small. Look up, turn a circle, and take twenty seconds before you drop the pack. It costs nothing, it works in every terrain, and it is the only defence that exists against a hazard which gives no warning and allows no response.

guides.title: Cold Air Drainage and Valley Bottoms
guides.summary: Why the bottom of a valley is reliably the coldest, dampest and most polluted ground in the landscape, how cold air is manufactured by radiative cooling and then flows downhill under gravity, and how to read terrain, choose a campsite, protect a crop and stay out of the trouble that pooled cold air causes.

sections.heading: The Coldest Ground for Miles Is Usually the Flattest
sections.body:
Anyone who has slept out in hill country has met this the hard way. You pitch on a level, sheltered patch of grass beside a stream, tucked out of the wind, on what looks like the best ground for a kilometre. You wake at three in the morning with your breath fogging inside the tent, frost furring the outside of the flysheet and the inside of the fabric wet with condensation. After sunrise you walk twenty or thirty metres up the hillside to relieve yourself and notice, quite distinctly, that the air up there is milder. Nothing about that is a fluke or a trick of a tired body. Under the right conditions the floor of a valley will sit five, ten, occasionally twenty-five degrees Celsius colder than a slope only a short walk above it, and the effect is regular enough that fruit growers, vineyard owners, glider pilots, air-quality regulators, mountain rescue teams and military planners all build it into their working assumptions.

The counterintuitive part is the flatness. Human beings instinctively read a sheltered hollow as a safe, warm place, because shelter from wind genuinely is warming during the day and in a storm. At night, in calm clear weather, that instinct inverts. Shelter from the wind is precisely what allows cold air to sit still and get colder, and a hollow is a container. The same basin that shields you from a breeze is a bowl into which every cubic metre of chilled air produced on the surrounding slopes will drain and accumulate for the whole length of the night.

Two separate processes are at work and it helps to keep them apart from the start. The first is manufacture: the ground radiates heat to space, chills the shallow layer of air touching it, and makes cold air. That happens everywhere, on flat plains as much as on mountains. The second is transport and storage: because chilled air is denser than the air around it, gravity pulls it downslope, and it collects wherever the terrain stops it going any further. Manufacture without transport gives you a uniformly cold night. Manufacture plus transport plus a container gives you a frost hollow, and frost hollows produce some of the most extreme low temperatures ever recorded outside the polar regions.

The practical consequences are wide. Ground frost kills a vine or a citrus crop on the valley floor while the same variety twenty metres higher on the slope comes through untouched, which is why terraced vineyards and hillside orchards are not merely picturesque but economically rational. Fog forms in the pooled layer and not above it. Woodsmoke, vehicle exhaust and industrial emissions released into a cold pool cannot escape upward and accumulate to concentrations that have historically killed people in their hundreds. Sound carries oddly. Radio and light refract. And a person sleeping without adequate insulation in the wrong spot loses body heat substantially faster than one who walked another five minutes and pitched on a shoulder of the hill.

sections.heading: Radiative Cooling: How the Ground Manufactures Cold Air
sections.body:
Everything that has a temperature radiates electromagnetic energy. The rate is governed by the Stefan-Boltzmann law, which says that the power radiated per unit area is the emissivity multiplied by the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth, multiplied by the absolute temperature raised to the fourth power. For ordinary natural surfaces such as soil, grass, rock and water the emissivity is high, typically between 0.90 and 0.98, so they are close to perfect radiators. A grass surface at 5 degrees Celsius, which is 278 kelvin, radiates roughly 330 watts per square metre upward. That is a large flux, comparable to weak sunshine.

During the day incoming solar radiation swamps this loss and the surface warms. After sunset the solar input is zero and the loss continues without interruption. The surface does receive some radiation back from the atmosphere above it, chiefly from water vapour, carbon dioxide and cloud droplets, and the balance between the upward and downward streams is what determines how fast the ground actually cools. This is where the sky matters enormously. Water vapour and carbon dioxide are strong absorbers and emitters across most of the infrared spectrum but they are relatively transparent between roughly 8 and 13 micrometres, a band known as the atmospheric window. Through that window the ground radiates more or less directly to the cosmic background, an effective sink at about 3 kelvin. A dry, cloudless, low-humidity night leaves the window wide open and the net loss from the surface can run at 70 to 100 watts per square metre all night.

Cloud closes the window. A low, thick overcast has a base temperature not far below the surface temperature and emits back almost as much as it receives, which is why an overcast night feels mild and why frost forecasts collapse the moment cloud arrives. High cirrus is thin and cold and only partially closes it. Humid air does much the same job as thin cloud: a dew point close to the air temperature means abundant water vapour, strong back-radiation, and a slow cooling rate. This is the physical reason the classic frost night is described as clear, calm and dry.

The air itself is nearly transparent to this exchange and barely cools by radiation at all. What cools the air is contact. The ground chills first and fastest, and the thin film of air touching it loses heat to the surface by conduction, then that chilled film mixes upward a little way by weak turbulence. The result is an extremely shallow but intense layer of cold: on a still night the temperature at the grass tips can be 4 to 6 degrees below the temperature measured in a standard instrument screen at 1.25 metres. This is exactly why meteorological services issue separate air frost and ground frost forecasts, and why a gardener can lose seedlings on a night when the official minimum never went below 3 degrees.

sections.heading: Why Cold Air Sinks: Density, Buoyancy and Gravity
sections.body:
Air behaves closely enough to an ideal gas that its density follows the relation density equals pressure divided by the product of the specific gas constant and absolute temperature. For dry air the gas constant is 287 joules per kilogram per kelvin. At sea-level pressure of 101,325 pascals and 15 degrees Celsius, which is 288 kelvin, the density comes out at about 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre. Hold the pressure fixed, which is a good approximation across the few tens of metres of a hillside, and density varies inversely with absolute temperature. Cooling a parcel from 288 kelvin to 283 kelvin, a drop of five degrees, raises its density by a factor of 288 divided by 283, which is about 1.8 per cent, taking it to roughly 1.247 kilograms per cubic metre.

Under two per cent does not sound like much, and in absolute terms it is not. But buoyancy does not care about the absolute density, only the difference. A cubic metre of that chilled air weighs about 22 grams more than the cubic metre of ambient air it displaces, so it experiences a net downward force of roughly 0.22 newtons. Spread across a whole hillside and sustained for hours, that small persistent force is entirely sufficient to drive a steady, organised flow. The relevant physical measure is the reduced gravity, sometimes written g-prime, equal to the acceleration due to gravity multiplied by the fractional density difference. For a five-degree deficit that is 9.81 times 0.018, about 0.18 metres per second squared. Acting down a slope of 10 degrees, the component along the surface is 0.18 times the sine of 10 degrees, roughly 0.031 metres per second squared, which in the absence of friction would accelerate the layer to 2.5 metres per second in eighty seconds.

Friction and mixing prevent runaway acceleration, so real drainage flows settle at a modest and fairly predictable speed. Over gentle grassy slopes the layer typically moves at 0.5 to 2 metres per second and is anything from one to twenty metres deep. Over steeper, longer mountain slopes speeds of 3 to 6 metres per second are ordinary. In the extreme case of the Antarctic ice sheet, where a continent-sized chilled surface feeds a continuous slope to the coast, the flow becomes a genuinely violent wind. At Cape Denison in Adelie Land, where Douglas Mawson's 1911 to 1914 expedition wintered and where he later coined the phrase home of the blizzard, the annual mean wind speed is around 19 metres per second and gusts have exceeded 90 metres per second. The physics is identical to the whisper of chilled air sliding off a Yorkshire field at midnight; only the scale differs.

Two further points matter. Water vapour is lighter than dry air, so humid air is slightly less dense at the same temperature, but the effect is small compared with a several-degree temperature deficit and rarely reverses the sign. And because the driving force depends on the temperature difference, drainage weakens as the pool it is feeding gets colder. A basin approaches an equilibrium rather than chilling without limit.

sections.heading: Katabatic Flow: The Mechanics of Air Running Downhill
sections.body:
The organised movement of chilled air down a slope is called katabatic flow, from the Greek katabatikos, going downhill; its daytime counterpart, warm air climbing a sunlit slope, is anabatic. The classic idealised description was set out by Ludwig Prandtl in 1942 and it still explains the observed structure remarkably well. Picture a uniform slope cooling at its surface. A shallow layer of chilled air forms and begins sliding downward. Its speed is limited by friction against the ground below and by turbulent exchange with the warmer, stationary air above. The result is a distinctive velocity profile: zero at the ground, rising to a maximum at a jet height typically only one to five metres above the surface, then falling back to zero at the top of the layer. Above that the air is undisturbed. A person standing on a slope on a still clear night often feels a cool draught around the ankles and calves while the air at head height is calm, and that is the katabatic jet passing beneath the knees.

The flow is fed continuously along its length. Every square metre of slope it passes over adds more chilled air, so the layer thickens downhill, much as a stream gathers water. By the time drainage from many side slopes has converged on the axis of a valley it is no longer a thin skin but a coherent down-valley wind, commonly 20 to 200 metres deep and moving at 2 to 6 metres per second. Mountain meteorologists distinguish these scales deliberately: the slope flow is the tributary, the down-valley wind is the river. The down-valley wind usually starts an hour or two after the slope flows, and in long alpine valleys it persists well after sunrise.

Katabatic flow is not smooth. Because a dense fluid running under a lighter one is the same configuration as water running under air, it develops the same instabilities: surges, pulsations with periods of several minutes, internal waves on the interface, and hydraulic jumps where the flow decelerates abruptly and thickens. Observers in valleys frequently report the temperature dropping two or three degrees in a minute and then recovering, which is a surge arriving. Cold air can also behave like water in a channel in a much more literal sense. It ponds behind obstructions, spills over low points in a ridge in concentrated streams, accelerates through gaps, and can be dammed by something as slight as a hedge, a railway embankment, a stone wall or a belt of conifers.

It is worth separating katabatic drainage from the violent downslope winds that share some of its geometry. The bora of the Adriatic, the mistral of the Rhone valley and the various foehn and chinook winds are driven principally by large-scale pressure gradients and by mountain-wave dynamics, not by local radiative chilling, and they can be warm on arrival because of adiabatic compression during descent. Genuine katabatic drainage is a local, nocturnal, gravity-driven phenomenon that dies within an hour or two of sunrise when the slopes begin to warm and the flow reverses into anabatic upslope wind.

sections.heading: The Thermal Belt: The Warm Band on the Hillside
sections.body:
If the valley floor is cold and the free air well above the valley is also cold, there must be a band in between that is warmer than either. There is, and it has a name. Appalachian orchardists in the nineteenth century called it the thermal belt, and the term has stuck in agricultural meteorology. On a clear calm night the warmest air in the whole cross-section of a valley sits on the slope somewhere between about 30 and 150 metres above the valley floor, often as a fairly narrow band. Measurements in the Blue Ridge, in Alpine valleys and in the vine-growing regions of central Europe repeatedly find the thermal belt running 4 to 10 degrees warmer than the valley bottom at the same hour.

The mechanism is straightforward once drainage is understood. Air on the mid-slope is chilled by the ground beneath it just as everywhere else, but it does not stay there; gravity keeps pulling it away downhill and replacing it with air drawn down from above. That replacement air comes from the free atmosphere, which has been cooling only slowly because it is not in contact with a radiating surface. The mid-slope is therefore constantly being flushed with relatively warm air, and it never gets the chance to build up the deep, stagnant, progressively chilling reservoir that forms on the floor. The valley bottom, by contrast, has nowhere to drain to and accumulates everything the slopes shed. Higher up, above the top of the inversion, temperature resumes its normal decline with height at something near the environmental lapse rate of 6.5 degrees per kilometre, so the summit is cold again for ordinary reasons.

The practical exploitation of the thermal belt is centuries old and largely predates any understanding of why it works. Vineyards across the Mosel, the Rhine, the Douro and Burgundy sit on slopes rather than floors. Citrus in California and Florida is planted on rises. Tea in the hill country of Sri Lanka and coffee in the Colombian cordillera occupy mid-slope terraces. In the English apple counties the old growers had a rule of thumb that the safest ground was above the highest point that the morning mist reached, which is a workable visual proxy for the top of the cold pool. Frost damage statistics support the practice. In a well-developed inversion the difference between the floor and the belt is routinely the difference between minus 3 and plus 3 degrees, which is the difference between a destroyed blossom and a full crop.

The belt is not fixed in height. It rises as the cold pool deepens through the night, and its position depends on valley width, slope angle and how much cold air the catchment can generate. In a narrow steep valley it may be only 20 metres above the stream; in a wide basin the pool can be 300 metres deep and the belt correspondingly high. Anyone planting a frost-sensitive crop, or simply choosing where to sleep, is better served by observing where frost and mist actually stop on a few clear mornings than by trusting any single published number.

sections.heading: Temperature Inversions and How Deep They Get
sections.body:
In the free atmosphere temperature normally falls with height. The global average rate, the environmental lapse rate, is about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre, and a parcel of dry air lifted without exchanging heat cools at the dry adiabatic lapse rate of 9.8 degrees per kilometre. An inversion is any layer in which that pattern is reversed and temperature increases with height. The nocturnal surface inversion produced by radiative cooling and drainage is the commonest kind on the planet, forming on most clear nights over most land surfaces.

Inversions are extraordinarily stable, and this is the single most consequential fact about them. In a normal atmosphere a parcel nudged upward finds itself warmer and less dense than its new surroundings and keeps rising, which produces convection and mixing. In an inversion, a parcel nudged upward cools adiabatically while the surroundings get warmer with height, so the parcel is immediately colder and denser than its environment and sinks straight back. Vertical motion is suppressed. Turbulence is damped. The layer becomes a lid, and anything released beneath it stays beneath it. Meteorologists quantify the stiffness of that lid with the Brunt-Vaisala frequency, the natural oscillation rate of a displaced parcel; in a strong nocturnal inversion the corresponding period is under a minute, meaning displaced air springs back very smartly indeed.

Depths vary enormously with terrain and season. Over open flat farmland on a summer night the inversion may be only 30 to 100 metres deep with a total strength of 3 to 6 degrees. In a moderate mountain valley in winter it is commonly 100 to 400 metres deep with strengths of 8 to 15 degrees. In large enclosed basins under a winter anticyclone the pool can be several hundred metres deep, 15 to 25 degrees strong, and persist for days or weeks because the low winter sun never delivers enough energy to erode it. The Salt Lake Valley in Utah is a much studied case, where persistent cold-air pools trap particulate pollution for a week or more at a stretch. Alpine basins such as the Inn Valley behave similarly.

Destruction of an inversion normally happens one of three ways. Sunrise heats the ground, convection begins at the bottom, and a growing mixed layer eats upward through the inversion; on a summer morning this can be complete within ninety minutes, in a deep winter pool it may never finish. Wind arrives and mechanically stirs the layer; a sustained wind of about 3 to 5 metres per second measured above any vegetation canopy is usually enough to prevent a surface inversion forming at all, which is why frost warnings are cancelled when a breeze is forecast. Or cloud moves in and shuts down the radiative loss that was feeding the whole system. The reverse case is worth knowing too: a fresh snow cover has an emissivity near 0.99, is an excellent insulator against heat coming up from the soil, and reflects most of the next day's sunshine, so snow-covered valleys generate the deepest and most persistent cold pools of all.

sections.heading: Frost Hollows, Sinkholes and the Extremes of Cold Pooling
sections.body:
When drainage feeds a container with no outlet, the result is a frost hollow, and frost hollows produce numbers that look like misprints. The best studied are limestone sinkholes and closed karst basins, because they are small, steep-sided, and completely enclosed. The Gstettneralm doline in the Austrian Alps, a modest funnel about 150 metres across sitting at only 1,270 metres above sea level, recorded minus 52.6 degrees Celsius in 1932, a reading far below anything measured on far higher Alpine summits. Peter Sinks, a limestone basin in the Bear River Range of northern Utah at about 2,500 metres, recorded minus 56.3 degrees Celsius on 1 February 1985, which stands as one of the lowest temperatures ever measured in the contiguous United States. In both cases the surrounding ridges are only a few tens of metres higher than the floor.

The cooling rate in such a hollow is startling. Instrumented sinkholes routinely show the floor dropping 10 to 20 degrees within the first two hours after sunset, then continuing more slowly all night while air only 20 metres higher on the rim stays 15 or 20 degrees warmer. What makes them so effective is the combination of a large chilled catchment feeding a small volume, a rim that stops any lateral escape, and a shape that shelters the pool from the slightest wind so nothing mixes it. Snow cover, which insulates the floor from soil heat and reflects daylight, makes them colder still. Anywhere else the pool would drain away and be diluted; here it just deepens.

You do not need mountains. Britain's celebrated frost hollows are gentle and low-lying. Rickmansworth in Hertfordshire, studied intensively in the 1930s by the meteorologist E L Hawke, sits in a shallow chalk valley partly dammed by a railway embankment and recorded minima routinely 8 to 11 degrees below neighbouring stations, along with astonishing diurnal ranges of well over 25 degrees on clear summer days. Santon Downham in the Norfolk Breckland, on sandy soil in a broad shallow depression, has produced air frost in every month of the year. The common factors are a mild slope collecting from a wide area, a low obstruction closing the outlet, and a dry sandy or chalky soil with poor heat conductivity so little warmth comes up from below to offset the radiative loss.

Artificial dams matter as much as natural ones. Railway and road embankments, flood levees, solid boundary walls, dense shelterbelts of conifer, and even large buildings will pond cold air and create a frost pocket where none existed before. The converse is a standard remedy: cutting a gap in a wall, thinning the lower branches of a windbreak to leave a metre of clearance at ground level, or installing a culvert through an embankment lets the pool drain away and can raise the local minimum by several degrees. If you are trying to work out whether a piece of ground is a frost pocket, trace with your eye the path that water would take if you flooded the landscape, then ask what would stop it. Cold air will do very nearly the same thing.

sections.heading: Reading Terrain to Predict Where Cold Air Will Sit
sections.body:
Cold air behaves enough like water that the hydrological analogy is the single most useful mental tool available, provided its limits are respected. Imagine the terrain slowly filling with a heavy, invisible, slow-moving fluid poured evenly over every slope. It runs downhill, follows gullies, converges into valley axes, backs up behind obstructions, spills through gaps, and ponds in anything closed. Contours on a topographic map are therefore the primary evidence. Any place where contour lines close on themselves around a low point is a basin and will pool. Any place where two or more valleys meet is a confluence and will receive the drainage of both. Any narrowing downstream of a wide flat reach is a constriction that will back the pool up behind it.

The catchment area is what sets the magnitude. A hollow that gathers from two hectares of slope collects modestly; a basin at the foot of a fifteen-square-kilometre bowl collects an enormous volume and will produce a much deeper, colder pool. Slope angle and surface cover set the delivery rate: short-cropped grass, bare soil, rock and snow chill fast and shed quickly, while dense forest canopy intercepts the radiative loss at treetop height and delivers noticeably less cold air to the floor beneath it. Water bodies are the important exception. Because water has a huge heat capacity, about 4,180 joules per kilogram per kelvin, and mixes internally, a lake cools very slowly and can hold a valley several degrees warmer along its shore than a dry hollow a kilometre away. This is exactly why vineyards cluster around large lakes and rivers.

Where the analogy breaks down is worth knowing. Cold air is only about two per cent denser than its surroundings, not eight hundred times as with water and air, so the driving force is feeble and easily overcome. It does not have a sharp free surface; the top of a cold pool is a diffuse transition several metres thick that waves and sloshes. It mixes with what it flows under, so a long, fast, turbulent descent dilutes and warms it, which is why the coldest ground is often not the very lowest point in a large drainage but a small sheltered basin partway down. And it can be blown clean out of a basin by a modest wind, which water cannot.

For quick field assessment, a short list of high-risk signatures serves well. Look for flat ground beside a stream in a steep-sided valley, the inside of a broad valley bend, the upstream side of any embankment or causeway, small closed depressions and old quarry floors, clearings surrounded by forest, and the flat apron at the foot of a long open slope. Look for low-risk ground on convex shoulders and spurs, on mid-slope benches roughly a third to halfway up the valley side, on the leeward side of a slight rise, and close to a large body of standing water. A single clear-night observation of where dew, frost and mist actually stopped will confirm or overturn every one of these inferences in about a minute.

sections.heading: The Landscape Tells You: Vegetation, Frost Lines and Mist
sections.body:
Terrain that pools cold air every clear night leaves marks, and reading them is faster and more reliable than any calculation. Vegetation is the longest-running record because plants integrate decades of minima. In temperate uplands a well-developed frost hollow often shows an inverted treeline: broadleaf and frost-sensitive species retreat to the slopes, while the floor carries only tough grasses, sedges, rushes, dwarf shrubs or nothing much at all. The Alpine and Carpathian dolines display this dramatically, with a rim of spruce, a band of dwarf pine below it, and a floor that supports only alpine herbs more usually found several hundred metres higher. In Britain the same signal appears in Breckland hollows and in the New Forest, where the valley bottoms carry bog and grass and the gorse and oak begin abruptly a few metres up the slope.

On farmland the record is written in crop damage and in what the previous generation chose to plant. A line of apple or plum trees that stops at a definite contour, an old vineyard that occupies only the middle third of a slope, a field of frost-scorched potato haulms with a clean upper boundary, or a hedge line marking the edge of a persistently poor-yielding corner are all direct evidence of the top of the cold pool. Farmers in frost-prone country very often know the exact line and will tell you where it is if asked. Local place names carry the same information across centuries: elements meaning cold, frost, ice, mist or winter attached to a valley bottom are a strong hint, and so are names referring to fog or steam attached to a particular meadow.

The most immediate indicator is available on any clear morning. Radiation fog forms when the pooled air cools to its dew point, and because the pool has a reasonably well-defined top, the fog fills it like liquid in a bowl and has a startlingly flat upper surface. Standing above it at dawn you are looking directly at the shape of the cold pool, in three dimensions, for free. Note where the fog surface meets the hillside and you have located the top of the inversion and the bottom of the thermal belt. The same applies to the frost line: on a marginal night frost whitens the ground only up to a certain height and stops, sometimes with a boundary sharp enough to photograph.

Two smaller signs are worth carrying. Dew and frost appear first, and most heavily, where the pool is deepest, so the wettest tent on a campsite marks the low point even when the ground looks level. And sound behaves strangely across an inversion: because the speed of sound increases with temperature, sound rays leaving a source in the cold layer bend back down toward the ground instead of escaping upward, so distant traffic, running water or voices carry unnaturally far and clearly. An unusually loud, crisp soundscape at two in the morning is a reliable, if easily missed, sign that you are lying in a well-developed cold pool.

sections.heading: The Weather That Makes or Breaks a Cold Pool
sections.body:
Cold pooling is not an every-night event. It requires a specific and easily recognised set of conditions, and knowing them turns an abstract hazard into something you can forecast for yourself from a doorway an hour after sunset. Three ingredients are essential and a fourth is helpful.

Clear skies come first, because the whole system is powered by radiative loss through the atmospheric window. Total cloud cover below about two eighths permits near-maximum cooling. Between three and five eighths the cooling is roughly halved. Above six eighths of low or medium cloud the surface barely cools at all and the drainage never starts. High thin cirrus is intermediate and often catches people out: the stars are still visible but cooling runs at perhaps sixty per cent of the clear-sky rate. Calm air comes second. Wind is the enemy of stratification because it mixes the chilled surface layer with the warmer air above and destroys the density difference before gravity can organise it into a flow. A sustained wind of roughly 3 to 5 metres per second, about 11 to 18 kilometres per hour, measured above the vegetation, is generally enough to prevent a surface inversion from forming. Below about 1.5 metres per second the inversion forms readily. This threshold is not sharp and depends on surface roughness: a smooth mown field stratifies at a higher wind speed than a rough hedged landscape.

Dry air comes third, and works two ways. Low humidity means less back-radiation from water vapour, so the surface loses heat faster. It also means the dew point is low, so the air can cool a long way before condensation begins. Condensation is a brake: every kilogram of water vapour that condenses releases about 2.5 megajoules of latent heat directly into the air, and once fog or dew formation gets going the cooling rate falls sharply. This produces a recognisable pattern in which the temperature falls fast until it reaches the dew point, then almost levels off. A humid night with a dew point of 12 degrees will not produce frost regardless of how clear and calm it is, because the air cannot get below 12 degrees without a great deal of energy being released. Conversely, very dry continental air with a dew point of minus 8 permits a plunge to severe frost.

The helpful fourth ingredient is a long night. Cooling is cumulative, so the total drop depends on how many hours the process runs. This is why the most dangerous frost dates in temperate agriculture are in late autumn and early spring rather than midsummer, and why a clear calm night in December in a mid-latitude valley, with sixteen hours of darkness, produces a far deeper pool than an identical night in June with seven. The synoptic pattern that supplies all four at once is a slack anticyclone: high pressure overhead, subsiding air suppressing cloud, weak pressure gradients giving light winds, and in winter often a dry continental airmass. When the forecast shows a ridge of high pressure building overnight with light winds and clear skies, expect the valley floors to be brutal.

sections.heading: Choosing Where to Sleep: Practical Campsite Selection
sections.body:
For anyone sleeping outdoors this is where the physics becomes personal. The temperature difference between a badly chosen and a well chosen pitch, separated by perhaps eighty metres of walking and thirty metres of ascent, is commonly 5 to 8 degrees Celsius and occasionally more. That is easily the difference between a comfortable night in a given sleeping bag and a miserable, sleepless, shivering one, and in marginal conditions with inadequate gear it is a genuine safety margin. It also determines whether your equipment ends up soaked, because a pitch inside the cold pool will reach the dew point and coat everything, inside and out, with condensation that then freezes.

The target is the lower part of the thermal belt: high enough to be above the pooled air, low enough to still have shelter from any general wind and access to water. In practice that usually means a bench, shoulder, spur or terrace some 20 to 60 metres in height above the valley floor, ideally on a slight convexity so that drainage passes around rather than over you. Avoid the obvious traps: the flat grassy patch immediately beside the stream, small closed hollows, the upstream side of any embankment or wall, clearings ringed by trees, and the foot of a long open slope. If you must camp low, prefer ground with a clear downhill exit so the cold keeps moving through rather than stopping, and prefer the immediate shore of a large lake, which is often several degrees milder than a dry hollow at the same elevation.

There is a real trade-off and it should be stated honestly rather than glossed. Higher ground is more exposed to wind and lightning, often further from water, rockier, and in a storm the valley floor may genuinely be safer. The decision depends on the forecast. If the night is clear and calm, go up. If it is windy or wet or a front is coming through, cold pooling will not develop and shelter matters more. This is a judgement, not a rule: read the sky at dusk.

Where you cannot move, mitigation helps more than most people expect. Ground conduction is a larger heat loss than air temperature for a sleeper, so insulation beneath the body matters most; a closed-cell foam mat or an inflatable pad with an R-value of 4 or above transforms a cold pitch. Raising the sleeping position even half a metre, on a camp bed, a thick bed of dry vegetation or a slight mound, puts you above the most intense part of the surface layer where the sharpest gradient sits. Pitching under a tree canopy rather than in the open reduces the radiative loss from the tent itself by several degrees, since the canopy radiates back at something close to air temperature instead of the tent seeing cold sky. Keeping ventilation open to manage condensation seems perverse when cold but a wet sleeping bag loses most of its insulating value, and a damp bag in a cold pool is the mechanism by which mild discomfort becomes hypothermia.

sections.heading: Frost Protection in Farming and Horticulture
sections.body:
Agriculture has fought cold air drainage for as long as it has grown fruit, and the countermeasures fall into four families: site selection, drainage management, mixing, and direct heat or latent-heat protection. Site selection is by far the cheapest and most effective, which is why the advice to plant on the slope and never in the bottom is universal. A frost-sensitive perennial planted in a hollow will be damaged repeatedly for its entire life, and no amount of later intervention fully compensates.

Drainage management means removing the dams. Cutting a gap in a hedge or wall at the low point of a field, trimming the skirts of a shelterbelt to leave a clear metre at ground level, removing a redundant bank, or installing a culvert under a track can raise the minimum temperature in the field above it by 1 to 3 degrees, which in marginal seasons is decisive. It also means not creating new dams: a newly planted evergreen windbreak across the bottom of a sloping orchard is a classic self-inflicted disaster. Keeping the orchard floor short and firm rather than long and loose also helps, because a compacted, moist, bare soil conducts stored daytime heat upward far better than a fluffy layer of dry grass or freshly cultivated tilth, and can supply 1 to 2 degrees of protection overnight.

Mixing exploits the inversion directly. A wind machine, typically a large fan on a ten to eleven metre tower, drags warmer air from the top of the inversion down to crop level and can protect roughly four to five hectares. It only works where an inversion actually exists: growers judge this by comparing temperature at 1.5 metres with temperature at 10 metres, and a difference of at least about 1.5 to 2 degrees is normally needed for the machine to be worth running. On a windy advective freeze, where cold air is being imported wholesale by a synoptic wind rather than generated locally, there is no reservoir of warm air aloft and wind machines are useless.

Latent-heat protection is the most counterintuitive and the most powerful. Water releases about 334 kilojoules per kilogram as it freezes. Continuous overhead sprinkling therefore holds the wetted plant tissue at almost exactly 0 degrees as long as liquid water keeps arriving and freezing, even while the surrounding air falls to minus 5 or lower. The technique is genuinely effective but unforgiving: application must be continuous, typically 2.5 to 3.5 millimetres per hour and more in wind, must start before the temperature reaches freezing, and must not stop until the ice has melted off in the morning. Stopping early is worse than never starting, because evaporative cooling from the wet, ice-laden plant then drives tissue temperature well below air temperature. The load of accumulated ice can also break branches, and the water demand is heavy. Older methods such as orchard heaters, smudge pots and burning straw work by direct heating and by placing a smoke layer under the sky to intercept radiation; they are effective but expensive, labour-intensive and now often restricted on air-quality grounds.

sections.heading: Trapped Air: Fog, Smoke and the Valleys That Killed People
sections.body:
An inversion is a lid, and everything emitted beneath it stays beneath it. Because the layer resists vertical motion, pollutants that would normally disperse through several kilometres of atmosphere are confined to a few tens or hundreds of metres, and concentrations rise in rough proportion to how much the mixing depth has shrunk. A tenfold reduction in mixing depth produces roughly a tenfold increase in concentration for the same emission rate. Add several days of stagnation and the arithmetic becomes lethal, and historically it has.

In the Meuse Valley in Belgium in early December 1930, a dense fog settled into a narrow industrial valley about twenty kilometres long under a persistent inversion. Emissions from steelworks, zinc smelters, glassworks and coke ovens accumulated for five days. Roughly sixty people died and several hundred fell acutely ill, with sulphur dioxide and sulphuric acid aerosol implicated as the principal agents. In Donora, Pennsylvania, in October 1948, an inversion held emissions from a zinc smelter and steel mill over the town for five days; twenty people died, and about six thousand of a population of fourteen thousand became ill. The Great Smog of London in December 1952, the largest such episode on record, arose when a cold anticyclonic inversion trapped domestic coal smoke and sulphur dioxide over the city for four days. Contemporary estimates put the excess mortality at about four thousand; later analyses that include the following weeks suggest figures around twelve thousand. That single event drove the British Clean Air Act of 1956 and, indirectly, much of the modern regulatory apparatus for air quality worldwide.

Modern versions are less spectacular but far from gone. Mountain basins with winter cold pools, such as the Salt Lake Valley in Utah, Fairbanks in Alaska, Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia and many Alpine and Himalayan valley towns, regularly exceed particulate health guidelines for days on end during persistent inversions, driven by traffic, wood burning and domestic heating. The chemistry can be unpleasant in its own right, since the cold moist stagnant conditions favour formation of secondary particulate from ammonia and nitrogen oxides.

Radiation fog belongs to the same family. When the pooled air cools to its dew point, water condenses on abundant condensation nuclei and fog forms, filling the pool from the bottom upward with a characteristically level top. Because it forms in exactly the ground that vehicles must drive through, valley-bottom radiation fog is a major road-safety hazard, and it is worst in the hour around and just after sunrise when the fog is thickest and the low sun destroys what visibility remains. Freezing fog, where supercooled droplets deposit rime on every surface, is a further stage. The lid also causes purely practical nuisances that matter to anyone living in a valley: a wood stove or bonfire that draws badly and fills the garden with smoke on a still evening, exhaust from a generator lingering around a camp, and the reason that any fuel-burning appliance used near sleeping people in a hollow deserves conspicuous respect.

sections.heading: Heavier-Than-Air Gases and the Same Terrain Trap
sections.body:
The physics that pools cold air also pools any gas denser than the surrounding atmosphere, and this is where the topic stops being a matter of comfort and becomes one of survival. Density is the whole story. Dry air at standard conditions is about 1.29 kilograms per cubic metre. Carbon dioxide, with a molar mass of 44 grams per mole against air's 29, is about 1.98, more than half again as dense. Hydrogen sulphide is about 1.54. Propane is roughly 1.9 and butane 2.5, which is precisely why leaked liquefied petroleum gas collects in cellars, bilges and inspection pits rather than dispersing. Chlorine is around 3.2. Every one of these will run downhill exactly as chilled air does, follow gullies, and fill any depression, and in the still, stratified conditions of a nocturnal inversion nothing will mix it away.

The worst recorded natural example is Lake Nyos in Cameroon. On the evening of 21 August 1986 a crater lake saturated with volcanic carbon dioxide overturned and released on the order of a cubic kilometre of gas, which formed a dense cloud, poured over the crater rim and ran down the valleys at speeds estimated in the tens of metres per second. It asphyxiated about 1,746 people and thousands of livestock in villages up to 25 kilometres away, in many cases while they slept. Survivors reported that people on higher ground lived while those in the valley bottoms did not, which is the entire lesson in one sentence. A smaller event at Lake Monoun in the same region in 1984 killed 37. Both lakes are now fitted with degassing pipes.

Volcanic terrain provides regular smaller versions. The Italian phrase for such places is grotta del cane, dog cave, from sites where carbon dioxide pooled at knee height would fell a dog while a standing human was unaffected. Mazuku in the Democratic Republic of Congo, dry gas-filled hollows near Lake Kivu and the Virunga volcanoes, kill people and animals every year. On Mammoth Mountain in California, tree kill zones and several deaths have been attributed to carbon dioxide accumulating in snow-covered depressions and in ski patrol structures.

The everyday versions matter more to most people than the exotic ones. Silage clamps and grain silos generate carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides that pool at the base. Slurry pits release hydrogen sulphide, which paralyses the sense of smell at exactly the concentrations that become dangerous, so the classic fatality pattern is one person overcome and two or three would-be rescuers dying alongside them. Wells, cellars, ship holds, tanks, trenches and manholes are all confined-space hazards in which the pooling behaviour is central. The universal rules follow directly from the physics: assume any depression may hold something you cannot see or smell, ventilate or test before entry, never enter to rescue without breathing apparatus, and remember that going downhill or downstairs toward a casualty is going deeper into the hazard.

sections.heading: Measuring and Forecasting a Cold Pool Yourself
sections.body:
You can characterise the drainage behaviour of a piece of ground with almost no equipment, and the resulting local knowledge is worth more than any general forecast. The basic instrument is a pair of cheap digital minimum-recording thermometers, of the kind sold for greenhouses. Place one at the suspected low point and one on the slope thirty to sixty metres higher, both at the same height above ground, both shielded from the sky by a simple radiation shield such as an inverted white plastic cup or a stack of drilled saucers, and both away from walls and hard surfaces. Read them for a dozen clear calm nights and you will have quantified your own inversion. Growers doing this properly use a standard screen height of 1.25 metres, and it is worth adding a third sensor at ground level, since the difference between grass minimum and screen minimum is typically 3 to 5 degrees and is what actually determines whether frost forms.

A rough forecast of the overnight minimum can be made from dusk observations with surprising accuracy under clear calm conditions. Several empirical schemes exist, most starting from the afternoon maximum temperature and the dew point and adjusting for cloud and wind. A simpler practical approach for a known site is to record the temperature at sunset and the dew point, note that under clear calm skies temperature typically falls fast for the first three hours then slows, and that it will rarely drop more than a degree or two below the dew point because condensation releases latent heat. If sunset temperature is 8 degrees and dew point is 1 degree, a clear calm night in a hollow will very likely reach frost; if the dew point is 7 degrees it almost certainly will not.

Simple qualitative observations are often enough. Step outside two hours after sunset. If the stars are sharp, the air is dead still, your breath is visible and the grass is already wet, the pool is forming and will continue. Walk fifty metres uphill; if you feel a distinct step up in temperature, the inversion is already established. If a breeze is stirring the treetops but the air at your feet is calm, the inversion has decoupled the surface from the flow above and will survive. If the wind reaches your face, it will not.

For serious work, remember what the standard forecast does and does not give you. Numerical weather prediction models run at grid spacings of one to ten kilometres and cannot resolve a fifty-metre hollow, and they are systematically warm-biased for frost hollows for exactly that reason; a forecast minimum of plus 2 for the region can easily mean minus 4 in a small basin within it. Some national services publish separate grass minimum forecasts and frost warnings, which are more useful. Above all, the local pattern is highly repeatable. A site that ran 7 degrees colder than the slope last October will do it again, and a season of observations gives you a personal correction to apply to any forecast for the rest of your life at that place.

sections.heading: Where the Rules Break and What to Do When They Do
sections.body:
The pattern described here is reliable but not universal, and knowing its failure modes prevents the overconfident errors that catch experienced people. The commonest failure is applying nocturnal logic to a windy or cloudy night. Cold pooling requires clear, calm conditions; under an active weather system there is no inversion, the valley floor may be the warmest and safest ground available, and a hard-won habit of always camping high can put you on an exposed shoulder in a gale for no thermal benefit whatever. Read the sky, not the rule.

The second failure is confusing a radiation frost with an advective freeze. A radiation frost is generated locally by a clear calm night and is intensely terrain-dependent, with several degrees of difference across a hillside. An advective freeze is a mass of cold air imported by a synoptic wind, is deep, well mixed, and blows straight over the terrain, and under it the slope is no warmer than the floor. Every terrain-based countermeasure including wind machines, site selection and drainage gaps loses most of its value in an advective freeze, and claims to the contrary should be treated sceptically. The distinguishing sign is simply wind: an advective freeze is windy and often cloudy, a radiation frost is still and clear.

The third is misjudging scale. Cold air drainage is diluted by mixing over long descents, so the coldest ground in a large mountain system is frequently not the main valley floor but a small, sheltered, high-altitude basin partway down that receives a concentrated supply and holds it. Conversely, a very wide valley floor may behave more like a plain than a container, with the pooled air spread thinly. Small closed depressions punch far above their apparent significance and are the single most underestimated feature on a map. The fourth is forgetting that people and machines create dams overnight: a new hedge, a parked line of vehicles, a plough-thrown snow bank.

When it does go wrong the responses are simple and should be automatic. If you wake cold in a hollow, the correct move is usually to move rather than to endure: gaining twenty or thirty metres of height in the dark is unpleasant but can be worth five degrees, and even shifting the pitch off the lowest ground onto a slight rise helps. If moving is impossible, get insulation underneath you before adding layers on top, since conduction into cold ground dominates the heat loss of a lying body; boost it with a rucksack, rope, dry vegetation, foam or spare clothing. Eat, because shivering is metabolically expensive, and drink, because cold-induced diuresis dehydrates people fast. If someone is showing early hypothermia, insulate them from the ground first, add windproof and vapour-proof layers, give warm sweet drinks if they are fully conscious, and get them moving or moved. And if you find yourself in a hollow that smells wrong, feels unaccountably heavy, or where an animal or a person has collapsed for no visible reason, do not go down into it. Retreat uphill and get help, because that depression may be holding something other than cold air.

guides.safetyNote: Cold pools kill in two ways. A valley bottom can run 5 to 25 degrees Celsius colder than ground a short walk uphill, so sleeping gear rated for the forecast regional minimum may be badly inadequate in a hollow, and ground conduction, not air temperature, is the dominant heat loss for a lying body: insulate underneath before adding layers on top. Separately, the same terrain that traps chilled air traps every gas denser than air, including carbon dioxide, hydrogen sulphide, LPG, chlorine and engine exhaust. Never run a stove, generator, heater or engine in a tent, hollow, cellar, pit or other depression; never enter a well, silo, slurry pit, tank or trench without testing and ventilating; and never descend into a depression to rescue a collapsed person or animal without breathing apparatus, because most fatalities in such incidents are would-be rescuers.

guides.title: Drainage and Runoff in Camp Selection
guides.summary: How to read ground, soil and weather for where water will go, and choose and prepare a campsite that stays dry and safe: infiltration and runoff mechanics, flash-flood and meltwater hazards, site survey procedure, shelter siting, and what to do when a camp starts flooding at night.

sections.heading: Why the ground decides the night
sections.body:
