Of all the choices made when setting up a camp, the one that most often determines whether the
night is restful or miserable is not the shelter, the sleeping bag or the fire. It is the patch
of ground chosen, and specifically what that ground will do with water. A tent pitched in a
shallow depression that looked flat and inviting in the afternoon becomes a basin at two in the
morning, and a sleeping bag that has absorbed a litre of cold water has lost most of its
insulating value for the rest of the trip. The same decision, made badly beside a desert wash,
has killed people.

The reason siting matters so much is that water is relentless and cumulative in a way that other
discomforts are not. Cold can be countered by adding layers; hunger tolerates delay; wet
insulation cannot be fixed by effort. Down loses nearly all its loft when saturated, and while
synthetic fill retains perhaps a third of its warmth, that is a third of a rating already chosen
with little margin. A wet sleeping system in cool conditions moves a person from uncomfortable
to hypothermic over a few hours, because the body loses heat to water roughly twenty-five times
faster than to still air of the same temperature. Most survival-course hypothermia cases do not
begin with immersion in a river; they begin with a night spent damp.

The encouraging fact is that water behaves predictably. It moves downhill by the steepest
available route, it concentrates where slopes converge, it accumulates where it cannot escape,
and it enters the ground only as fast as the soil will accept it, with the excess flowing across
the surface. Every one of those behaviours leaves visible evidence, and all of it can be read in
a few minutes by someone who knows what to look for. Sediment fans, matted grass, water-stained
bark, a change in vegetation, a line of debris caught in a bush at knee height: the landscape
has already recorded what happens in weather worse than today's.

This is a skill of observation rather than equipment, and it improves quickly with deliberate
attention. A useful habit when arriving at a candidate site is to spend two minutes not looking
at the site at all, and instead looking uphill, asking a single question: if fifty millimetres
of rain fell on the ground above this spot in the next hour, where would it go? That question
reframes the site from a flat piece of ground into a point in a drainage system with an upstream
and a downstream. Once a camp is seen that way, most of the classic mistakes become obvious
before they are made, and almost all of them are cheaper to avoid by walking another hundred
metres than to fix at midnight in the rain.

sections.heading: Where rain actually goes: interception, infiltration and runoff
sections.body:
When rain reaches the ground it divides between a small number of destinations, and the
proportions determine whether a site stays workable. Some is intercepted before it lands, caught
on leaves and branches and evaporated without ever touching soil; a dense conifer canopy can
intercept 15 to 30 per cent of light rainfall, which is why the ground under mature spruce stays
dry through a passing shower and why the same ground becomes a series of concentrated drips once
the canopy saturates and begins to shed. Some of what reaches the surface is stored in
depressions, from puddles down to the roughness between soil crumbs. Some infiltrates into the
soil. What is left over runs off across the surface, and it is that leftover, called overland
flow or Hortonian flow after the hydrologist Robert Horton who described it in 1933, that soaks
camps.

The governing comparison is simple and worth internalising: runoff occurs when rainfall
intensity exceeds the soil's infiltration capacity. Intensity is measured in millimetres per
hour. Light rain delivers under 2.5 mm per hour; moderate rain 2.5 to 7.5; heavy rain 7.5 to 50;
and a vigorous convective thunderstorm cell can deliver 50 to 100 mm per hour for a short
period, with extreme cells exceeding that. Infiltration capacity varies over an even wider
range: clean sand may accept 20 to 200 mm per hour, a well-structured loam perhaps 10 to 20, a
silt loam 3 to 8, and a heavy clay only 1 to 5. Bare compacted ground, a well-used path or a
vehicle track may accept almost nothing.

Two consequences follow. First, the same storm produces a dry camp on sandy soil and a flooded
one on clay a hundred metres away, so soil type is a site-selection criterion in its own right.
Second, infiltration capacity is not constant. It starts high on dry soil and falls as the pore
spaces fill, typically declining towards a steady final rate within twenty to sixty minutes of
continuous rain. This is why the third hour of a storm produces far more surface water than the
first, and why a site that handled an afternoon shower without difficulty may not handle the
same rainfall arriving at the end of a wet week.

Beneath the surface, water continues to move. Some percolates to the water table; some travels
laterally through the upper soil as throughflow, especially where a permeable layer sits over an
impermeable one, emerging downslope as a seep. A patch of ground that is wet without rain, or
which supports rushes, sedges, mosses or bright green growth in an otherwise dry setting, is
very likely fed by throughflow, and it will be wettest precisely when you least want it to be.

sections.heading: Reading terrain: catchments, contours and convergence
sections.body:
Every point on the landscape has an upslope catchment, the area of ground from which water would
eventually flow across or past it. The size and shape of that catchment is the single strongest
predictor of how much water a site must deal with, and it can be estimated by eye with practice
or read directly from a contour map.

The essential distinction is between convergent and divergent ground. Convergent ground is any
hollow, swale, gully, draw or valley: the land curves inward, so flow lines from a wide area
funnel into a narrow one. Divergent ground is any spur, nose, ridge, rib or shoulder: the land
curves outward, so flow lines spread apart and each square metre sheds water in slightly
different directions. On a contour map the difference is unambiguous. Contours form a V pointing
uphill, towards higher ground, where they cross a watercourse or hollow; they form a V or U
pointing downhill where they cross a spur. That rule, sometimes taught as the rule of Vs, is the
most useful single piece of map reading for campsite selection, because it lets you identify
convergent ground from a map before you have walked a step.

Slope angle matters less than most people assume, and slope position matters far more. Steep
ground sheds water fast but delivers it somewhere, and being on that somewhere is the problem.
The best positions are typically a broad, gently convex bench, terrace or spur shoulder: high
enough that no significant catchment lies above, and shaped so that whatever falls on the site
itself moves away in several directions. The worst positions are the base of a slope where
several hollows meet, the inside of a concave hillside, and the flat floor of any valley narrow
enough that its walls are visibly steep.

Scale deserves attention because catchments nest. A slight swale two metres across may drain
only a tennis court and produce a trickle. The same swale a hundred metres downhill may be
collecting from several hectares. When judging a site, trace the hollow you are standing in
upwards with your eyes until you can see where it begins; if you cannot see the top, the
catchment is bigger than you think.

Finally, remember that the surface you can see may not be the surface that governs. In limestone
country, water disappears into fissures and reappears unpredictably; in glaciated terrain, a
flat hollow may be a kettle hole with no outlet at all, which is why it holds a bog. And in any
terrain, human works redirect flow at a scale that overwhelms natural drainage: a road, a
forestry track, a culvert or a ditch can deliver the runoff of a whole hillside to a point that
natural topography would never have concentrated.

sections.heading: Soil, texture and the ground you cannot see
sections.body:
Two sites on the same slope, in the same weather, can behave completely differently because of
what lies under the surface. Soil texture, the proportion of sand, silt and clay, sets the size
of the pore spaces through which water must travel, and pore size dominates everything. Sand
particles are 0.05 to 2 millimetres across and leave large channels between them, so water
drains through quickly and the surface dries within hours of a storm. Clay particles are smaller
than 0.002 millimetres, with pores so fine that water moves through them at a crawl, so clay
holds water at the surface, turns greasy underfoot and stays wet for days.

You can identify texture in the field in under a minute without any equipment. Take a small
handful of soil from a few centimetres down, wet it to the consistency of putty and work it
between finger and thumb. If it feels gritty and will not hold a shape, it is sand-dominated and
will drain well. If it feels smooth and floury, like talc, and forms a weak ball that crumbles,
it is silty; silt drains moderately but is prone to forming a surface crust that sheds water. If
it feels sticky, takes a polish when smeared, and can be rolled into a thread two or three
millimetres thick without breaking, it is clay-rich, and a tent on it after rain will be sitting
on a shallow pond.

Structure matters as much as texture. Well-aggregated soil under undisturbed vegetation,
threaded with root channels, worm burrows and decayed organic matter, accepts water far faster
than the same texture compacted. This is why the most attractive-looking spot in a popular area,
the bare flat patch where everyone camps, is frequently the wettest: hundreds of nights of boots
and tent floors have destroyed the structure of the top few centimetres, and a compacted surface
can lose eighty per cent or more of its infiltration capacity. The corollary is useful in
reverse: a patch of ground with intact leaf litter and springy organic duff will absorb a
surprising amount of rain.

Depth to an impermeable layer is the third variable and the one most often missed. Soil sitting
over bedrock, a clay pan, permafrost or a compacted plough pan can only store the water its own
depth allows. Fifteen centimetres of loam over rock holds perhaps 25 to 45 millimetres of rain
before it saturates, after which every additional drop runs off, and the site turns from
apparently sound to waterlogged very suddenly. Probing with a tent peg or a stick before
pitching, and noting where it stops, is a five-second test worth making a habit.

Finally, two soils behave counter-intuitively. Severely dried clay cracks, swallowing the first
rain fast and then swelling shut. And soils under recently burned ground or under some pine and
eucalyptus litter become hydrophobic, coated with waxy organic compounds that actively repel
water; rain beads on the surface and runs off almost entirely, which is why burned catchments
produce flash floods and debris flows from rainfall that would previously have soaked in.

sections.heading: How much water: intensity, duration and simple runoff arithmetic
sections.body:
It helps to convert weather into volumes, because the numbers are larger than intuition
suggests. One millimetre of rain falling on one square metre is one litre. A modest overnight
fall of 20 millimetres therefore delivers 20 litres to every square metre, which is 20 cubic
metres, or 20 tonnes, to a patch of hillside 100 metres by 10. Only a fraction of that becomes
surface flow, but even a fraction is a great deal of water to have arriving at a tent door.

The standard tool for estimating that fraction is the rational method, published in essentially
modern form by Emil Kuichling in 1889 and still used for small catchments. It states that peak
runoff equals a runoff coefficient multiplied by rainfall intensity multiplied by catchment
area, usually written Q equals C times i times A. The coefficient C is the proportion of rain
that becomes surface flow, and typical values are instructive: dense forest on sandy soil 0.05
to 0.15; grassland on loam with gentle slope 0.15 to 0.35; the same grassland on clay or on
steep ground 0.4 to 0.6; bare, compacted or saturated ground 0.6 to 0.8; rock slabs, hardpan or
pavement 0.85 to 0.95. Steepness, wetness and compaction all push C upward, and they commonly
occur together.

Worked through, this gives a feel for the risk. Suppose a shallow draw drains half a hectare of
steep grassy hillside, so A is 5,000 square metres, and a thunderstorm delivers 40 millimetres
per hour with C at 0.5. The runoff rate is 0.5 times 0.04 metres per hour times 5,000 square
metres, which is 100 cubic metres per hour, or about 28 litres per second flowing through that
draw. That is a stream you would not step across casually, produced by a catchment small enough
to see across, from a storm that might last twenty minutes. Doubling the catchment doubles it; a
burned or frozen surface with C near 0.9 nearly doubles it again.

Two refinements matter in the field. Time of concentration, the time for water from the furthest
point of the catchment to reach you, sets how quickly flow builds; on a small steep catchment it
may be five to fifteen minutes, meaning that trouble arrives almost with the rain, while a
larger catchment delivers its peak an hour or more after the downpour has stopped and the sky
has cleared. And antecedent conditions dominate: identical rainfall onto soil already at field
capacity produces far more runoff than onto dry ground, which is why the last day of a wet week
is the dangerous one.

None of this requires calculation in the field. The point of the arithmetic is calibration, so
that when you look uphill at a hectare of steep bare ground above a tempting flat spot, you
recognise it as tens of litres per second in a serious storm rather than as scenery.

sections.heading: Flash floods and dry channels: the hazard that kills
sections.body:
Every other drainage error costs comfort. This one costs lives, and it deserves to be treated as
a separate category with an absolute rule attached: do not camp in a dry wash, arroyo, gully,
canyon floor, culvert outfall or any other channel, however dry and however convenient the flat
sand looks.

The mechanism is what makes it lethal. A flash flood is generated by rain falling on a
catchment, often far away and out of sight, that cannot absorb it. Desert soils are frequently
crusted or hydrophobic and shed water almost like pavement, so runoff coefficients approach 0.9.
The catchment funnels that flow into a narrow channel with smooth, steep, confining walls, which
converts a broad sheet of shallow water into a deep, fast-moving wall. Arrival can be sudden
because debris temporarily dams a constriction and then fails, releasing a surge. The result is
that a channel can go from bone dry to two metres deep in a matter of minutes, under a blue sky
directly overhead, from a storm 15 or 30 kilometres upstream that was never audible.

The historical record is unambiguous. On 12 August 1997, eleven hikers died in Lower Antelope
Canyon in Arizona when a thunderstorm dropped rain into the catchment more than 20 kilometres
away; the sky above the canyon was clear. In Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon on 31 July 1976,
roughly 300 millimetres of rain fell in about four hours over the upper canyon, producing a
flood wave that killed 144 people, many of them campers. In arid regions worldwide, flash
flooding is consistently among the leading causes of weather-related death, and a large share of
the victims were in vehicles or camped in the channel.

The physical thresholds are worth memorising because they are lower than people expect. Moving
water only 15 centimetres deep at a walking pace can sweep an adult off their feet, because drag
force rises with the square of velocity and a person presents a large area. Thirty centimetres
will float many cars; 60 centimetres will move most vehicles, including four-wheel drives.
Floodwater in a wash is opaque, laden with sand and cobbles, and often carries logs, so it
strikes rather than merely pushes.

The evidence of past floods is always present if you look for it. Scour lines and undercut
banks; a clean, sorted, unvegetated channel floor; sand and gravel bars deposited on the inside
of bends; debris, grass or plastic caught in branches above head height; trees stripped of bark
on the upstream side; and an absence of mature vegetation on the flat that surrounds you while
the ground three metres higher supports established shrubs. Any of these means the channel runs,
and the height of the debris tells you how deep. Camp above that line by a good margin, ideally
on a terrace that is separated from the channel by a distinct step, and choose a site with an
escape route to higher ground that does not require crossing the channel.

sections.heading: Reading the evidence: vegetation, sediment and ground signs
sections.body:
The landscape keeps a record of water, and learning to read it converts campsite selection from
guesswork into inference. The evidence falls into three families: what grows, what has been
moved, and what the surface itself looks like.

Vegetation is the most reliable long-term indicator because plants integrate conditions over
years rather than hours. Rushes, sedges, reeds, horsetails, willows, alders and cottonwoods all
indicate water at or near the surface for much of the year; a stand of them in the middle of
otherwise dry ground marks a seep or a high water table with near certainty. Mosses and
liverworts thrive where the surface stays damp. Bright, lush green grass in a dry season, or a
distinct colour change visible from a distance, follows the wet ground almost exactly.
Conversely, lichens on rock, drought-tolerant shrubs, cacti and deep-rooted bunch grasses
indicate ground that dries thoroughly. Trees are informative in a second way: species that
cannot tolerate waterlogged roots, and mature specimens of any kind, indicate ground that has
not been scoured or drowned within their lifetime, which for a mature tree is decades of
evidence.

Absence is as informative as presence. A flat, open, unvegetated strip running through vegetated
ground is a channel, whether or not it holds water today. Vegetation that is all the same young
age, where older trees stand slightly higher, indicates that everything older was removed by
flood or debris flow. Grass combed flat and all pointing the same way was laid down by flowing
water, and the direction it points is the direction that water went.

Moved material tells you about the last event and its magnitude. Look for sorted sediment:
rounded gravel and coarse sand indicate fast flow, fine silt indicates standing or slow water,
and a fan of sediment spreading where a slope meets flatter ground marks where flow regularly
loses energy. Debris caught in branches, fences or shrubs gives a direct height reading for the
last flood, and it is worth walking to touch it, because the eye consistently underestimates it.
Undercut banks, exposed roots and a step or scarp in the ground surface indicate scour. Pebbles
perched on top of vegetation or leaf litter arrived recently and by water.

The surface itself completes the picture. A dry, cracked, polygonal crust is a former puddle and
will be one again. A fine, smooth, uniform silt layer marks slack water. Water stains or a
distinct colour band on rock, tree trunks or masonry mark a former water level. Animal signs
help too: worm casts and mole hills need moist but not saturated soil; ant nests, especially
large mounds, are almost never built where ground floods, so a mature ant colony is a reasonable
indicator of ground that stays dry.

Finally, a physical test settles most doubts in ten seconds. Press a boot heel firmly into the
ground. If water pools in the print, or if the ground feels springy and rebounds like a sponge,
the soil is at or near saturation now, in the current weather, and will be worse after rain.

sections.heading: A ten-minute site survey
sections.body:
A structured survey turns scattered observations into a decision, and it can be completed in
about ten minutes with no equipment. The value of doing it in a fixed order is that the fatal
problems are checked first, so that a site can be rejected before any effort is invested in
liking it. Arrive with enough daylight to do this properly; the single most common cause of a
bad site is arriving too late to have a choice, so plan to stop earlier than feels necessary in
unfamiliar country.
steps: Stand at the candidate spot and look uphill first. Trace the ground above you with your eyes and estimate the catchment feeding this point. If you cannot see the top of the slope or hollow above you, treat the catchment as large and be conservative.

Reject outright any position in a channel: a wash, gully, draw, canyon floor, streambed, culvert line or ditch, however dry. Check for scour, sorted gravel, undercut banks and debris caught above ground level, and if any is present move to ground above the highest such mark by a clear margin.

Identify whether the ground is convergent or divergent. Sight along the slope and look for a hollow that funnels flow towards you, or a nose or shoulder that sheds it away. Prefer a broad convex bench, spur shoulder or terrace with little ground above it.

Check for a low point. Walk the perimeter of your intended pitch and confirm that no part of the tent footprint is the lowest ground within about ten metres. A depression of even five centimetres will hold water once the soil saturates.

Test the soil. Probe with a tent peg or stick to find depth to rock or a hard layer, then take a pinch of soil from a few centimetres down, wet it and feel it. Grit means sand and good drainage; smooth and sticky means clay and standing water. Press a boot heel in and see whether water appears.

Look for standing evidence of wet ground: rushes, sedges, moss, bright green grass, springy organic ground, worm casts in a saturated surface, or any patch that is damp with no rain today. A seep line running across the slope is a hard reject.

Assess overhead and adjacent hazards while you are here, since they cost nothing to check: dead branches, leaning or undercut trees, loose rock above, and undercut banks that could collapse if saturated.
Plan where your own runoff will go. Identify the direction water will leave the pitch, and confirm it does not run towards a fire site, a food store, a latrine, or the door of the shelter.
Identify an escape route to higher ground that can be walked in the dark without crossing a channel, and confirm everyone in the party knows it before dark.

Only then judge the comfortable factors: flatness, wind exposure, shade, view, distance to water and firewood. Comfort is chosen from among sites that have already passed the drainage test, never instead of it.

sections.heading: Choosing the microsite: high and dry, but not too high
sections.body:
Once a broad area is accepted, the final choice is measured in metres, and it involves a genuine
conflict between two objectives that most guidance mentions only one side of. The drainage
objective says go higher: get above the hollows, off the valley floor, onto ground that sheds
water. The thermal objective says the opposite in one specific respect, because cold air drains
too.

Cold air drainage is a real and often dramatic effect. On clear, calm nights the ground radiates
heat to the sky, chilling the air immediately above it. That chilled air is denser and flows
downhill, pooling in valley floors, basins and hollows exactly as water does, forming what is
called a frost hollow or cold sink. The temperature difference is not trivial: a valley bottom
can be 5 to 10 degrees Celsius colder than a slope 30 to 60 metres above it, and in extreme
sheltered basins the difference has been measured at over 20 degrees. Above the cold pool sits a
warmer layer, called the thermal belt, typically on the mid-slope. This is why orchards are
planted on slopes rather than valley floors, and why an experienced camper who wants a warm
night looks for a bench part way up a slope.

Fortunately the two objectives usually agree. A mid-slope bench or spur shoulder is both above
the cold pool and above the water. The place they conflict is a ridge crest or summit, which is
excellently drained and thoroughly exposed to wind, and wind removes far more heat than a few
degrees of air temperature. The workable rule is to camp on the shoulder rather than the crest
or the bottom: high enough to be off the valley floor and out of the cold pool, low enough and
sheltered enough to be out of the wind, and on convex ground so that water leaves in every
direction.

Several finer points refine the choice. Prefer ground with a gentle slope of one to three
degrees over dead flat, because a slight fall guarantees drainage while remaining comfortable to
sleep on; sleep with your head at the upslope end. Avoid the base of any slope, where both water
and cold air accumulate and where soil is deepest and wettest. Beware the apparently ideal flat
clearing in woodland, which is often flat because it is a filled hollow with poor drainage.
Avoid the ground immediately beside a stream even where it is above the channel, because the
humidity there guarantees condensation and dew. And keep a distance of at least 60 metres,
roughly 200 feet, from open water where regulations or good practice apply, which incidentally
puts you above most of the flood risk as well as protecting the water from your camp.

sections.heading: Preparing the ground and pitching for water
sections.body:
Good siting does most of the work, but the last few centimetres are decided by how the shelter
is prepared and pitched. The governing principle is that water must be kept from reaching the
sleeping surface by three independent means: it should not arrive, it should not enter, and if
some enters it should have somewhere to go that is not your bedding.

Ground preparation begins with clearing. Remove stones, sticks and cones, which puncture floors
and create high points that pool water around them, and clear any built-up leaf dam that would
hold water against the uphill side of the tent. Do not remove the whole organic layer: intact
duff is absorbent and insulating, and stripping it exposes bare soil that seals and sheds. If
the ground has a slight fall, orient the shelter so the fall runs along its length rather than
across it, and sleep with the head uphill.

A groundsheet is the primary barrier and the most commonly misused item of kit. A footprint
placed under a tent must be smaller than the tent floor, or trimmed and tucked so that no edge
protrudes; an exposed lip collects rain running off the flysheet and channels it directly under
the floor, which turns a protective layer into a water tray. Inside a tarp shelter the reverse
applies: fold the edges of the ground cloth upward against the sides to make a shallow bathtub,
so that surface water flowing across the ground is turned aside rather than running underneath.
A modern tent with a bathtub floor, seams sealed and rising 10 to 15 centimetres up the walls,
performs the same function.

Pitch tautly, because slack fabric sags, holds water and eventually leaks by capillary action
where it touches the inner. Set guys so the flysheet is held clear of the inner everywhere, and
where a fly reaches the ground, ensure it sheds outside the footprint rather than onto it. Keep
the sleeping mat and bag off the floor edges, and packs raised rather than resting against the
inner wall where condensation and seepage collect. Re-tension the guys before sleeping and again
if rain begins, because nylon and polyester stretch when wet by several per cent, and a fly that
was taut at dusk will be resting on the inner by midnight.
ingredients: A groundsheet or footprint cut smaller than the tent floor, or a plain polythene sheet trimmed to size; hardware shops sell heavy builder's polythene cheaply, and 125 micron or thicker resists punctures.
A tarp with reinforced tie-outs for a separate rain roof or a covered working area, plus 15 to 20 metres of 2 to 3 millimetre cord.
Pegs suited to the ground: long thin skewers for soft soil, wide stakes for sand or snow, short steel pins for stony ground, plus a few spares.
A small trowel or lightweight digging tool, for latrine catholes and for restoring disturbed ground.
Dry bags or heavy-duty bin liners to isolate sleeping insulation and spare clothing from any water that does get in.
A microfibre or sponge cloth for mopping condensation and small ingress before it soaks into bedding.

sections.heading: Diverting runoff: berms, drainage and the trenching question
sections.body:
When a site is good, no earthworks are needed. When a site is merely acceptable and the weather
turns, a small amount of water management can save the night. The technique to understand is
diversion: intercepting flow above the shelter and leading it around, rather than trying to hold
it back or bail it out.

The traditional method is a drainage trench, a shallow ditch dug around the uphill side of a
tent, with a leg running downhill on each side to carry water away. It is effective, and in the
era of canvas tents without sewn-in floors it was standard practice. It is also, in most modern
circumstances, both unnecessary and unacceptable. A tent with a sealed bathtub floor does not
need a trench, because water flowing under it cannot get in. Trenching scars ground that takes
years to recover, concentrates flow into an artificial channel that then erodes, and is
prohibited in most national parks and under Leave No Trace guidance. The honest position is that
trenching is a genuine emergency tool, justified when flooding threatens shelter or safety and
no better site can be reached, and that in that case the trench should be as small as will work
and must be filled and the turf replaced before leaving.

The preferred alternatives are non-destructive. A berm built from loose material already on the
surface, such as leaf litter, gravel, deadfall or a rolled log laid across the slope a metre or
two above the shelter, will turn a sheet flow aside without cutting the ground. Existing
features can be recruited: a log, a rock ledge, a bank or a dense clump of vegetation upslope
will already be diverting water, so pitching immediately behind one is free protection. If a
tarp is available, an extra low-pitched panel angled across the slope above the sleeping area
will intercept and shed overland flow entirely.

Three principles govern any diversion. It must begin above the shelter and extend past both
sides, because water that reaches the flank simply turns downhill into the pitch. It must lead
somewhere that can accept the flow, since concentrating half a hillside onto a single point of
bare soil creates a gully within one storm. And it must not deliver water towards anyone else's
camp, the fire, food stores or the latrine.

Within the pitch itself, keep the interior floor as the driest point. A small sump dug just
outside the door in a tarp or basha shelter, ten centimetres across and filled with gravel,
gives incoming water somewhere to collect and is easily restored. If water is already inside,
mop it with a cloth and wring it out rather than trying to sweep it, because sweeping spreads it
into bedding and clothing where it will do far more damage than it does on a groundsheet.

sections.heading: Snow, frozen ground and meltwater
sections.body:
Cold conditions do not remove the drainage problem; they postpone and then concentrate it.
Frozen ground has essentially zero infiltration capacity, because the pore water is ice, so rain
or meltwater onto frozen soil produces a runoff coefficient approaching that of concrete. This
is the mechanism behind many spring floods: a moderate rainfall that summer soil would have
absorbed entirely runs off almost completely, and it arrives with the meltwater the same rain is
releasing from the snowpack.

Snowmelt itself follows a strong daily cycle that is easy to observe and easy to forget. Melting
is driven by sun and warm air, so streams fed by snow rise through the afternoon and peak in the
late afternoon or evening, with the lag depending on how far the water has to travel; they fall
overnight and are lowest around dawn. A dry gravel channel crossed comfortably at eight in the
morning may be a thigh-deep torrent at six in the evening. Camping on a bar or bank in such a
channel, or planning a return crossing for the end of the day, are both predictable mistakes.

Camping on snow brings its own drainage logic. Water runs on top of frozen ground and beneath
the snowpack, so a platform that appears solid may sit over a running channel; listen for water
and avoid depressions and the low points of gullies. Tree wells, the hollows of loose snow
around trunks where the canopy has intercepted snowfall, are both a collapse hazard and a drip
trap once the canopy warms. A snow platform should be stamped out and left for thirty to sixty
minutes before pitching so the disturbed crystals sinter and harden, which produces a firm
surface that does not develop body-shaped hollows overnight. Those hollows matter because your
own heat melts the surface beneath you, and the meltwater has nowhere to drain.

Ground insulation becomes the primary defence rather than a comfort item. Snow conducts heat far
better than air, and any melt refreezes as ice against the sleeping mat. A combined insulation
value of about R-5 or more is usually recommended for winter ground, commonly achieved by
pairing a closed-cell foam mat with an inflatable one; the foam layer goes underneath, where it
continues to work if the inflatable fails.

Spring conditions require the most caution because they combine the worst of both. Snow bridges
over streams weaken from beneath and are least reliable in the afternoon. Ground that is thawed
at the surface and frozen below sheds water sideways, producing saturated slush over ice on
slopes that appeared dry. And a site chosen on hard morning snow may become, by evening, a pool
of standing meltwater within an impermeable basin, which is why a winter camp should be sited
with the same uphill catchment question in mind as a summer one.

sections.heading: Water that arrives from elsewhere: rivers, lakes and coasts
sections.body:
The hazards considered so far are local, driven by rain falling on ground you can see. Camping
beside larger water bodies introduces a different class of risk, in which the water level
changes because of something happening far away or on a schedule that has nothing to do with
today's weather.

Rivers rise from upstream rain, and the lag can be many hours. A camp on a gravel bar under a
clear evening sky can be flooded before dawn by a storm that fell fifty kilometres upstream at
dusk. The practical rules are to camp on a terrace with a distinct step above the active channel
rather than on any bar, beach or flat within it; to read the debris and scour lines that mark
previous high water and add a substantial margin above them; and, before settling in, to look
upstream and consider what weather the catchment has had. Rising, discoloured, debris-laden
water at dusk is a signal to move immediately, not to watch.

Regulated rivers add an entirely artificial hazard. Below a dam or hydroelectric station,
releases can raise the level by a metre or more in minutes, on a schedule set by electricity
demand rather than by rainfall. Sirens and posted warnings exist on many such rivers and should
be taken literally. Irrigation canals and sluices behave similarly. If there is a dam upstream,
do not camp within the channel at all.

Lakes seem benign but can be driven by wind. A strong sustained wind pushes water to the
downwind end of a lake, raising it there and lowering it at the upwind end, an effect called
wind setup; when the wind stops, the water sloshes back in a slow oscillation known as a seiche.
On large lakes the setup can reach several tens of centimetres and occasionally more, and it
coincides with the largest waves, so a camp on the downwind shore can be flooded and wave-washed
simultaneously.

Coasts require the most disciplined arithmetic, because tides are predictable and therefore
inexcusable. Semi-diurnal coasts see two high tides about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart, so high
water shifts roughly 50 minutes later each day. Tidal range varies enormously by location, from
under a metre in parts of the Mediterranean to over 15 metres in the Bay of Fundy, and it varies
through the month: spring tides, at new and full moon, have the greatest range, while neap tides
at the quarter moons have the least. Camping above today's high water line is not enough if
tomorrow is a spring tide. The reliable field marker is the wrack line, the band of dried
seaweed, driftwood and litter deposited at the highest recent water, with the highest of several
such lines marking recent springs. Camp well above the highest wrack line, and add margin for
storm surge, which in an onshore gale with low atmospheric pressure can add a metre or more on
top of the predicted tide.

sections.heading: Hard ground, human ground and vehicle camps
sections.body:
Human-modified surfaces change drainage more than any natural variation, and the changes are
usually in the wrong direction. Roads, tracks, compacted campsites, car parks and roofs shed
almost everything that falls on them, with runoff coefficients from 0.85 to 0.95, and they
collect that water into ditches and culverts that concentrate it at chosen points. The result is
that a small storm can deliver, to one culvert outfall, the runoff of an area many times larger
than the natural hollow there would ever have drained.

The practical consequences for camp selection are direct. Never pitch below a culvert, drain
outfall, downpipe or the low point of a road, however dry and level the ground appears; that
flat sandy patch is flat and sandy because it is a discharge point. Roadside ditches are
channels and are subject to the same rule as any other channel. Where a track crosses a slope,
its uphill ditch collects the hillside and the crossing point becomes a stream in rain, so
camping just downhill of a track is camping in a concentrated flow path. Old wheel ruts perform
the same function on a smaller scale, and they are one of the most reliably wet places in any
field.

Vehicle-based camping adds specific hazards. A vehicle parked on soft, saturated ground can sink
or lose traction with no warning once the surface fails, and recovery in the dark in rain is
genuinely dangerous; test ground with a boot before driving onto it, and think about how you
would drive out rather than in. Do not park in a wash or on a beach below the high water line.
Rooftop tents and vehicle awnings put the sleeping platform above the water, which solves the
wet-bedding problem entirely but does nothing about the vehicle being in a flood path.

In urban or disaster settings the analysis is the same with different vocabulary. Underpasses,
subways, basements, stairwells and the downhill side of any large hard surface are sumps, and
they flood rapidly and deeply. Storm drains reverse and surcharge in heavy rain, so a gutter or
drain grate is not an escape route for water but potentially a source. Anywhere sheltered and
dry-looking beneath a structure deserves the question of where the roof drains. Contamination is
the second problem: urban runoff carries fuel, oil, sewage from surcharged systems, and whatever
was on the ground, so shelter that is merely above the water may still be in a zone that should
not be slept in or that requires strict hand hygiene afterwards. In all these settings the same
principle holds as in wild country: find the high, convex, well-drained ground and accept the
walk to reach it.

sections.heading: Keeping water clean: hygiene, greywater and latrine siting
sections.body:
Drainage runs in both directions. The same flow paths that can soak a camp will also carry
whatever the camp puts on the ground into the nearest watercourse, and from there potentially
into someone's drinking water, including your own downstream. Siting for cleanliness uses the
identical reading of the ground, applied in reverse.

The dominant pathogens are faecal in origin. Giardia lamblia cysts, Cryptosporidium oocysts and
bacteria such as Campylobacter and pathogenic Escherichia coli travel readily in surface runoff,
and Cryptosporidium in particular resists chlorine at the concentrations used in field
treatment, which is why filtration or boiling matters. Cysts survive for weeks in cool water and
for months in cold, so a poorly sited latrine remains a hazard long after the party has left.

The standard distance guidance is at least 60 metres, about 200 feet or roughly seventy adult
paces, from any watercourse, lake, spring or seep, and equally from trails and camp. That
distance is a rule of thumb, not a physical barrier, and it should be increased where the ground
between is a concentrated flow path. Site the latrine on ground that is divergent, well-drained
and unlikely to carry overland flow, and never in a hollow, a gully, a seep line or a dry wash.
Dig a cathole 15 to 20 centimetres deep so waste is within the biologically active layer where
soil organisms break it down; deeper is not better, because below that depth decomposition slows
markedly. In fragile alpine, desert or heavily used environments, and on rivers where
regulations require it, the correct answer is to carry waste out in a sealed system.

Greywater from washing follows the same logic with an extra consideration. Even biodegradable
soap is a pollutant in water, since biodegradability describes what happens in soil over time
and not what happens to aquatic life immediately. Wash at least 60 metres from water, use the
minimum soap or none, strain food particles out and pack them with rubbish, then scatter the
water broadly over absorbent ground rather than pouring it in one place, so that soil filters
it. Never wash directly in a stream or at a spring.

Camp layout should keep these functions separated along the flow direction, and this is where
the drainage reading pays off directly. The water collection point goes upstream and uphill of
everything. The cooking and washing area sits below it. The latrine goes furthest downhill and
well off to the side, out of any flow path leading back to camp or to the water source. Where
the ground has a consistent fall, arranging camp in that order takes no extra effort and removes
most of the risk; where the ground is flat or complex, spend a moment identifying the flow
direction before deciding, because guessing wrong puts the latrine upstream of the kitchen.

sections.heading: When it goes wrong at two in the morning
sections.body:
Even careful siting occasionally loses to weather beyond what the ground has seen in years. What
matters then is recognising the situation early, and knowing in advance which of two very
different responses applies, because the wrong one is dangerous.

The distinction is between nuisance water and rising water. Nuisance water is seepage,
condensation, splash and a slowly spreading damp patch: unpleasant, manageable, and survivable
in place. Rising water is flow that is getting deeper or faster, or standing water whose edge is
visibly advancing. The second is an evacuation trigger and there is no safe amount of waiting to
see. If moving water in or around camp reaches ankle depth and is still rising, leave for higher
ground immediately, on foot, carrying only what comes without delay. Fifteen centimetres of
moving water can take an adult off their feet, water at night is opaque and its depth cannot be
judged, and the ground beneath it may have been scoured away. Gear is replaceable and can often
be recovered downstream in daylight.

For nuisance water, act sooner rather than later, because the deciding factor is whether
insulation gets wet. Get the sleeping bag and mat physically off the floor and onto anything
that lifts them. Mop standing water with a cloth and wring it outside rather than sweeping it.
Move packs off the floor. If water is entering along one edge, build a small berm of leaf
litter, a rolled mat, spare clothing in a bag or loose soil outside that wall to turn the flow
aside, and re-tension the guys, since a sagging fly touching the inner will wet everything it
contacts.

The judgement most often got wrong is whether to move camp in the dark. Moving is right when
water is rising, when the sleeping insulation is already soaked and a better site is genuinely
close and reachable, or when the ground shows signs of instability such as a slumping bank.
Staying is usually right when the problem is confined to a wet floor with dry insulation, when
the alternative site is unknown and the walk involves crossing water or moving on steep ground
in the dark, or when a member of the party is already cold enough that a wet, wind-exposed walk
would make things worse. Between those cases, the strongest argument for moving is that
conditions are still deteriorating.

Recovery afterwards has a clear order. Get the coldest person warm and dry first, using dry
insulation from anyone who has spare. Change into dry clothing even if it is thin, since dry
thin beats wet thick. Wring and body-dry synthetic insulation, which works surprisingly well,
and avoid trying to dry down in the field. Then, before anything else, apply the lesson: walk
the site in daylight, find where the water actually came from, and note what evidence was
present the previous afternoon that you did not read. That evidence is almost always there, and
it is the cheapest teacher available.

guides.safetyNote: Never camp in a dry wash, canyon floor, gully or any channel with scour marks or debris lodged above ground level: flash floods arrive from rain you cannot see, often with no warning and faster than you can run. If moving water in camp reaches ankle depth and is still rising, leave immediately for higher ground and leave the gear. Only 15 cm of moving water can knock an adult off their feet, and 30 cm will float most cars.

guides.title: Using Terrain for Wind Protection
guides.summary: How wind behaves over ridges, valleys, forests, snow, and open ground, and how to read and use that terrain to shelter a camp, a shelter, or yourself, including the hazards that sheltered ground trades in return.

sections.heading: Why wind protection can decide survival
sections.body: Of all the weather a person can face outdoors, wind is the most underestimated killer, because it does its work invisibly, by arithmetic. The human body loses heat to moving air by forced convection, and the rate of that loss climbs steeply with wind speed: moving air continuously strips away the thin blanket of warmed air that clings to skin and clothing, replacing it with cold air that must be warmed in turn. The wind chill index published jointly by the United States National Weather Service and Environment Canada since 2001 quantifies the effect on exposed skin. Air at 30 degrees Fahrenheit with a 20 mile per hour wind removes heat as fast as calm air at 17 degrees. At an air temperature of minus 5 Fahrenheit with a 30 mile per hour wind, the equivalent is roughly minus 31, and exposed flesh can freeze in about ten minutes. Cut that wind by three quarters, which good terrain routinely does, and the same air becomes survivable with ordinary clothing. Wind attacks in other ways as well. It multiplies the drying and cooling of wet clothing, since evaporation is also convection-driven, which is why a wet, windy 40 degree day kills more hikers than a calm day at zero. It tears at shelters: the force on a tent panel grows with the square of wind speed, so a 40 mile per hour gust pushes four times as hard as a 20 mile per hour breeze, and gusts in mountain terrain routinely double the average speed. It steals fire, scattering heat, flinging embers into dry fuel, and doubling or tripling stove fuel consumption; field trials with backpacking stoves show boil times stretching from four minutes to ten or worse in even a moderate unshielded breeze. It exhausts and demoralizes, because walking into a 30 mile per hour headwind can raise energy expenditure by a fifth, and the constant noise and buffeting degrade sleep, judgment, and fine motor control. The remedy costs nothing. Terrain, the shape of the ground and what grows and accumulates on it, modifies wind enormously over distances of a few meters. The lee of a boulder, the floor of a shallow swale, the inside of a spruce stand, or a spot eight wall-heights downwind of a ridge of snow can run at a quarter or less of the free wind speed, and the difference between camping in the wrong spot and the right one fifty meters away can be the difference between a torn tent and a quiet night. Using terrain well requires understanding three things: how wind actually behaves when it meets an obstacle, which is often contrary to intuition; how to read the permanent evidence of wind written into vegetation, snow, and sand; and what dangers sheltered ground trades in return, because the calmest places in the landscape collect cold air, snow, falling rock, and flood water. This guide takes each in turn.

sections.heading: How wind behaves near the ground
sections.body: Wind is a fluid in motion, and near the ground it obeys the physics of boundary layers. Far above the surface, air moves at the gradient speed set by large-scale pressure differences; at the surface itself, friction drags the speed toward zero. Between lies the atmospheric boundary layer, and within its lowest tens of meters wind speed increases roughly logarithmically with height above ground. The practical consequence is that conditions at head height are always gentler than at the ridgetop or at the treetops, and gentler still at ankle height: a wind measured at 20 miles per hour at the standard 10 meter weather-station height may be 13 or 14 at two meters over open grass, and a person lying prone experiences far less than a person standing. The rougher the surface, the steeper this gradient. Aerodynamicists describe surfaces by a roughness length: a few millimeters for smooth snow or mown grass, several centimeters for crops and low scrub, a meter or more for forest and broken rock, which is why the same synoptic wind that howls across a frozen lake merely sighs inside timber. Wind is also never steady. Friction and obstacles break the flow into turbulence, swirling eddies of many sizes, so the wind arrives as a mean speed plus gusts, and over rough terrain gusts commonly reach 1.5 to 2 times the mean. Structures and shelters fail in gusts, not averages, and any plan should assume them. Two more behaviors matter for shelter-seeking. First, air has inertia: when wind meets an obstacle it cannot turn instantly, so it separates from sharp edges, leaving behind zones of slow, recirculating air, the eddies that make the lee of an object calm, but also the rotors that make certain lees violently turbulent. Second, air is compressible in effect if not in fact: when terrain squeezes a flow, through a pass, between a cliff and a forest wall, over a crest, the same mass of air must pass through a smaller cross-section, so it accelerates, the same principle, named for the Italian physicist Giovanni Battista Venturi, that speeds water in a narrowed hose. Terrain therefore never merely blocks wind; it redistributes it, robbing speed from some places and paying it to others, and the skill lies in predicting which is which. Finally, wind direction near the ground is shaped by the terrain itself: valleys steer flow along their axes regardless of the free wind above, coastlines generate their own sea and land breezes on a daily cycle, and slopes manufacture their own winds by heating and cooling. A traveler who thinks of the forecast wind as a single arrow will be surprised constantly; one who thinks of it as water flowing over the landscape, pooling, spilling, accelerating through gaps, curling behind obstructions, can usually predict what the air will do in any given spot before feeling it.

sections.heading: The shape of a shelter zone: windward, leeward, and porosity
sections.body: Every object standing in wind, whether a boulder, a hedge, a snow wall, or a hill, creates a predictable pattern of disturbed flow, and decades of shelterbelt research, much of it from the agricultural stations of the American Great Plains and the Canadian prairies, has mapped that pattern in detail. The numbers are usually expressed in multiples of the barrier's height, written H, because the pattern scales: a two-meter wall and a twenty-meter tree line produce geometrically similar zones ten times different in size. Upwind of a barrier, air begins slowing before it arrives, pushed by the pressure that builds against the obstruction, producing a modest sheltered wedge extending roughly 2 to 5 H to windward. Downwind lies the main shelter zone. Behind a solid barrier, wind speed near the ground falls to a small fraction of the free stream in the first few heights, but the flow that jetted over the top curls back down in a strong recirculating eddy, so the calm is deep but short, and the zone from about 3 to 8 H can be gusty and reversed in direction; measurable protection is largely gone by 10 to 15 H. Behind a porous barrier, one that lets perhaps 40 to 60 percent of the flow bleed through, such as a belt of trees, a slatted fence, or a brush wall, the bleed flow prevents the over-the-top jet from slamming back to the surface, so the maximum wind reduction is somewhat less, but the protected zone stretches much farther, with useful reductions of 20 to 50 percent persisting to 15 or even 20 H, and the turbulence within it is far gentler. This is the single most useful quantitative rule in the subject: for a quiet camp close in, a solid barrier is fine at 1 to 3 H; for protecting a long area, moderate porosity beats solidity. Barrier length matters too, because wind wraps around ends: protection is only reliable in the middle of a barrier at least ten times as long as it is high, and behind anything short, the ends generate accelerated, swirling flow, which is why the corner of a building or the end of a rock outcrop is often the windiest place in the landscape. Orientation matters in the obvious way, maximum shelter when the barrier stands perpendicular to the wind, but oblique winds slide along a barrier and lose less speed, effectively lengthening the fetch. All of this applies identically at every scale, from a hand cupped around a match, to a sleeping position behind a log, to siting a cabin in the lee of a shelterbelt, and a person who internalizes the two canonical pictures, short deep calm behind solid objects, long moderate calm behind porous ones, with trouble at ends, tops, and 3 to 8 H behind solid walls, can read almost any situation.

sections.heading: Reading the landscape for prevailing wind
sections.body: The wind that matters for siting a shelter is not the breeze of the moment but the wind the place usually receives, and the landscape keeps honest records of it for anyone who learns to read them. Trees are the most legible archive. Persistent strong wind kills buds and desiccates growth on the windward side, so exposed trees grow asymmetric crowns streaming away from the prevailing direction, an effect called flagging or banner growth. Botanists grade it with the Griggs-Putnam index, a zero-to-seven scale developed in the 1970s for wind-energy prospecting, running from perfectly symmetrical crowns where mean winds are light, through brushing and moderate flagging near mean annual winds of 4 to 6 meters per second, to complete flagging, throwing, and finally carpet-like krummholz, from the German for crooked wood, the prostrate mat form that conifers adopt at timberline where wind and blowing ice prune anything that rises above the snowpack. A flagged tree is a compass that has been recording for decades: its bare side faces the prevailing wind, and finding several in agreement is strong evidence. Snow writes shorter-term but equally clear records. Drifts form in the lee of every obstruction, so the tails of drifts point downwind; sastrugi, the hard sculpted ridges of polar and alpine snowfields, lie parallel to the wind that carved them with their steep, undercut prows facing upwind; cornices, the overhanging waves of snow along ridgelines, always project over the lee side. Sand obeys the same physics: the gentle slope of a dune faces the wind that built it and the steep slip face lies downwind, and crescent barchan dunes stretch their horns downwind. Grass and sedge bend and stay bent after storms; lichen often favors the sheltered side of exposed rocks; on coasts, salt-pruned shrubbery slopes upward from the sea like a hedge trimmed by a giant. Even human artifacts testify: stock shelters, old farmsteads with their windbreak plantings, and the doors of older barns tend to turn their backs on the local prevailing wind. These permanent records must be combined with knowledge of the wind of the day, because weather systems bring wind from any quarter, and a camp perfectly sheltered from the prevailing westerly is exposed if tonight's storm blows from the southeast. The synthesis is straightforward: use the landscape record to understand the dominant pattern and the likely worst direction, use the sky and forecast to anticipate tonight's direction, and prefer sites sheltered from both, or sites that can be improved quickly if the wind swings. It is also worth remembering that mountain and valley terrain manufactures its own directions on a daily schedule regardless of the synoptic flow, upslope and up-valley by afternoon, downslope and down-valley by night, so in such country the record in the trees may reflect thermally driven winds as much as weather winds, and both must be planned for.

sections.heading: Ridges, gaps, and acceleration zones
sections.body: The most dangerous misreading of terrain is to treat high ground and gaps as neutral. They are not: terrain concentrates wind exactly where travelers most often want to walk and camp, and the acceleration is large. When wind crosses a ridge, the streamlines squeeze together over the crest and the flow speeds up, commonly by 50 to 100 percent over rounded hills and more over sharp ones, which is precisely why wind turbines are planted on crests. The zone of maximum speed is the crest itself and the upper windward slope; a tent pitched there endures both the acceleration and the strongest gustiness, and mountaineering accident reports are thick with camps destroyed on cols and summit plateaus. Saddles and passes are worse than they look. A pass is a gap in a barrier, and the pressure difference that builds between the windward and lee sides of a range drives air through the gap like water through a breach; gap winds in famous locations, the Columbia River Gorge separating Oregon and Washington, the passes of the Tehuantepec isthmus in Mexico, the mistral funneling down the Rhone valley between the Alps and the Massif Central, and the bora spilling through the gaps of the Dinaric Alps onto the Adriatic, routinely double or triple the regional wind and reach hurricane force in storms. The same physics operates at every scale: the notch between two knolls, the alley between two buildings, the gap between a cliff and a stand of timber, all are nozzles, and the acceleration is greatest in the narrowest section and for some distance downwind of it, where the jet spreads and breaks into turbulence. Canyons and gorges aligned with the wind channel and accelerate it similarly, and a bend in a canyon can hurl the jet against one wall while leaving the other calm. For the shelter-seeker the operational rules follow directly. Never camp in a saddle, a pass, or a notch unless there is truly no alternative, however inviting the flat ground; the flatness usually exists because wind sweeps it. Avoid the crest and the upper windward slope of any ridge; if high ground is unavoidable, the best of the bad options is usually a bench on the lee side several heights below the crest, beyond the immediate rotor zone. When traveling in strong wind, expect the worst blasts at crests and gaps, time movements between gusts, and lower your profile through the worst sections, because the force on a body scales with the square of speed and a gust that doubles the wind quadruples the push. Conversely, the concentration effect can be exploited deliberately: a fire needing draft, a wet garment needing drying, or a buggy camp needing insects blown away all benefit from a few minutes in an acceleration zone, provided the visit is on your terms and brief.

sections.heading: Valley winds: katabatic flows, cold pools, and the thermal belt
sections.body: Mountain and valley country runs a wind machine of its own, powered by the daily cycle of heating and cooling, and it works even when the weather map shows calm. By day, sun-warmed slopes heat the air touching them; the warm air rises along the slopes as anabatic wind, and by late morning a general up-valley wind develops, typically a moderate breeze strongest in the afternoon. By night the machine reverses with more consequence for the camper. Ground radiates heat away to a clear sky, the air in contact with it chills, becomes denser than the free air at the same altitude, and slides downhill under gravity as katabatic or drainage wind, from the Greek katabasis, a going down. Individual slope flows are gentle, but they gather in the drainage network exactly as water does, so by the small hours a steady cold river of air flows down every gully, ravine, and valley axis, strongest where the drainage is constricted, and it persists until morning sun rewarms the slopes. Where the terrain has the character of a basin or a dead-end valley floor, the cold air cannot drain away and instead pools, forming a cold pool or frost hollow in which temperature inversions of 10 to 20 degrees Celsius between the floor and the slopes a hundred meters higher are routinely measured on clear calm nights. The world's most extreme examples are limestone sinkholes: the Gstettneralm sinkhole in Austria has recorded temperatures near minus 53 Celsius, and Peter Sinks in Utah reached minus 56 Celsius in 1985, in both cases tens of degrees colder than the surrounding country that night. Above the pool, on the lower-middle slope, lies what fruit growers call the thermal belt, the band high enough to sit above the pooled cold air yet low enough to escape the stronger winds and colder absolute temperatures of the upper slopes; orchards and vineyards have been sited in it for centuries, and it is very often the best camping elevation in a valley as well. Glaciers add a special case: the air over ice is chilled all day, so glacier snouts exhale a persistent cold katabatic wind day and night, and in the great ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica the same mechanism scales up to relentless winds that can exceed hurricane force where the drainage converges, which is why polar travelers treat any camp in a katabatic outflow zone as a serious engineering problem. The operational summary for ordinary terrain: expect a down-valley breeze at night and plan fires, shelter doors, and smoke accordingly; do not camp on the floor of a basin, a frost hollow, or the axis of a gully on a clear night, both for cold and for the drainage wind itself; favor the thermal belt on a slope out of the drainage lines; and remember that valley-bottom calm at sunset says nothing about what the drainage will deliver at three in the morning.

sections.heading: The leeward slope: where the calm actually is
sections.body: Lee means the side away from the wind, and the lee of a hill is the obvious refuge, but the calm is not distributed the way intuition suggests, and finding it requires understanding flow separation. When wind crosses a gentle, rounded hill, the flow may stay attached, following the surface down the far side; the lee slope then receives wind only somewhat reduced, and the calmest air is found low on the slope and in the first valley beyond. When the crest is sharp or the lee slope steep, roughly steeper than one in four, the flow cannot follow; it separates at the crest, continuing more or less straight while a large, slowly rotating eddy fills the space below and behind. Inside that separation bubble the near-ground wind is light but unsteady and frequently reversed, blowing back toward the hill, a fact that surprises campers who feel wind in their faces while standing in the lee of the ridge that is supposedly protecting them, and that matters enormously for fire management, because smoke and embers in a lee eddy drift toward the slope, not away. Downwind of the bubble, where the separated flow reattaches to the ground, turbulence is at its worst, with strong erratic gusts from shifting directions; over big terrain in strong winds this structure organizes into true rotors, horizontal vortices downwind of mountain ranges that are violent enough to be charted as aviation hazards, and their ground-level signature is a band of chaotic gusts some distance out from the range front. The practical geometry for the shelter-seeker is therefore not simply behind the hill but specifically: close in under the steep lee, within the first two or three crest-heights, where the eddy is gentle, accepting the unsteady back-flow there; or well back, beyond roughly eight to ten heights, past the reattachment zone; and avoiding the middle band where reattachment gusts strike. Snow country adds two decisive cautions to the lee. Wind erodes snow from windward slopes and deposits it in the lee, so lee slopes carry wind slabs, dense cohesive layers loaded onto weaker snow, and lee deposition zones immediately below ridgelines are precisely where slab avalanches release most often; a lee camp in avalanche terrain must sit far from any slope of roughly 30 to 45 degrees and out of runout paths. Cornices, the snow waves projecting over the lee side of ridges, break farther back than they appear and fall on the lee slope, adding overhead hazard to it. In sand country, lee slip faces of dunes are soft, unstable, and prone to burying gear, though the hollow between dune arms is often an excellent camp. The refined instinct, then, is not lee equals safe, but read the crest: rounded and gentle means moderate shelter all down the back; sharp and steep means a calm pocket close in, chaos farther out, and in snow, a loaded slope that may be a trap rather than a refuge.

sections.heading: Boulders, outcrops, caves, and overhangs
sections.body: Rock features offer the most immediate wind protection in open country, and the rules for using them follow from the flow patterns around bluff bodies. A single large boulder creates a calm wedge on its windward base, where pressure piles air into stagnation, and a deeper calm pocket in its lee extending one to three boulder-heights downwind before the flow closes back in; the flanks, where the wind squeezes around, are accelerated, often noticeably windier than the open ground. The best bivouac position is therefore tight against the lee face, within about one height, with the understanding that eddying there can swirl light snow or sand over you, or against the windward base if the boulder overhangs enough to deflect flow overhead. Groups of boulders are better than singles, because their combined wakes overlap, and a field of large talus can offer nearly windless corridors, at the price of ankle-breaking travel and, in cold climates, cold air drainage settling among the stones. Rock outcrops and low cliffs act as solid barriers with all the caveats already described: deep calm close in, a turbulent reattachment zone farther out, wrap-around acceleration at the ends, and, at the top edge, a jet that makes the clifftop itself one of the worst places in the landscape. Two hazards attend camping under any steep rock. The first is falling material: freeze-thaw cycles pry rock loose, and the base of a cliff, the very place the wind shelter is best, is by definition the impact zone, so the overhead face should be inspected for perched blocks, fresh scars, and debris on the ground that testifies to recent falls, and camps moved out from under anything doubtful. The second is water: overhangs and cliff bases in canyon country often mark flood-carved terrain, and a sheltered alcove in a desert wash may lie in the path of a flash flood generated by rain fallen far away and hours before. Caves and deep overhangs deserve their own respect. They provide superb wind and precipitation shelter, but they belong to whatever lives there, snakes, spiders, rodents, bats, and occasionally larger animals, so entries deserve a slow inspection by light; their still air holds smoke, so an open fire inside a low or deep chamber can render it uninhabitable or dangerous within minutes, and carbon monoxide from any flame accumulates in poorly ventilated rock chambers; and in cold weather the rock itself, a massive conductor, will drain heat from a body lying on it far faster than soil, demanding thick insulation beneath. A shallow south-facing overhang with a high ceiling, a dry floor above any flood line, a clean face above it, and a fire built near the drip line where smoke can escape while heat reflects off the back wall, is the classic and genuinely excellent configuration, used by humans since the Paleolithic for exactly these reasons.

sections.heading: Forests, treelines, and living windbreaks
sections.body: Vegetation is terrain that grew, and for wind purposes it behaves as a porous barrier of enormous extent. Inside a closed-canopy forest, wind at head height typically runs at 10 to 25 percent of the speed over open ground nearby, and in dense conifer stands with low branching, near calm persists through all but the strongest storms; this is why forest camps are the default in wooded country and why winter travelers drop below treeline to camp almost regardless of the distance cost. The protection is not uniform. The windward edge of a forest takes the brunt, with the first 50 to 100 meters acting as the sacrificial rampart, and it is there that storm-thrown trees concentrate; the downwind edge experiences a modest jet as flow spills off the canopy; small clearings within the forest funnel and swirl wind; and large clearings behave as open ground. The safe, calm zone is the forest interior, several tree-heights in from any edge, and away from any gap aligned with the wind. The forest trades its shelter for one deadly serious hazard: falling timber. Dead standing trees, live trees with dead limbs, called widow-makers in the logging trade for exact reasons, and shallow-rooted species on wet or thin soils all come down preferentially in the very storms that drive a camper under cover, and deaths of campers in tents from tree fall occur every year in otherwise mild conditions. The camp drill is to look up before pitching: identify every stem and limb within striking radius, meaning anything whose height exceeds its distance from the bed, reject sites under dead wood, leaning trees, cracked forks, or fresh root heave, and prefer stands of young, uniform, deep-rooted trees over old broken ones. At the cold and windy limits of tree growth, vegetation itself records and offers refuge: the stunted, matted krummholz belts at alpine and arctic treeline, tuckamore in Newfoundland English, grow precisely where wind is fiercest, and a krummholz island's downwind side conceals genuinely calm pockets a meter high, enough for a bivouac when nothing else stands. Humans have long engineered living barriers on the same principles. The shelterbelt programs of the 1930s American plains, planted after the Dust Bowl under the Prairie States Forestry Project, set out some 220 million trees in belts whose measured effects match the porous-barrier science: a belt of height H with about half its face open reduces wind usefully from a few H upwind to 15 or more H downwind, cutting soil erosion, home heating costs, and livestock losses. A traveler can borrow any of these, hedgerows, farm windbreaks, plantation edges, remembering the geometry: the middle of a long belt beats the end, several meters in beats the exact edge, and the leeward 3 to 8 H zone is the prize. In every case the payment demanded is vigilance about what stands overhead.

sections.heading: Snow country: drifts, walls, and shelters that wind builds
sections.body: Snow changes the game twice over: it makes wind more dangerous, through wind chill, ground blizzard, and avalanche loading, and it supplies, uniquely, an unlimited stock of building material that wind itself has pre-compacted. Wind-worked snow sinters into a dense, carvable medium, and a wall cut from it is the fastest effective windbreak in nature. Polar and high-mountain practice is standardized: quarry blocks from a nearby drift with a snow saw or shovel, stack a wall one to one and a half meters high on the windward side of the tent at a distance of one to two wall-heights, longer than the tent by a generous margin because wind wraps ends, and expect the wall to buy a large reduction in wind load and spindrift at the cost of half an hour of labor. Two placement subtleties come straight from barrier aerodynamics. A wall too close couples the tent into the wall's own eddy and buries it in the drift that inevitably forms in the lee; a wall too far puts the tent in the reattachment gusts; and every barrier in blowing snow is also a drift-maker, so the wall must be positioned so that its drift, which grows downwind of it night by night, lands in front of the tent, not on it. The same drifting behavior explains both an opportunity and a trap in natural terrain: the lee of every rock, bank, and krummholz island carries a drift, and a deep, consolidated drift is the raw material for the two great snow shelters. The snow cave is dug into a steep drift or bank at least two meters deep, entrance low, sleeping platform high so that the coldest air drains out the door, roof a hand's-length to an arm's-length thick and dome-shaped for strength. The quinzhee, from the Athabaskan, is built where no drift exists by piling loose snow into a mound two to three meters high, letting it sinter for one to two hours while the disturbed crystals bond, then hollowing it out. Both exploit snow's remarkable insulation, holding interior temperatures near freezing regardless of the storm outside, and both silence wind completely, a psychological relief that anyone who has spent a night in a flogging tent will value at its true worth. Both also impose the same non-negotiable rules: keep a ventilation hole open and maintained, never run a stove inside without generous ventilation because carbon monoxide kills quietly in snow shelters most seasons somewhere, mark the shelter's location, and dig with your body low so a collapse during construction leaves your airway clear. The lethal caveat overhanging all of it is avalanche terrain. The drifts and lee deposits that make the best quarries and cave sites form by the same loading that creates wind slabs, so the siting question must always be asked in this order: is this slope, or anything above it that could reach me, steeper than about 30 degrees, and is it loaded? Only after a no does snow-craft begin.

sections.heading: Coasts, plains, and deserts: shelter where the land looks flat
sections.body: The hardest wind problems are the landscapes with no obvious lee at all: open coast, prairie, steppe, tundra, and desert. The solution in all of them is the same shift of scale: stop scanning the horizon for a wall and start reading micro-relief, because a meter of vertical difference is a fortune when the wind owns everything taller. On plains and tundra, the land is corrugated with swales, stream cuts, buffalo wallows, dry ditches, and the banks of even trivial watercourses; a coulee two meters deep with the wind blowing across it holds near-calm air at its floor, and simply lying in a plow furrow or behind a field bund halves the wind over a sleeping body. Cutbanks, the small eroded cliffs on the outside of stream bends, give true vertical shelter, with the usual cautions about camping in any channel that can carry water and about undercut banks collapsing. Isolated objects are precious: a single erratic boulder, a stock tank, a line of fence brush, a grain bale, each casts a usable wake sized by its height. In true shortgrass or snow-covered prairie with nothing at all, the answer is to make relief: dig a shallow trench for the body, bank the spoil windward, and the effective wind at skin level drops dramatically, a technique as old as soldiers and shepherds. On coasts, wind arrives with a long fetch over water, uninterrupted, salt-laden, and often on a daily rhythm, onshore sea breeze by afternoon as the land heats, offshore land breeze at night, superimposed on whatever the weather is doing. The shelter assets are the back sides of foredunes, the hollows between dune ridges, driftwood accumulations above the wrack line, and the vegetation line where salt-pruned scrub begins; the constraints are that a camp must sit above the reach of the tide, including the larger spring tides near new and full moon and any storm surge, that dry loose sand anchors nothing and demands buried deadman anchors rather than pegs, and that the lee of a dune, like all sharp-crested lees, swirls fine sand into everything while remaining far better than the crest. Deserts combine the plains and coastal problems and add heat: shade may matter more than wind by day, while clear skies make nights cold and drainage winds real among mesas and canyons. Dune fields offer generous shelter in their interdune hollows and lee slopes; slot canyons and washes offer superb wind protection and must be refused anyway whenever regional rain is possible, because flash floods travel far from their storms and arrive as a wall. Dust and sand storms, haboobs on the desert margins, reverse the usual instinct: the ground-hugging blast is worst near the surface obstacle field, and the practical drill is to get behind any solid mass available, seal eyes and airway with cloth, orient feet toward the wind, and wait it out low rather than walking blind.

sections.heading: Micro-siting a camp: putting the principles together
sections.body: Choosing the actual square meters where a shelter stands is the moment all the theory cashes out, and it is worth a deliberate ten minutes even at the end of an exhausting day, because no amount of guyline heroics fixes a bad site at two in the morning. The sequence that follows condenses the craft. First establish the wind of the night, not merely the wind of the moment: the forecast if one exists, the sky if not, the permanent record in trees, drifts, and dunes for the prevailing pattern, and in mountain country the expectation of down-valley drainage after dark. Then survey candidate features with the barrier geometry in mind, the middles of long barriers rather than ends, distances of one to three barrier-heights behind solid objects or several heights within porous ones, out of saddles, off crests, above valley-floor cold pools, and audit every candidate for the tolls sheltered ground charges: what can fall from above, what can flow through in water or cold air, what has been loaded above it in snow.
