Test the finalist by standing in it and feeling, or by watching thrown grass, dust, or a strip of flagging tape held at shelter height, remembering that a brief calm proves little in gusty flow. Only then pitch, and pitch for the gusts, not the average: the tail or lowest, strongest aspect of the tent into the expected wind, the door on the lee side or quartered away, so that opening it does not turn the shelter into a scoop, every guyline rigged before the wind demands it, anchors matched to the ground, pegs in loam, rocks and deadmen in sand and snow, and everything loose either inside, weighted, or tied, because gear blows away in exactly the gust that flattens the stove. Fire and smoke belong downwind of living space but within the sheltered zone, with an ember-fall watch downwind of the fire itself. Sleep slightly elevated above the very lowest ground so cold air and any rain runoff drain past rather than pooling under the bed. Finally, plan the failure before sleeping: know which way the wind is most likely to swing, identify the fallback spot or the re-rig that a swing would demand, and keep headlamp, gloves, and spare cord where hands can find them in the dark.
steps: 1. Determine tonight's likely wind direction and strength from forecast, sky, and the terrain's permanent wind records, and assume gusts near double the average.
2. Shortlist sheltered features: mid-barrier lees, forest interiors, swales, thermal-belt benches; reject saddles, crests, gully floors, and basin bottoms.
3. Audit each candidate overhead and upslope: dead limbs, perched rock, cornices, loaded snow slopes, and any channel that could carry flood water.
4. Feel-test the finalist at shelter height with thrown grass or flagging tape, allowing for gust cycles before trusting a calm.
5. Pitch lowest-and-strongest aspect to windward, door leeward, all guylines rigged, anchors matched to soil, sand, or snow.
6. Place fire downwind of the shelter, secure every loose item, sleep slightly above the lowest ground, and stage light, gloves, and cord for a night re-rig.

sections.heading: Improving on nature: built windbreaks that extend terrain
sections.body: Natural shelter is rarely perfect, and the highest form of the craft is hybrid construction: letting terrain do most of the work and building the missing piece. The physics already described dictates the designs. A built windbreak of height H protects usefully for roughly five to eight H downwind if solid, longer if porous, so even a knee-high wall meaningfully shelters a sleeping body, and a chest-high wall shelters a tent; the labor question is only ever where the material is and how fast it stacks. In stone country, a drystone crescent one meter high against an existing boulder closes the wrap-around flow at the boulder's flanks, converting a mediocre single-object lee into a genuine pocket; the crescent's horns should curl downwind, and the courses should lean slightly into the wind for stability, with the biggest stones at the base and ends, where gusts pry hardest. In forest and brush country, a lattice of stakes driven upright with brush, boughs, or bark woven through it makes a barrier of exactly the 40 to 60 percent porosity that the shelterbelt studies favor, gentler in its lee than any solid wall and far faster to build than one; piled slash and root wads work cruder but faster. In snow, quarried blocks are the premium material, as treated at length elsewhere in this guide, but even shoveled loose snow banked against a tent's windward wall adds real protection within minutes. On sand and gravel, where nothing stacks, the answer is to dig rather than build, lowering the living space instead of raising a wall, and to anchor fabric structures with buried deadmen, stuff sacks or sticks buried horizontally with the guyline girth-hitched to their middles, which hold in loose ground where pegs will not. Fabric itself extends terrain: a tarp pitched as a steep lean-to with its low edge staked hard to windward and its face quartering the wind turns a mediocre lee into a dry, calm room, while the same tarp pitched broadside and high becomes a sail that will destroy itself, so the rule is low, taut, small angles to the flow, and no large flat faces presented to gusts. Vehicles, sledges, and canoes are prefabricated windbreaks, and parking or overturning one to windward of a bivouac is standard practice in open country, with the caution that vehicles rock in gusts and drift badly in blowing snow, so the sleeping position belongs clear of any direction the object could shift. Two general construction rules close the subject. First, every barrier you build is also a drift-and-eddy maker: in blowing snow or sand it will bury its own lee, so position the structure so accumulation lands where you want it, never on the door. Second, build for double the current wind, because the night that needed a windbreak at dusk usually needs a better one by midnight, and adding a course of stone by headlamp is miserable exactly in proportion to how little was added in daylight.

sections.heading: The price of calm: hazards that sheltered ground collects
sections.body: Everything that stops wind collects something else, and the experienced eye audits every sheltered site for what it gathers. Cold is the first toll. The calmest air in any landscape on a clear night is also the coldest, because the same stillness that spares a camp from wind chill lets radiatively chilled air pool undisturbed; hollows, gully floors, and walled basins routinely run 5 to 15 degrees Celsius colder than slopes a short climb above, and the wind-sheltered floor of a frost hollow can be the coldest spot for miles. The remedy is elevation in moderation: the thermal-belt bench a few tens of meters above the drainage floor keeps most of the wind protection and sheds the pooled cold. Falling material is the second toll. Lees are lees because something stands above them, and what stands above sheds: dead limbs and whole stems in forest, pried blocks under cliffs, cornice fragments and slab avalanches under loaded ridgelines, and the audit is always upward and upslope, asking what can reach this spot and what has already reached it, since fresh debris on the ground is the terrain's own accident report. Water is the third. Wind-sheltered channels, washes, alcoves, and canyon floors are sheltered precisely because flowing water carved them, and they remain its property; flash floods in desert systems arrive from storms too distant to see or hear, so the rule is absolute rather than judgment-based: do not sleep in a wash or slot when rain is possible anywhere in the catchment, and read every bank for the high-water line of debris and stain before trusting ground below it. Snow burial is the fourth: every barrier in blowing snow grows a drift in its lee at rates that can exceed a foot per hour in ground blizzard, so a too-close snow wall, cutbank, or boulder can entomb a tent by morning, and doors and vents must be sited and re-cleared with drift growth in mind. Stagnant air itself is the fifth toll. The stillness that comforts also fails to carry away smoke, stove exhaust, and carbon monoxide, and it concentrates them in exactly the pockets, caves, snow shelters, deep hollows, tight tent vestibules, where wind protection is best; carbon monoxide is odorless, and cooking in an unventilated sheltered space is a leading cause of backcountry poisoning deaths, so ventilation is a design requirement of every calm camp, not an option. Insects are the sixth, in season: mosquitoes and blackflies are weak fliers that wind suppresses, so the windless pocket that would be paradise in October is torment in June, and summer campers in fly country often deliberately choose breezy knolls, accepting wind to escape bites. Lightning, finally, complicates storm shelter: the tall isolated tree and the cliff base offer wind refuge and are respectively a strike target and a ground-current path, so in electrical storms the crouch belongs in low, uniform cover away from both. None of these tolls forbids sheltered ground; each simply has a price tag that must be read before paying.

sections.heading: When the wind shifts: failure modes and recovery
sections.body: Wind protection fails in predictable ways, and the difference between an anecdote and an emergency is usually whether the failure was anticipated. The commonest failure is directional shift. Wind is not a fixed property of the night: frontal passages swing it, often abruptly and by large angles, in the northern hemisphere characteristically from southerly quarters ahead of a cold front to west or northwest behind it, with the strongest gusts arriving at the change itself; thermally driven mountain winds reverse on schedule at morning and evening; and sea breezes swing onshore by afternoon. A camp perfectly sheltered from the evening wind can be perfectly exposed by the shift, which is why the siting drill includes asking where the wind goes next and why all-around defilade, a swale, a forest interior, a boulder cluster, outranks a single wall facing a single direction. The signs of a coming enforcement are readable: pressure falling, cloud lowering and thickening, the wind backing and freshening, lenticular clouds capping ridges in mountain country, and a rising roar in the trees upwind that arrives seconds before the gust does. The second failure is underestimating growth: wind that doubles quadruples its force, so a shelter adequate at dusk fails at midnight not by degrees but suddenly, when a panel, peg, or pole crosses its load limit. The countermeasures are engineering margins set in daylight, double anchors windward, low profiles, and the discipline of re-rigging at the first flap rather than the fifth, because fabric that has begun to luff hammers its own stitching and its anchors with impact loads far beyond the static push. When a shelter does fail in strong wind, the priorities are sequence-critical: secure yourself and insulation first, since sleeping bags and pads blow away faster than they can be chased; collapse the shelter deliberately rather than letting it thrash itself to rags, kneeling on it and pulling poles; then either re-rig low, a flattened tarp weighted with rock and snow over a body is a survivable shelter in almost anything, or move to the pre-identified fallback. Moving in violent wind is its own hazard, and the decision rule is honest triage: move if the present site is dangerous, from tree fall, drift burial, rising water, or hopeless exposure, and the fallback is close and known; stay and dig in if travel means stumbling in the dark through blowdown toward a guess, since a bad night in a degraded shelter is recoverable and a fall or separation from gear may not be. Rehearsal converts all of this from prose to reflex: practicing a storm re-rig in daylight, once, teaches more than any text, and the habit of glancing at every camp with the question of what the wind would have to do to make this site wrong is, in the end, the entire skill of using terrain compressed into a single reflex.

guides.safetyNote: Sheltered terrain collects its own hazards: never camp under dead limbs, loaded snow slopes, cornices, or unstable rock; never sleep in washes, slots, or gully floors when rain is possible anywhere upstream; keep ventilation open in caves, snow shelters, and closed tents whenever anything burns, because carbon monoxide is odorless and lethal; and treat any lee slope steeper than about 30 degrees in snow country as potential avalanche terrain.

guides.title: Slope Aspect and Solar Warmth
guides.summary: Why the compass direction a slope faces controls how much solar heat it receives, and how to read and use aspect — for warmer campsites, safer snow travel, better growing sites, and smarter shelter and building placement.

sections.heading: Why the direction a slope faces matters
sections.body: Stand in a mountain valley on a clear late-winter morning and you will often see two different seasons on the two walls: one side bare, brown, and steaming as frost burns off, the other still locked under snow, dark with dense conifers. Nothing about the rock or the weather differs between them. What differs is aspect — the compass direction toward which each slope faces — and aspect decides how directly, how long, and at what time of day the sun strikes the ground. That single geometric fact drives differences that matter to almost every outdoor decision a person makes. Aspect determines which campsite thaws your boots and which keeps them frozen, which slope sheds its snow by March and which holds avalanche-prone layers into May, which hillside grows grapes and which grows moss, which house needs half the heating fuel of its neighbor across the valley. The temperature difference between opposing aspects is not subtle: on mid-latitude mountains, surface soil on the sunny side can run five to fifteen degrees Celsius warmer at midday than the shaded side a few hundred meters away, and the growing season may differ by several weeks. Ecologists have long treated a slope's aspect as one of the strongest predictors of what lives on it, so strong that many mountain languages carry ordinary words for the two sides: in the French and Swiss Alps the sunny side is the adret and the shaded side the ubac; Spanish uses solana and umbría; and settlement maps of the Alps show villages, fields, and orchards clustered on the adret while the ubac was left to forest. The underlying rule is simple to state. In the northern hemisphere the sun spends its day in the southern half of the sky, so south-facing slopes lean toward the sun and receive its rays more squarely, while north-facing slopes lean away and receive them at a grazing angle or not at all. In the southern hemisphere the geometry mirrors: north-facing slopes are the warm ones. East-facing ground gets its sun in the morning, west-facing ground in the afternoon, and that timing difference has its own consequences for frost, drying, and comfort. Everything else in this subject is the working-out of that rule — how strong the effect is at a given latitude and season, how slope steepness amplifies or defeats it, how it interacts with wind, cold-air drainage, and cloud, and how to read it quickly from a map, from vegetation, or from the sun itself. The reward for learning it is a kind of quiet competence: the ability to look at terrain and know, before you touch it, where warmth will pool and where cold will linger. For someone choosing a survival shelter site in the cold, that knowledge can be worth more than any single piece of equipment, because it costs nothing, weighs nothing, and works every clear day the sun comes up.

sections.heading: The sun's path: elevation, azimuth, season, and latitude
sections.body: To reason about aspect you need a working model of where the sun actually is, and the model has only a few moving parts. The sun's position at any moment is described by two angles: elevation, its height above the horizon, and azimuth, its compass bearing. Both change through the day and through the year in a pattern fixed by latitude and by the tilt of Earth's axis, which is about 23.44 degrees. Because of that tilt, the latitude at which the noon sun stands directly overhead migrates annually between the Tropic of Cancer at 23.44 degrees north, reached at the June solstice, and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.44 degrees south, reached at the December solstice, crossing the equator at the March and September equinoxes. A remarkably useful formula follows: the sun's elevation at solar noon equals ninety degrees minus your latitude plus the solar declination, where declination is the latitude the sun stands over that day, positive when north. Worked examples make it concrete. At 45 degrees north — roughly Ottawa, Milan, or the U.S.-Canada border in the west — the noon sun at the June solstice stands at 90 minus 45 plus 23.44, about 68 degrees, high overhead; at the equinoxes it stands at 45 degrees; at the December solstice at 90 minus 45 minus 23.44, barely 21.6 degrees above the southern horizon. Winter, precisely when warmth matters most, is when the sun is lowest — and a low sun is exactly the condition under which aspect matters most, because a slope tilted toward a low sun can nearly face it square-on while flat ground catches only a glancing blow. Azimuth behaves just as systematically. At mid-northern latitudes the sun rises exactly east and sets exactly west only at the equinoxes; in summer it rises well north of east and sets north of west, taking a long high arc through the southern sky; in winter it rises south of east and sets south of west, taking a short low arc. Day length swings with the arc, from around fifteen and a half hours at midsummer to under nine hours at midwinter at 45 degrees latitude, with the swings growing more extreme toward the poles and vanishing at the equator. Two consequences for terrain follow directly. First, a slope facing the equator — south in the northern hemisphere — faces the sun's entire daily arc in winter and so collects nearly all the direct sunlight the day offers; a pole-facing slope steeper than the sun's noon elevation receives no direct sun at all for weeks or months, sitting in continuous shadow. Second, near the equator the sun is high year-round and passes north of overhead for part of the year and south of it for the rest, so aspect contrast is weak and seasonal in the tropics, while at high latitudes the contrast is enormous. Local solar noon, when the sun crosses your meridian at its daily highest, rarely matches clock noon — time zones, daylight saving, and the equation of time shift it — but shadows point their shortest at that moment, which makes it findable without instruments.

sections.heading: The physics of warmth: the cosine law and the atmosphere
sections.body: The warmth a surface gains from the sun comes down to one dominant piece of geometry and two smaller atmospheric effects. The geometry is Lambert's cosine law: the power a surface intercepts from a beam of light is proportional to the cosine of the angle between the beam and the surface's perpendicular. A surface facing the sun dead-on collects the full beam; tilt it and the same beam spreads over a larger area, diluting the energy per square meter. Above the atmosphere sunlight delivers about 1361 watts per square meter, the solar constant; after clear-sky absorption and scattering, roughly 1000 watts per square meter reaches the ground when the sun is high. Now apply the law to terrain. At 45 degrees north on the winter solstice the noon sun stands about 21.6 degrees above the horizon. Flat ground receives the beam diluted to the sine of 21.6 degrees, about 37 percent of face-on intensity. A slope inclined 25 degrees toward the sun presents itself at 21.6 plus 25, about 46.6 degrees, and receives the sine of that, about 73 percent — essentially double the energy per square meter of the flat field beside it, from identical sunshine. A north-facing 25-degree slope, by contrast, would need the sun 25 degrees up just to be grazed edge-on; at a 21.6-degree noon sun it receives no direct beam whatsoever, only diffuse skylight, which on a clear winter day may amount to barely a tenth of the direct beam's power. This is the entire secret of aspect in one calculation: at low sun angles, modest slopes double their solar income or forfeit it entirely. The atmospheric effects sharpen the contrast. Sunlight reaching a low sun must traverse a longer slant path through air — path length grows roughly as one over the sine of elevation, so a sun at 20 degrees shines through nearly three times the air mass of an overhead sun — losing more energy to scattering and absorption; low-angle sun is therefore weaker per beam as well as more diluted per square meter. Second, what the ground does with absorbed energy depends on the surface: fresh snow reflects 80 to 90 percent of incoming sunlight, dry soil perhaps 15 to 30 percent, dark rock and conifer forest less than 15, so a snow-covered slope resists warming until something exposes darker material, after which absorption, melt, and further exposure feed each other — one reason snow cover often collapses quickly once it starts to go. Finally, sunshine hours integrate the whole story: over a clear midwinter day at mid-latitudes, an open equator-facing mountainside can absorb several times the total solar energy of its pole-facing twin, and that daily surplus, repeated for months, is what builds the biological and human geography of sunny and shady sides. Cloud, of course, taxes everything: under heavy overcast nearly all light arrives diffusely from the whole sky dome, and the aspect advantage shrinks toward zero, a point that matters in chronically cloudy regions.

sections.heading: Hemisphere rules: equator-facing and pole-facing ground
sections.body: The most important practical vocabulary in this subject is the pair equator-facing and pole-facing, because the familiar shorthand about south slopes silently assumes the northern hemisphere and will mislead you badly south of the equator. The rule that always works: the warm aspect faces the equator, the cold aspect faces the pole. In the northern hemisphere the equator lies to the south, so south, southeast, and southwest aspects are the solar collectors and north-facing ground is the cold store. In the southern hemisphere — Patagonia, New Zealand, southern Africa, Australia — the sun tracks through the northern sky, so north-facing slopes are the warm ones, a reversal that northern-trained hikers, gardeners, and builders forget at real cost: the classic error is an Australian house built with its big windows facing south out of imported European habit, collecting no winter sun at all. Between the tropics the picture softens: the noon sun stands north of overhead for part of the year and south of it for the rest, so no aspect is reliably the sunny one year-round and other factors — rain-bearing winds, cloud patterns, elevation — usually dominate site choice. Poleward of the polar circles the geometry goes to extremes: in midwinter the sun never rises and aspect briefly means nothing; in spring and autumn, with the sun skimming the horizon for long hours, even gentle equator-facing tilts capture dramatic energy advantages. The strength of the equator-facing advantage peaks in the mid-latitudes, roughly 35 to 60 degrees, where winter sun is low but present — which is also where most of the world's population lives. The advantage also has a seasonal shape worth internalizing: it is largest in winter, when the sun is low and every degree of favorable tilt counts; moderate at the equinoxes; and smallest in high summer, when the sun rides high enough that flat ground and most slopes are all well lit — indeed in summer a steep equator-facing slope at noon can receive slightly less than a moderately tilted one, because the high sun overshoots it. The compass fine-structure matters too. Due-equator aspects maximize total daily energy. Aspects rotated toward the east get their share early, warming quickly after dawn and going shady by mid-afternoon; aspects rotated toward the west start cold and collect their heat in the afternoon, on top of air already warmed by the day, which is why in many climates the hottest, driest microsites are southwest-facing in the northern hemisphere and northwest-facing in the southern. Pole-facing ground has its own uses precisely because it is cold and stable: it holds snow for late-season water and skiing, shelters heat-intolerant plants, keeps root cellars and food caches cool, and in hot climates the shaded aspect is the livable one — an inversion of preference that reminds you aspect is not about seeking warmth in itself, but about knowing where the sun's energy goes so you can seek or avoid it deliberately.

sections.heading: Morning slopes and afternoon slopes: the east-west asymmetry
sections.body: If equator-versus-pole is the first axis of aspect, east-versus-west is the second, and it is a story about timing rather than totals. Over a full clear day, an east-facing and a west-facing slope of equal steepness receive nearly identical amounts of solar energy — the sun's morning and afternoon arcs are mirror images. What differs is when the energy arrives and what the air is doing at the time, and those differences are large enough to feel on your skin and read in the vegetation. An east-facing slope takes the sun's beam from shortly after sunrise, when the air is at its coldest and everything is wet with dew or frost. Its mornings are therefore kind: tents warm early, frozen boots soften, wet gear dries, frost burns off in the first hours. But its heat input ends by early afternoon, and it faces away from the warmest part of the day, so its afternoons and evenings cool early. A west-facing slope inverts the schedule: it sits cold and shaded through the morning, sometimes holding frost hours after the valley's east wall is bare, then receives its full solar dose through the afternoon, when air temperature is already near its daily peak. Afternoon sun on top of warm air makes west aspects the thermal extreme of the day — in hot climates the punishing side, in cold climates the side where snow turns sloppy and wet avalanches release late in the day. The asymmetry has a second driver: atmospheric moisture. Mornings tend to be clearer; afternoons breed convective cloud and thunderstorms, especially in mountains in summer. East slopes thus often collect their sunshine before the clouds build, while west slopes lose part of theirs to afternoon overcast — a systematic bias that in some mountain climates makes east aspects the sunnier ones in total, not just the earlier ones. Ecologically, the west and southwest aspects in the northern hemisphere are typically the driest and most fire-prone, because their heat arrives when evaporation is most efficient; the combination of afternoon sun and daytime wind pulls more moisture from soil and plants than the same energy delivered at dawn would. Practical consequences follow. For a campsite in cold weather, an easterly component to your aspect buys the thing you want most: early warmth at the hour you break camp. For drying gear at midday or stretching warmth into the evening — around a fixed shelter you will occupy at day's end — a westerly component serves better. Fruit growers have long favored gentle east and southeast slopes for blossom-frost country, partly for early warming, though gradual thawing is a subtler business: rapid morning thaw of frozen tissue can itself injure blossom, and some growers prefer sites that warm progressively. For water, the shaded morning side holds snowbanks and seeps later into the season. None of this changes total energy much; it changes the schedule — and in the field, the schedule is often what you are actually living by.

sections.heading: Slope steepness meets aspect: tilting toward the sun
sections.body: Aspect says which way a slope leans; steepness says how far, and the two multiply. A useful way to think about it is effective latitude: tilting ground toward the equator makes its sun geometry behave like ground at a lower latitude, and tilting it poleward like ground at a higher one, degree for degree. A 30-degree south-facing meadow at 47 degrees north intercepts the noon sun the way flat ground at 17 degrees north does — Caribbean geometry in the Alps, which is why alpine haymeadows and vineyards on steep adrets ripen crops their valley floors cannot. A 30-degree north-facing slope at the same spot behaves at noon like flat ground at 77 degrees north, well inside the Arctic Circle, and its ecology says so. The amplification is strongest when the sun is low. In midwinter at mid-latitudes, each degree of equator-ward tilt adds roughly two to three percent to noon beam intensity in the range where most real hillsides fall, which is why even a 10-degree rise behind a campsite noticeably changes the feel of a January noon. There is a geometric optimum: a surface catches the maximum possible noon beam when its tilt equals the angle between the sun and the zenith — for the winter-solstice noon sun at 45 degrees north, that is a slope of about 68 degrees, essentially a cliff face, which explains the surprising warmth of sunlit rock walls in winter and why climbers find bare dry rock on south faces while the gullies beside them hold ice. For year-round energy collection the practical compromise is familiar from solar-panel design: a tilt roughly equal to latitude maximizes annual capture, tilting latitude plus about fifteen degrees favors winter, latitude minus fifteen favors summer. Steepness also controls shadowing. A pole-facing slope steeper than the sun's noon elevation is in total shadow all day; at 45 degrees north that threshold is about 21.6 degrees at the winter solstice, and slopes of that pitch are everywhere in hill country, so whole hillsides go sunless from November to February. Deep valleys add horizon shadowing on every aspect: a wall to your equator side can bury even a perfectly oriented site in shade for months — mountain towns like Rjukan in Norway famously lose direct sun for half the year to the ridge above them — so the real question is never aspect alone but the whole sky view: which way you lean, how steeply, and what stands between you and the sun's winter arc. Very steep terrain brings one more warmth-relevant behavior: slopes above roughly 35 to 40 degrees shed snow continuously in small sluffs rather than accumulating deep slabs, while their bases collect the debris; the warm-looking sunlit bowl at the cliff foot may thus carry both extra sun and extra tons of relocated snow. Aspect, pitch, horizon, and what falls from above must be read together.

sections.heading: Microclimates: how aspect writes local temperature and moisture
sections.body: The energy differences between aspects turn into microclimates — persistent local departures from the regional weather — and the mechanism runs through the ground itself. Sunlight absorbed at the surface heats the top layer of soil or rock; the surface re-radiates and conducts that heat to the air above it, so near-ground air temperature tracks surface heating far more closely than the free atmosphere does. On a clear winter midday, the few centimeters of air above sunlit dark soil can run ten degrees Celsius or more above the shaded equivalent across the valley, and the soil itself stores part of the surplus, re-releasing it after sunset so the sunny slope's evening lasts longer. Season by season the surpluses integrate into different local climates on what the map shows as one place. The warm aspect's soil thaws and dries out weeks earlier in spring, reaches higher summer maxima, and refreezes later in autumn; its snow-free season and its frost-free growing season are both extended, in mid-latitude hill country commonly by two to six weeks relative to the pole-facing side. Moisture follows temperature with a twist: the sunny slope receives the same precipitation but loses far more of it, because evaporation from soil and transpiration through plants scale steeply with surface temperature and sunshine. The equator-facing slope is therefore not just the warm side but the dry side — thinner soils, sparser litter, more drought stress, more wildfire — while the pole-facing slope, cool and shaded, keeps its moisture: deeper humus, denser shade-tolerant forest, moss, seeps that run into summer. Ecologists measuring opposing aspects in temperate ranges routinely find the shaded slope's soil moisture half again or more that of the sunny slope in late summer, a bigger biological difference than the temperature gap itself. The dryness feedback can even invert expectations: in semi-arid mountains the warm aspect may carry only sparse grass and rock while the cold aspect carries the trees, since water, not warmth, is the binding constraint. Aspect microclimates also govern freeze-thaw behavior, which matters for more than comfort. The sunny side cycles through freezing repeatedly in winter — thawing by day, refreezing at night — which pries rock apart, heaves soil, ices trails glaze-smooth by morning, and rots snow into melt-freeze crusts; the shaded side may stay continuously frozen for months, preserving powder snow, firm trails, and intact ice. Human comfort sits inside these same gradients. A shelter dug into the base of an equator-facing slope enjoys radiant heat from the warmed ground behind it; laundry dries on the sunny side while it mildews on the shaded one; and the difference in perceived warmth between sitting in winter sun and sitting in adjacent shade — often felt as fifteen degrees, though the air temperature is identical — is direct radiant heating of your body, the same cosine law applied to skin and clothing. Learning to see terrain as a mosaic of these small climates, rather than as one place with one weather, is the core skill this subject teaches.

sections.heading: Reading aspect in plants, snow, and soil
sections.body: Terrain broadcasts its aspect through what grows and lingers on it, and a practiced eye can read compass direction from a hillside miles away. The signals are most honest at the scale of whole slopes; any single tree or boulder can be an exception. Vegetation contrast is the loudest signal in temperate latitudes. In the northern hemisphere, pole-facing slopes hold the moisture-loving, shade-tolerant community: dense conifers such as spruce, fir, and hemlock, thick moss and fern understories, deep leaf litter. Equator-facing slopes carry the drought-tolerant, light-hungry community: open pine or oak woodland, grass, sagebrush and other scrub in dry country, thin rocky soils. Where a valley runs east-west the contrast is often visible as a hard line — solid dark forest on one wall, open savanna on the other. The famous rule that moss grows on the north side of trees is this same physics applied to a cylinder: the shaded, damp side favors moss — but a single trunk's shading is contaminated by leaning, overhanging canopy, and prevailing rain-bearing wind, so treat moss as a weak vote, never a verdict, and poll many trees before believing it. Snow is the second great indicator, and in winter and spring it is close to a printed map of insolation. Snow lingers on pole-facing slopes and in shaded hollows weeks after equator-facing slopes are bare; late-season snow patches mark the coldest aspects and the terrain that shades them. Watch also the texture: sun-cupped, refrozen, dirty snow speaks of strong sun exposure and melt cycles, while cold dry powder persisting on one aspect tells you that side has stayed shaded. On big mountains the pattern extends upward: the elevation of the snowline on a given day is typically hundreds of meters higher on the sunny aspect, and glaciers in each hemisphere cluster on the poleward and shaded quadrants. Soil and rock carry quieter signatures. The sunny aspect's soil is paler, drier, often thinner, with bare patches and more surface stone; the shaded aspect's is darker and more organic. Lichens paint rocks differently by moisture and light, and in freeze-prone country the sunny side shows more frost-shattered talus, since it cycles through zero degrees far more often. Human land use is a readable proxy too, because generations of farmers performed this analysis before you: vineyards, orchards, terraced fields, haymeadows, and old villages sit on the adret; timber lots, and in hot countries the summer pastures and shade crops, sit on the ubac. Even animal behavior votes — grazing animals favor sunny slopes in cold weather and shaded ones in heat, game trails contour accordingly, and south-facing rock outcrops are where reptiles bask. Reading these signs together gives you a compass that works under overcast, at night with snowpatches faintly visible, or on a map's vegetation and land-use symbols — and, run in reverse, it lets you predict from a compass bearing what growth, snow, water, and footing you will find on a slope before you commit to it.

sections.heading: Snowpack and avalanche: aspect as a safety variable
sections.body: Nowhere does aspect carry higher stakes than in snow country, because the same solar geometry that makes one slope pleasant makes another one lethal, and the pattern flips with the season. In winter, the danger concentrates on the shaded aspects. Pole-facing and heavily shaded slopes stay cold, and a cold shallow snowpack develops strong temperature gradients between the relatively warm ground and the frigid surface; water vapor migrating along that gradient rebuilds snow grains into large, cohesionless faceted crystals and depth hoar — sugar-like layers with almost no strength. Bury such a layer under subsequent storms and you have a persistent weak layer: a slab avalanche waiting for a trigger, and one that can stay triggerable for weeks or months precisely because the shaded slope never gets the warmth that would heal it. This is why mid-winter avalanche accidents in continental climates cluster so strongly on north through east aspects, and why avalanche bulletins describe danger by aspect and elevation on a compass rose — the pattern is that predictive. Sun-exposed slopes in midwinter are generally more settled but not innocent: strong sun can build melt-freeze crusts that later become the sliding surface for new snow, and sun-warmed rocks shed the season's first wet sluffs. In spring the danger migrates to the sunny aspects and acquires a clock. As strong sun and warm air soak the equator-facing snowpack with meltwater, the snow loses cohesion and wet avalanches release — typically in the afternoon, on the aspects that have faced the sun longest, which at mid-northern latitudes means east faces failing by midday and south and west faces through the afternoon. The travel discipline that follows is one of mountaineering's oldest rules: in spring, be on and under sunny slopes early, when the overnight refreeze still carries your weight, and be off them before they go isothermal and sloppy; a corn-snow descent that is perfect at nine in the morning can be a wet-slide hazard by two. Cornices — wind-built snow roofs on lee ridgelines — add a sun term too: they sag and calve in afternoon warmth, bombarding the slopes below, so the sunny side of a corniced ridge is worst visited late. Aspect likewise organizes glacier travel: crevasse bridges soften first on sun-facing sections; icefall zones under sunlit seracs are morning objectives or no objectives. For a winter traveler the synthesis is a habit of asking, for every slope you touch or pass beneath: which way does it face, what has the sun done to it this season and today, and what does that make it right now — cold and hollow, or warm and rotten? Neither answer is safe or unsafe in itself; the shaded aspect offers better skiing and colder camps, the sunny aspect offers firm morning travel and warmth. What aspect gives you is the ability to time and route your exposure — and no rule of aspect ever substitutes for the local avalanche bulletin, test pits, and the humility to turn around.

sections.heading: Cold-air drainage, frost hollows, and the thermal belt
sections.body: Solar aspect explains the daytime map of warmth; the nighttime map is drawn by a different mechanism that every site-chooser must hold alongside it. On clear, calm nights the ground radiates heat to the sky and chills the air in contact with it; that chilled air is denser than the air above, and on any slope it begins to flow downhill like a fluid — a katabatic drainage. It gathers in valley floors, basins, and hollows, ponding behind any obstruction the way water would, and the result is a temperature inversion: cold air below, warmer air above, the reverse of the daytime norm. The numbers are not small. Valley floors on clear nights commonly run five to ten degrees Celsius colder than the slopes a hundred meters above them, and enclosed sinkholes take the world records — the Gstettneralm sinkhole in Austria has recorded minus 52.6 degrees Celsius, in a country whose mountaintops rarely approach such cold. Farmers name these places frost hollows and learned their boundaries the hard way: the first and last frosts of the year strike the low ground weeks apart from the slopes, and a single bad night in a hollow can kill a season's blossom. Out of the same physics comes the prize real estate: the thermal belt, the band of slope above the pooled cold air and below the exposed heights, which enjoys the warmest nights on the hillside. Orchards, vineyards, and old hill towns sit in this belt across the world, typically some tens to a couple of hundred meters above the valley floor, on the equator-facing side where the belt's mild nights combine with sunny days. For a camper or survivor the lesson is direct and frequently counterintuitive: in clear, calm weather, do not camp at the bottom. The sheltered-looking creek flat, the meadow in the basin, the mouth of a draw — these are exactly where the night's cold will pool, where frost and condensing damp will load your gear, and where morning fog will sit longest. Climb even ten or twenty vertical meters onto a bench or shoulder — ideally with an easterly or equator-facing exposure for early sun — and you sleep in measurably warmer air, above the fog, with drier gear at dawn. The same drainage explains familiar field sensations: the icy river of air that slides down a gully after sunset, crossable in a few strides from warm to cold and back; the way a fire's smoke at dusk creeps downhill, tracing the drainage; the frost stripe along the fence line where cold air dams up. Wind rewrites all of it — a breezy night mixes the layers and erases the inversion, and windward slopes lose to wind chill what they gained in sun — so the complete nighttime rule reads: on clear calm nights avoid the bottoms and the summits and take the slope between, favoring tomorrow morning's sun.

sections.heading: Finding aspect in the field and on the map
sections.body: Determining a slope's aspect precisely is straightforward with a map or compass and still perfectly feasible with neither, and the skill is worth drilling because so many decisions hang on it. On a topographic map, aspect is written in the contour lines: water and fall lines run perpendicular to contours, and a slope's aspect is the direction of that perpendicular pointing downhill. Read it by finding which way the terrain descends — closed contour rings step down toward valleys, elevation labels confirm — and imagine standing on the slope facing downhill; the bearing you face is the aspect. Valley shapes help: contour V's point upstream in valleys and down-ridge on spurs, so a valley running east-west necessarily has a south-facing wall on its north side and a north-facing wall on its south side, a pattern you can read at a glance across a whole sheet. With a compass on the ground, simply face squarely downhill and sight the bearing, then correct for magnetic declination — the local difference between magnetic and true north, printed on the map margin, up to tens of degrees in some regions — because an uncorrected reading can move a slope a full compass sector. Without instruments, the sun itself is the tool. Shadows at local solar noon point toward the pole — north in the northern hemisphere, south in the southern — and noon is findable as the moment shadows are shortest, or roughly as the midpoint between sunrise and sunset. The shadow-stick method needs only a stick and two stones: mark a shadow tip, wait fifteen or more minutes, mark again; the line between marks runs west to east in order of marking, and the perpendicular gives north-south. An analog watch held flat gives a rougher answer: in the northern hemisphere point the hour hand at the sun and bisect the angle between it and twelve for south; in the southern hemisphere point twelve at the sun and bisect toward the hour hand for north; halve clock errors from daylight saving. At night, Polaris marks true north in the northern hemisphere, and the Southern Cross's long axis extended about four and a half lengths finds south in the southern. Then let the terrain vote: snowpatches, moss, dense shade forest, and lingering frost mark the poleward quadrant; open dry grass, basking lizards, vineyards, and early bare ground mark the equatorward one. In cloud or darkness those biological signs may be the only compass you have, which is reason enough to have practiced them in good weather.
steps: On the map, establish downhill: use contour elevation labels, stream lines, and the rule that contour V's point upstream.
Imagine standing on your slope facing straight downhill; the direction you face is the aspect. Read its bearing off the map with a protractor or compass baseplate.
On the ground, face squarely downhill, sight your compass, and apply the local magnetic declination to get a true bearing.
No compass: plant a stick in sunlight, mark the shadow tip, wait 15-30 minutes, mark again; the first-to-second line runs west to east, and its perpendicular is the north-south line.
Confirm with terrain evidence — lingering snow, moss, and dense conifers vote poleward; dry grass, bare early-season ground, and sun-loving growth vote equatorward.
State the result usefully: aspect to the nearest eighth (for example south-southeast), plus slope steepness and any horizon shading, since all three set the site's real solar income.

sections.heading: Choosing campsites and shelter sites by aspect
sections.body: Site selection is where all the pieces — aspect, steepness, horizon, drainage, wind, and schedule — get weighed together, and it helps to run the analysis as a deliberate sequence rather than a vibe. Start with the thermal problem you actually have. In cold conditions you are buying solar warmth and avoiding pooled cold; in heat you are buying shade and moving air; in wet cold you may care most about drying opportunities. For the classic cold-weather case in the northern hemisphere, the specification reads: a site on a slope or bench, ten to two hundred meters above the local valley floor to stand clear of the nighttime cold-air pool, on ground with a southerly through easterly aspect so the sun arrives early and stays through midday, with an open horizon toward the winter sun's low arc — no wall of terrain or dense timber to the south — and with wind shelter that does not cost you that solar window. The easterly component deserves emphasis for camps you strike each morning: the first two hours of sun do the day's most valuable work, thawing boots, drying bags, melting frost, and lifting morale, and an east-facing bench delivers them at the hour a west-facing one is still in shadow. For a fixed shelter you return to at evening, shift the weighting west of south so warmth extends into late afternoon. In hot climates, invert the search: the pole-facing aspect, the shade of a north wall in the northern hemisphere's summer, morning-sun-then-afternoon-shade easterly exposures, and elevated breezy positions beat the airless sun-trap bowls; the ground itself is cooler where it has not baked all afternoon. Some cautions cut across all climates. Do not let solar greed put you under hazard: the sunny base of a snow-loaded or rockfall-prone slope, the warm mouth of an avalanche runout, and the pretty meadow below a corniced ridge are all classic bad trades, and in canyon country neither aspect matters more than staying out of flash-flood washes. Check the microsite as well as the slope: a boulder or dark rock face on your equator side becomes a radiant heater and windbreak in one, warming a tent site long after sunset, while a single shading tree can cost a winter camp its whole solar morning. Test your horizon honestly — crouch at ground level and trace where the sun will actually travel, remembering the winter arc is short and low; a site that was sunny at your summer scouting can be sunless in December. Finally, remember snow and frost as site materials: the shaded aspect keeps snow usable for water and building late in the season, and the sunny aspect gives you bare dry ground to sleep on weeks earlier — sometimes the best camp uses both, bedding on the sun-dried bench and harvesting the shaded drift thirty meters away.

sections.heading: Aspect in farming, building, and energy
sections.body: The oldest applied science of aspect is agriculture, and its monuments are visible from any mid-latitude train window. Wine grapes are the textbook case: at the poleward limit of viticulture, around 50 degrees north in Germany's Mosel and Rheingau, vineyards climb only the steep south- and southwest-facing river slopes, where tilt-toward-the-sun geometry adds the heat units the flat fields lack; the slate soils store daytime heat, the river reflects extra light, and wine from the shaded bank is simply not made. The same logic sites orchards and market gardens on equator-facing thermal-belt slopes above frost hollows, tea and coffee on aspects that trade maximum heat against cloud and moisture regimes, and in hot dry country reverses to favor shaded aspects and valley bottoms where moisture, not warmth, is scarce. Traditional architecture encodes the same analysis. Alpine villages cluster on the adret with their long glazed faces toward the sun; Mediterranean and Middle Eastern towns turn courtyards and thick walls against it; the classic farmhouse anywhere sets its main rooms and biggest windows toward the equator and its stores, stables, and blank walls toward the pole. Modern passive-solar design makes the rules quantitative: orient the long axis of a building east-west so the big glazing faces the equator; size the roof overhang so that the high summer sun is excluded while the low winter sun penetrates deep into the rooms — the geometry works because at, say, 45 degrees north the noon sun stands near 68 degrees in June but only 22 in December; put thermal mass such as masonry floors where that winter sun lands to store the day's gain into the evening; and keep pole-facing glazing modest, since it loses heat all winter and collects little. Done well in a suitable climate, these free choices cut heating demand by a quarter to a half before any machinery is bought. Solar energy hardware obeys the same cosine law: fixed photovoltaic panels yield most annually when facing the equator at a tilt near the site latitude, with winter-weighted systems tilted steeper by ten to fifteen degrees and summer-weighted ones shallower; a panel flat on the ground at 50 degrees latitude in December collects a small fraction of what the same panel properly tilted collects, which is also why a phone or emergency panel propped perpendicular to the winter sun charges dramatically faster than one lying flat. Even road and trail engineering reads aspect: highway departments know their black-ice belts are the pole-facing cuts and shaded curves that never see winter sun, gardeners start seedlings against equator-facing walls that re-radiate stored heat overnight, and fruiting espaliers trained on such walls ripen varieties a full climate zone beyond their nominal range. The through-line in every trade is identical: aspect is free energy or free cooling, permanently attached to the land, and the craft lies in siting the activity where the geometry already does part of the work.

sections.heading: When aspect rules mislead: limits and failure modes
sections.body: Aspect reasoning fails politely — it keeps giving answers — so you must know the conditions under which the answers go wrong. The first limit is cloud. The entire sunny-slope advantage rides on direct beam radiation; under thick overcast, light arrives diffusely from the whole sky and aspects nearly equalize. In chronically cloudy maritime climates — coastal ranges, the British Isles, Pacific Northwest winters — the measured difference between opposing aspects shrinks dramatically, and moisture-driven factors like drainage and wind exposure deserve the larger weight in your decisions. The second limit is wind. A perfectly oriented slope that faces the prevailing winter gale can be colder in effect than a shaded but becalmed one, because convective heat loss from wind routinely outweighs radiative gain; in many ranges the aspect of the storm wind, not of the sun, decides which side of the mountain is survivable, and wind-loading of snow onto lee slopes creates avalanche hazard on a compass bearing set by weather, not by the sun. Read both compasses. Third, the sun rule inverts by season and by need: the southwest slope you prized in January is the heat-stroke and wildfire aspect of August; the shaded ubac you dismissed is where the water, the cool, and the late-season snowbank live. Aspect is not a ranking of good and bad sides but a map of where energy goes; your needs decide the sign. Fourth, small-scale evidence lies. Moss on one tree, one snowpatch, one thriving shrub — each is contaminated by local shade, drip lines, soil, and chance; poll whole hillsides, not individuals, and prefer converging independent signs. Fifth, the tropics and the polar night are edge cases where mid-latitude intuition breaks: near the equator the sunny aspect changes with the calendar and the contrast is weak; in polar winter there is no sun to face, and everything is drainage, wind, and stored heat. Sixth, hazards outrank comfort with no exceptions: a warm bench under a cornice, a sunny runout zone, a dry south-facing scree gully that funnels rockfall as soon as the frost releases — the same solar loading that makes a slope pleasant is often precisely what makes it shed things, and afternoon rockfall on sun-warmed faces is a scheduled event in the mountains. When your aspect prediction and the ground evidence disagree — the south slope that is inexplicably boggy, the north slope that is inexplicably bare — believe the ground and look for the hidden variable: a spring line, a wind funnel, a horizon wall, a soil change. And when you have gotten it wrong — camped in a frost hollow, committed to a sun-rotted snow slope at two in the afternoon — the recoveries are boringly consistent: move up out of the pooled cold even a few meters; get off the softening slope by the shortest safe line and wait for the refreeze; re-time the route so sunny ground is used in the morning and shaded ground in the heat. The geometry never stops working; the skill is noticing which variable is in charge today.

guides.title: Sizing a Shelter to Your Body
guides.summary: Why an emergency shelter must be measured against your own body rather than built by eye, with the heat physics, body-based measuring techniques, and specific interior dimensions for debris huts, snow shelters, tarp rigs, and hot-weather shade.

sections.heading: Why shelter size is a survival variable, not a comfort choice
sections.body: Ask an untrained person to build an emergency shelter and they will almost always build a small house: something they can sit up in, turn around in, store gear in. It feels right, and in a cold-weather survival situation it can kill them. The single most common and most consequential shelter-building error recorded by survival instructors and search-and-rescue debriefs is oversizing, because the physics of staying warm without a stove is unforgiving: your resting body produces roughly as much heat as a single old-fashioned incandescent light bulb, around 100 watts, and that trickle of energy must warm every cubic meter of air your shelter encloses, replace everything the walls leak, and still keep your core temperature within about two degrees Celsius of 37 before hypothermia begins to degrade your judgment and coordination. Double the interior volume of a shelter and you have roughly halved its warmth for the same wall construction, yet the builder has also spent perhaps twice the calories and daylight building it. Sizing a shelter to your body, deliberately, with measurements taken from your own limbs rather than by eye, is therefore not a refinement for experts; it is the difference between a microclimate you heat successfully and a cold cavern you shiver in until morning. The stakes justify precision. Hypothermia can incapacitate in hours at air temperatures well above freezing when wind and wet are working against you; the often-quoted survival rule of threes puts exposure ahead of water and food for good reason, allowing perhaps three hours in severe conditions without protection. A correctly sized shelter, snug enough that your body heat meaningfully raises the air temperature around you, loose enough that you can enter it, insulate beneath yourself, and plug the entrance, converts your 100 watts from a rounding error into a heating system. There is also an equally real opposite case: in hot, sun-hammered environments the logic inverts, and a shelter must be sized generously for airflow and shade rather than snugly for heat retention, because the enemy is heat gain and the body's cooling budget is sweat, not metabolism. In other words, sizing is not one rule but a reasoned decision that starts from what the shelter must do thermally. This guide works through that reasoning: how much heat you actually have to spend, where shelters lose it, how to measure a shelter with no tape measure using the one measuring instrument you always carry, your own body, and then the specific interior dimensions that make a debris hut, a snow shelter, a tarp rig, or a desert shade structure work. The habit to build from the first paragraph is this: never build by eye. Lie down on the ground where the shelter will stand, scratch your outline, and let that outline, plus a hand's width here and a forearm there, dictate every dimension that follows.

sections.heading: Your heat budget: about one light bulb
sections.body: Every sizing rule in shelter craft descends from one number: the human body at rest produces roughly 80 to 120 watts of heat, a figure that comes directly from metabolism. An adult burning about 2,000 kilocalories per day is converting chemical energy at an average rate of close to 100 joules per second, and since the body's mechanical efficiency at rest is essentially zero, nearly all of it leaves as heat. Shivering, the body's emergency furnace, can multiply that output several-fold for a while, to perhaps 300 to 500 watts in strong bursts, but it burns glycogen quickly, exhausts you, and fails altogether as core temperature falls, so a shelter designed around shivering is a shelter designed to fail. Work, walking, chopping, digging, can push output past 500 watts, which is why you sweat while building a shelter and why you must manage that sweat: water conducts heat about 25 times better than air, and clothing soaked from the inside will spend the night stealing the very heat the shelter is meant to keep. The budget has a second side: the losses. A naked human in still air loses heat across the skin's roughly 1.8 square meters fast enough that air below about 25 to 27 degrees Celsius already feels cool; clothed, the balance point drops, but in a 0 degree night a poorly sheltered body can easily lose 200 to 400 watts, two to four times income, and the deficit is drawn down from core temperature. Mild hypothermia begins around a core of 35 degrees with violent shivering and fumbling hands; by 33 degrees thinking is visibly impaired; below about 30 degrees shivering stops, consciousness fades, and the heart becomes electrically unstable. The entire aim of a survival shelter is to close that gap between 100 watts of income and several hundred watts of potential outgo, and it does so by shrinking the volume of air your body must heat and slowing every channel through which that heated air and your radiant heat escape. This is why volume appears in every rule that follows. Air itself is a superb insulator when trapped and still, its thermal conductivity is about 0.026 watts per meter-kelvin, worse than almost any solid, which is why fluffed debris, snow, and lofted sleeping bags work; but air that can circulate carries heat away by convection, and a large shelter interior is precisely a volume in which warm air rises off your body, cools against distant walls, and returns as a draft. A snug shelter interrupts that loop: with only a few hundred liters of air around you, your body warms the whole envelope a few crucial degrees, and the trapped-air walls slow the rest. One light bulb can keep a phone booth warm; it cannot warm a garage. Every measurement in this guide is an application of that sentence.

sections.heading: How shelters lose heat: the four channels
sections.body: A shelter is a filter placed across four distinct heat-loss channels, and sizing decisions affect each one differently, so it pays to know them by name. Conduction is heat flowing through direct contact, and in shelter craft its overwhelming source is the ground. Earth is dense, effectively infinite in heat capacity, and on a cold night it will drink heat out of your body all night long through whatever touches it; lying on bare ground can outpace every other loss combined. Sizing consequence: the shelter must be big enough to contain a thick insulating bed, a point builders forget when they size the floor to their body and then discover the bed of boughs and leaves has nowhere to go. Convection is heat carried away by moving air, and it operates at two scales. Outside, wind strips the thin layer of warmed air clinging to surfaces, the wind-chill effect, which can make minus 5 degrees with a 40 kilometer-per-hour wind remove heat like still air at minus 15; a shelter's first job is simply to be a windbreak. Inside, the same physics appears as drafts: any opening low and high creates a chimney, cold air entering at the floor and warm air leaving at the peak, and an oversized interior gives warm air room to circulate and shed its heat against cold walls. Sizing consequence: minimize interior air volume, keep the ceiling low, and make the entrance small and pluggable. Radiation is heat leaving as invisible infrared light, and it needs no air at all; on a clear night the sky behaves like a surface tens of degrees below air temperature, and an exposed body or shelter roof radiates to it relentlessly, which is why frost forms on open ground but not under trees. Overhead mass, debris, snow, boughs, even a tarp, intercepts that radiation and returns some of it, and a low roof close to your body returns more than a high one. Evaporation is heat spent turning liquid water into vapor, about 2,400 kilojoules per kilogram, a huge number, which is the body's deliberate cooling mechanism when sweating and an accidental catastrophe when clothing or bedding is wet; it is also why breath and body moisture matter in tightly closed shelters, where condensation soaks insulation and then conducts. Sizing consequence in the cold: build snug but never airtight, leave a deliberate vent, and manage sweat during the build by shedding layers before you soak them. In the heat, every consequence flips: you want the wind you were blocking, a high roof to let hot air stratify above you, shade to block solar radiation gain, and free airflow so sweat can evaporate and do its job. One framework, four channels, two opposite climates: cold-weather sizing shrinks convection volume and blocks wind and sky; hot-weather sizing maximizes shade while opening the convection paths wide.

sections.heading: Your body is the tape measure
sections.body: Survival situations do not come with measuring tools, but you carry a calibrated set everywhere: your own limbs. Anthropometry, the measurement of the human body, has been the basis of practical units for all of recorded history, the foot, the cubit, the fathom, precisely because body proportions are consistent enough to build with. Before you ever need it, spend ten minutes calibrating yourself against a ruler and memorize five numbers. First, your height, the master dimension every shelter length derives from. Second, your armspan, fingertip to fingertip with arms outstretched: for almost everyone it equals height within a few centimeters, a relationship noted since antiquity and drawn famously in Leonardo da Vinci's Vitruvian Man of about 1490, so a shelter you cannot span is longer than you are tall. Third, the cubit, elbow to fingertip, typically 42 to 48 centimeters in adults, the ideal unit for clearances and insulation depths. Fourth, the hand span, thumb tip to little-finger tip stretched, usually 18 to 23 centimeters, and the fist, roughly 9 to 11 centimeters across the knuckles, the small change of shelter measurement, used for gaps, wall thickness checks, and door margins. Fifth, your boot length, commonly 28 to 32 centimeters, convenient for pacing off floor dimensions heel-to-toe. With these, every dimension in this guide translates into counts of your own body: a bed a cubit deep, a ridgepole a hand span taller than your height plus a boot, a clearance of one fist around the shoulders. Using them well has techniques. To lay out a floor, lie down where the shelter will stand, on your back for a snow trench, on your side with knees slightly bent for a debris hut, since that is how you actually sleep in the cold, and scratch or stamp your outline; this single act, taking fifteen seconds, prevents the classic error of building for an imagined body rather than your real one wearing every layer you own, and you should do the lie-down dressed in, or accounting for, your full night clothing and boots. To measure a pole against your height, stand it upright beside you and grip it; to measure horizontal spans, use armspan for coarse work, cubits laid end over end for fine. To check a wall's thickness, push a fist or a measured stick into it. To size a roof height above your chest, sit or lie beneath the frame before you commit to covering it. Groups should calibrate on the tallest member. It is worth stating the underlying rule plainly, because the rest of this guide leans on it: never trust visual estimation of enclosed space. Interiors look larger than they are while digging and smaller than they are while framing, errors of 20 to 30 percent are routine, and the lie-down test plus limb units replaces that unreliable eye with measurements that are always in reach.

sections.heading: The core rule: fit like a sleeping bag, not a room
sections.body: Here is the sizing philosophy for any unheated cold-weather shelter in one sentence: build a garment, not a building. A survival shelter you will heat with nothing but your body should fit you the way a good sleeping bag does, close everywhere, touching almost nowhere, with just enough clearance to enter, turn over with effort, and avoid compressing the insulation around you. Instructors teaching the classic debris hut phrase it memorably: if it does not feel slightly coffin-like inside, it is too big. The reasoning is arithmetic. Suppose your snug shelter encloses about half a cubic meter of air around your body; air's volumetric heat capacity is about 1.2 kilojoules per cubic meter per degree, so raising that pocket 10 degrees takes only around 6 kilojoules, a couple of minutes of your body's output, and thereafter your 100 watts fights only the leakage through the walls. Make the interior five times larger, a modest-looking crawl space, and everything scales against you: five times the air to heat, several times the wall area to leak through, and enough headroom for a proper convection loop to establish itself, warm air rising off you, cooling on the roof, and falling back as a draft. The same construction that felt warm now plateaus barely above outside temperature. Fit has a second, less obvious benefit: structural. Small spans are strong spans; a debris hut whose ridgepole clears your shoulder by a hand span carries its load of insulation easily, while a roomy one needs heavier framing you must find, cut, and lift, spending calories and daylight. And a snug interior means less material for the same wall thickness: insulation depth, not interior grandeur, is where surplus material should always go. The rule has limits that keep it honest. You are not building an actual coffin: you must be able to get in and out without demolishing the entrance, turn from one side to the other, since everyone turns during sleep, pull insulation over yourself, and keep your face near ventilation; claustrophobic panic in a shelter too tight to move in is real, and a shelter you dread entering will not be used. Clearance targets that respect both physics and sanity: about a fist to a hand span of free space beyond your body at the shoulders and hips when lying in your sleeping position, a hand span to a cubit above your chest and face when lying down, roughly 15 to 30 centimeters of length beyond your head and feet, and no more. Sitting headroom is a luxury that costs volume; in a one-night survival shelter you give it up, and in a multi-day camp you add a small sitting alcove near the entrance rather than raising the whole roof. Everything that follows, hut, snow shelter, tarp, is this rule dressed in specific numbers.

sections.heading: The numbers: length, width, and height for a solo cold shelter
sections.body: Translating the sleeping-bag rule into dimensions produces a specification you can memorize, and it is worth memorizing because you will apply it tired, cold, and in failing light. Length: your height plus 15 to 30 centimeters, that is, your height plus roughly half a cubit at each end, and no more. The extra accounts for the fact that a sleeping body is not a standing one, toes point, the head needs a margin from the wall so breath and face stay clear of cold surfaces, and some length is consumed by the insulation packed at each end. For a person 175 centimeters tall, that is an interior of 190 to 205 centimeters, which you lay out by lying down and adding a boot length beyond your head and another beyond your feet. Width: your shoulder width, typically 45 to 55 centimeters, plus a fist to a hand span of clearance on each side, giving an interior of roughly 65 to 90 centimeters at the shoulders for a single occupant; if you sleep curled on your side, check the layout against your drawn-up knees, which often govern. Many builders taper the floor plan, widest at the shoulders, narrower at the feet, which saves material and heat; a debris hut is naturally a tapered wedge for exactly this reason. Height: measured from the top of your bed, not from the ground, since a proper bed is 20 to 30 centimeters of compressed insulation, the ceiling should clear your body by a hand span to a cubit when you lie in your sleeping posture, which for a side sleeper means clearing the upper shoulder and hip. Interior heights of 45 to 60 centimeters above the bed surface are typical and correct; a ceiling you can sit under, 90 centimeters or more, roughly doubles the enclosed volume and should be rejected in a body-heated shelter. Run the volume check as a final audit: length times average width times average height. The target for a solo unheated shelter is roughly 0.4 to 0.8 cubic meters of air space, of which your body occupies about 0.07; a 2.0 by 0.8 by 0.5 meter interior gives 0.8 cubic meters and is on the generous end. If your plan computes to more than about one cubic meter for one person, shrink it before you build, not after. Two audits catch the standard errors. The lie-down audit: before covering the frame, lie inside in your sleeping clothes; you should be able to turn over with deliberate effort, and your nose should not touch the roof, but you should be able to touch every wall without stretching. The fist audit: probe the gap between your shoulder and the wall, one to two fists is right, four is a heat leak you will feel at 3 a.m. Oversize discovered early costs minutes to fix; discovered at night it costs the night.

sections.heading: The bed is part of the size: ground insulation first
sections.body: No dimension in shelter sizing is more commonly omitted than the vertical space consumed by the bed, and the omission is expensive, because the ground is usually the largest single heat thief in an unheated shelter. Conduction into soil dwarfs losses to still air: deep earth holds a temperature near the local annual average, commonly 5 to 12 degrees Celsius in temperate latitudes and far lower in winter surface layers, and its capacity to absorb your heat is effectively unlimited on the timescale of a night. Sleeping directly on cold ground can move more heat out of you than the air does, which is why experienced practitioners repeat the maxim that one blanket beneath you is worth two on top. Insulation works by trapping air in small, still pockets, dry leaves, grass, pine needles, bracken, moss dried of surface wet, conifer boughs laid like shingles, and it only works at depth: a survival bed should start as a loose pile 30 to 60 centimeters deep, knowing that your body weight will crush it to a fraction of that. The operative measurement is compressed thickness, the loft remaining under your hips and shoulders once you are lying on it, and the target is a minimum of 10 centimeters compressed, a hand span, with 15 to 20 centimeters better in hard cold. Test it the reliable way: lie on the finished bed for a full minute, then reach beneath your hip, the heaviest point, and feel for ground; if you can feel firm ground or cold coming through, double the pile and test again. Now the sizing consequence, which is the reason this subject sits in a guide about dimensions: the bed must be built into the shelter's measurements from the start. Vertically, an interior planned at 50 centimeters of headroom loses 20 to 30 of them to bedding; if you sized the roof off the bare floor, you will finish the bed and discover you no longer fit, and the common bodge, thinning the bed, trades your warmest component away to preserve a framing error. Size the frame from the top of an imagined finished bed: bed thickness plus body depth plus a hand-span clearance. Horizontally, the bed must extend beyond your body outline by at least a hand span on every side, because a bed exactly your width lets your shoulders and hips roll off its edge onto cold ground at every turn, and edges compress and scatter with use; that margin, in turn, sets the floor dimensions. A useful discipline is to gather bedding before framing the shelter, or at minimum to stake out the bed's footprint first and frame around it. In snow, the same role is played by a thick platform of boughs or gear insulating you from the snow floor, and in hot climates the logic inverts again: elevation and airflow beneath you cool, so desert practice favors a raised bed or thin mat rather than deep loft.

sections.heading: Sizing the debris hut
sections.body: The debris hut is the canonical body-sized shelter of temperate woodland survival, essentially a giant natural sleeping bag: a low A-frame wedge framed with a single ridgepole, ribbed with sticks, and buried under a meter of leaf litter. Its dimensions come straight from your body. The ridgepole, a stout pole that must bear the full insulation load without cracking, wants to be about 1.5 times your height, for most adults 2.5 to 3 meters; the traditional field measure is your height plus the distance from your fingertips to your opposite shoulder with arm outstretched, and a pole as thick as your upper arm is about right. One end rests on the ground beyond where your feet will lie; the other is propped in a crotched tree, on a stump, or on two crossed sticks at hip height, roughly 70 to 90 centimeters up. That prop height is a genuine sizing decision: set the high end at your hip and the interior at the head end will clear a side-sleeping body by about a hand span once the bed is in, which is the target; set it at chest height because it looks roomier and you have doubled the air volume and flattened the roof pitch that sheds rain. Check it directly: crawl under the bare ridgepole and lie in your sleeping posture; your shoulder and hip should nearly graze it. The footprint is a taper. At the head end, interior width is shoulder width plus a fist or two per side, about 70 to 90 centimeters; it narrows continuously toward the foot end, ending just wider than your boots. Lay it out by lying beside the ridgepole and scratching your outline, then adding the bed margin of a hand span per side. Ribs, sticks leaned against the ridgepole every 15 to 20 centimeters, should just clear the intended interior; longer ribs steepen and widen the hut, so trim or shove them in rather than letting them dictate size, and keep the rib angle at 45 degrees or steeper so debris and rain shed outward. A lattice of light brush over the ribs keeps the insulation from sifting through. Then the component that does the thermal work: debris piled over the whole structure to a thickness of at least 60 centimeters on every surface, a full arm's length, and closer to a meter in real cold, measured by plunging your arm to the shoulder into the pile; anything less than knee-deep is decoration, not insulation. Stuff the interior loosely with the driest leaves available, you will burrow in, displacing what your body does not need, and finish the entrance at the head end just larger than your shoulders, with a plug of packed debris, a stuffed jacket, or a rucksack pulled in behind you. Built to these numbers, a debris hut has kept people functional through freezing rain with no fire and no bag; built twice as large, the same materials produce a damp, cold woodpile.

sections.heading: Sizing snow shelters: quinzee, snow cave, and snow trench
sections.body: Snow is a paradoxical building material: it is frozen water, yet fresh settled snow is 50 to 90 percent trapped air, giving it a thermal conductivity in the same league as commercial insulation, and a properly sized snow shelter will hold its interior near 0 degrees Celsius while the night outside falls to minus 30. The sizing rules, though, are stricter than for any other shelter type, because errors here can suffocate or bury the occupant rather than merely chill them. The quinzee is the most broadly usable form: pile snow into a dome, let it sinter, the snow crystals fusing and strengthening over 1 to 3 hours, then hollow it out. Size the pile from your body: diameter of about your height plus a cubit, commonly 2.2 to 2.6 meters for one or two people, and height 1.5 to 1.8 meters, chest to chin high. Before hollowing, push two or three dozen sticks about 30 centimeters long into the dome all over; digging from inside, you stop excavating each direction when you meet a stick's end, leaving walls a uniform 30 centimeters, a forearm, thick, the gauge that balances insulation against collapse strength. The interior you carve is not a room but a sleeping slot per person: shoulder width plus a hand span, your height plus a boot, and a ceiling a hand span above your lying body, smoothed into a dome so meltwater runs down the walls instead of dripping. Critically, carve the sleeping platform higher than the top of the entrance opening: cold air is denser than warm and pools downward, so a raised platform sits in the warm pocket while the doorway acts as a cold sump and drain. A snow cave dug into a deep drift follows identical interior numbers, entrance tunnel low, sleeping bench high, roof at least a forearm thick and dome-smoothed, with the added rule that you dig the entrance slightly uphill into the drift so the sleeping chamber sits above the door.
