The snow trench is the fast, low-energy option for exhausted or poorly equipped parties: dig or stamp a slot just wider than your shoulders, a fist deeper than your body height is long, and about waist deep, then roof it with skis, poles, branches, or a tarp anchored by snow blocks, and floor it with every scrap of insulation available. Its virtue is that minimal volume comes automatically. Two non-negotiable sizing accessories apply to all three. First, a vent: punch a fist-sized hole through the roof at an angle, and keep the entrance loosely blocked with a pack or snow block rather than sealed airtight, because a sealed snow shelter accumulates carbon dioxide and, if any stove or flame is inside, carbon monoxide. Second, mark and probe your walls; a roof thinned below about 20 centimeters sags and collapses, and quinzees have killed diggers whose walls were carved too thin, which is what the gauge sticks exist to prevent. Always dig with a partner watching if one is available, and keep your shovel inside with you.

sections.heading: Sizing fire-heated shelters: the lean-to and its fire
sections.body: Everything changes when the heat source is a fire instead of a body, and the shelter type that expresses the change is the open lean-to: a single sloped roof, a windbreak with a bed beneath it, facing a long fire with a reflector wall behind the flames. Where the unheated shelter's rule is enclose as little as possible, the fire-heated shelter's rule is expose the occupant to the fire and trap as little smoke as possible, and its dimensions are set jointly by your body and the fire's. The roof: a ridgepole lashed or wedged between two trees or propped on sheer poles at about hip to chest height, 90 to 120 centimeters, with rafters sloped back at roughly 45 to 60 degrees to shed rain and reflect heat down onto the bed. Lower is warmer but harder to work under; higher than chest height turns the lean-to into a sail that catches wind and holds no heat. The footprint under the roof should fit your lying body plus bedding with a hand span to spare on each side, exactly as in any shelter, with the long axis parallel to the fire so your whole body faces it; depth from the open face to the back wall of about one meter, just past your body's depth plus bedding, keeps you within the heated zone rather than leaving a cold corridor behind you. Now the fire, which is a sized component of the shelter, not an accessory. The classic arrangement is the long fire: a bed of flames as long as your body, your height in fire, laid parallel to the shelter opening at a distance of roughly one to 1.5 meters from your bed edge, about an armspan; closer risks ember burns on bedding, farther wastes most of the radiant arc. Behind the fire, at another half meter to a meter, stands a reflector, a knee-to-waist-high wall of green logs, rocks, or piled earth, which does less true reflecting than people imagine but usefully blocks wind from driving the flame and re-radiates some heat once hot, closing the system: fire radiates in all directions, the reflector returns part of the back lobe, and your sloped roof intercepts the upward lobe and presses warmth down over the bed. Sizing errors here have their own catalogue. A roof too high or a fire too small produces the familiar misery of a roasting face and a frozen back, partly correctable by the long-fire length and by turning periodically. A fire too close to a low roof ignites it, snow-laden boughs overhead melt and dump, and resinous rafters catch; keep flames at least 1.5 meters from any flammable roof edge and clear overhead branches. Wind direction is a sizing input too: the open face must sit crosswind, not upwind or downwind, or smoke fills the shelter or the wind strips its heat. Fuel is the final dimension, a long fire burns roughly an arm-thick log's worth per hour, so a night demands a knee-high stack as long as the fire, gathered before dark.

sections.heading: Hot-climate shade shelters: size for air, not warmth
sections.body: In hot environments the shelter problem inverts completely, and so does every sizing rule. The threats are now solar radiation, which can deliver over 1,000 watts per square meter onto exposed skin and raise ground surface temperatures past 60 degrees Celsius, and dehydration, because the body's only cooling mechanism, evaporating sweat, spends water you may not be able to replace; heat exhaustion and then heat stroke, a core temperature above about 40 degrees with failing consciousness, are the end state. A hot-weather shelter is therefore a parasol and a wind tunnel, and it should be sized generously where the cold shelter was snug. Shade footprint first: the shadow must cover your whole body through the hours you will occupy it, and shadows move; the sun swings roughly 15 degrees of azimuth per hour, so a canopy sized to your exact outline at noon leaves your legs in the sun by mid-afternoon. Size the roof at least half a meter beyond your body on every side, a lying body of 1.8 meters wants a canopy of roughly 2.5 by 1.5 meters, and orient its long axis east-west so the low morning and evening sun still lands on canopy, not on you. Height is the second reversal: raise the roof. A tarp pitched high, waist height or above, lets breeze pass over your body, and hot air, which rises, stratifies against the underside of the canopy well above you instead of pooling around your face as it would under a low cold-weather pitch. The desert refinement is the double-roof shelter: two layers of material, a tarp over a second tarp or cloth, separated by an air gap of 20 to 40 centimeters, a forearm, so the top layer absorbs the solar load and the moving air in the gap carries that heat away before it re-radiates onto the lower layer; field measurements and long military practice in hot deserts credit the double roof with keeping the shaded space several degrees below single-layer shade. Get off the ground as well: the surface you avoid conducting to in winter now cooks from above, while soil 30 to 45 centimeters down remains dramatically cooler, so desert practice either raises the bed, a platform or hammock catching the breeze, or lowers it, a scraped trench floored with the cooler subsurface soil, shaded by the double roof, with the excavated spoil banked as low walls that block ground-level hot wind without stopping the higher breeze. Walls otherwise stay open: enclosing sides that face the wind throws away convective cooling, and only the upwind side of a dusty gale deserves a screen. Finally, size your labor to the clock, not the shelter: build in early morning or evening, rest through the 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. furnace, and remember that a generous shade shelter that cost you a liter of sweat to build has already paid a worse price than a slightly smaller one built in the cool.

sections.heading: Tarp pitches and how size follows configuration
sections.body: A tarp is the shape-shifter of shelter craft: the same 3 by 3 meter square can be a wide-open sunshade, a rain fly, or a nearly closed cocoon, and choosing the pitch is choosing the size, so a tarp user must understand how configuration trades coverage against enclosed volume. The A-frame, the tarp thrown over a ridgeline and staked along both edges, is the standard rain pitch: with a 3-meter tarp and the ridge at 60 to 80 centimeters, knee to hip height, it encloses a wedge with generous rain coverage and a moderate volume; pitch the ridge lower, 40 to 50 centimeters, storm pitch, and the volume shrinks toward body-heated territory while wind resistance improves dramatically, at the cost of crawling entry. The lean-to pitch, half the tarp as a sloped wall, is the fire-facing and shade configuration, all coverage and no enclosure. The plow point, one corner staked into the wind with the opposite corner raised on a pole or line, produces a half-cone that is remarkably storm-worthy and naturally body-tapered, wide at the mouth where your shoulders lie, tight at the point where your feet go: an inherently well-sized solo shelter. The C-fly or body bag folds, wrapping the tarp under, over, and around, produce minimum-volume cocoons for worst conditions. Across all pitches, three sizing checks decide whether the tarp will actually protect you. Coverage check: rain does not fall vertically; wind drives it at 20 to 45 degrees, so your body and bedding must sit inside the tarp's footprint with a margin, at least 30 centimeters, a cubit, of tarp beyond your head and feet, and more on the windward side; lie under the pitched tarp and have a partner sight along the likely rain angles, or do it yourself by eye from outside. Splash check: rain striking ground at the tarp's edge bounces inward 10 to 20 centimeters, so bedding should stay at least that far inside the drip line, another argument for margin. Sag check: a tarp pitched drum-tight in the evening will sag under rain load and stretch, and a roof that touches your bag transmits water straight through; leave a hand span between fabric and body at the tightest point, and re-tension guylines before sleeping. Tarp dimensions map to bodies simply: a 2.4 by 3 meter tarp shelters one person with margin in most pitches; 3 by 3 handles one person in storm folds or two in an A-frame; two people under smaller tarps must accept lean-to or shade configurations. Ground-cloth arithmetic matters too, if the tarp must also be the floor, subtract that area from the roof. The deeper lesson the tarp teaches is that size is not a property of material but of geometry: you carry a fixed number of square meters, and every pitch is a decision about how to spend them, coverage for volume, ventilation for warmth, speed for security, made correctly only when you start from where your body will lie and work outward.

sections.heading: Doors, entrances, and plugs: sizing the hole
sections.body: The entrance is the most thermally expensive opening in any cold-weather shelter, a deliberate breach in the envelope you spent hours sealing, and it deserves the same measured treatment as the walls. Size it to the minimum that admits you: just wider than your shoulders and just taller than your body's depth when crawling, for most adults an opening roughly 50 to 60 centimeters wide and 40 to 50 centimeters high. You enter a well-sized survival shelter the way you enter a sleeping bag, by wriggling, and that is correct; a doorway you can walk or crouch through is a heat gate that will empty the shelter's warm pocket in minutes. Orientation is part of sizing: place the entrance at 90 degrees to the prevailing wind, crosswind, never facing into it, and where terrain allows, slightly downhill of the sleeping platform, since cold air drains downward and an entrance below bed level becomes a cold sump that traps the densest, coldest air where you are not. In snow shelters this rule is structural doctrine: the entrance tunnel enters low, the sleeping bench sits high, and the vertical offset of half a meter or more is what lets the bench hold near-freezing warmth while the tunnel below reads far colder. Every cold-weather entrance needs a plug, and the plug should be planned when the entrance is cut, not improvised at midnight. Effective plugs are a rucksack pulled in behind you, a block of snow shaped to the opening, a tight roll of debris bound with cordage, or a jacket stuffed with leaves; the plug should fill most of the opening snugly but must never be an airtight seal, and it must be operable from inside with cold hands. That last clause is a genuine safety specification: you may need to exit fast, to vomit, to dig out, to escape a collapse or a fire, and a plug that jams, or an entrance so tight it binds your shoulders when you are stiff with cold, converts a shelter into a trap. Test the full cycle before dark: enter, plug, unplug, exit, three times, wearing everything you will wear at night. Alongside the door, size the vent: a dedicated fist-sized opening high in the shelter, kept clear, on the opposite side from the entrance where possible so a slow air exchange path exists. In debris huts and tarp shelters the structure usually leaks enough air that the loosely fitted plug suffices; in snow shelters and any shelter tightened with plastic sheeting, the vent is mandatory, because carbon dioxide from breath accumulates in sealed spaces and any flame, a candle, a stove, produces carbon monoxide, which is odorless and lethal. The finished standard for door and vent together: lying inside, plugged in, you should feel no draft along your body, yet a bare wisp of air movement should be detectable at the vent, and your candle, if you have one, should burn steadily, its flame neither guttering in a gale nor dimming in dead air.

sections.heading: Sizing for two or more: shared heat, shared volume
sections.body: Multiple occupants change shelter arithmetic in the builder's favor, and knowing the numbers lets a group exploit it. Two bodies in one shelter double the heat income, roughly 200 watts, while the shared shelter's air volume and wall area grow far less than double, because the occupants lie side by side and share the walls between them; the result is that a correctly sized two-person shelter runs distinctly warmer than either person's solo shelter would, and huddling, direct body contact, cuts each person's exposed surface further. Cold-weather doctrine therefore favors consolidation: one shelter for two, or two shelters for four, beats a scatter of solo shelters whenever the group is cold, and splitting up should be justified by something, injury, terrain, materials, not assumed. The width arithmetic: lying adults occupy about 50 to 60 centimeters of width each when packed shoulder to shoulder, slightly less if alternating head-to-toe, an arrangement that fits shoulders against hips and is warmer still, though many people reject sleeping beside boots and it complicates conversation and mutual monitoring. Interior width for N occupants is N times 55 centimeters plus a single fist of clearance at each outside wall, no clearance between bodies, contact is the point, giving roughly 120 centimeters for two, 175 for three. Length remains the tallest occupant's height plus the usual margins; height above the bed remains a hand span to a cubit over the bulkiest lying body. Volume check: about 0.4 to 0.5 cubic meters of air per person is a sound target in a shared unheated shelter, slightly less per capita than solo because shared warmth covers the difference. Structure must keep up with span: a debris-hut ridgepole for two is carrying nearly double the insulation load over a wider wedge, so step up pole diameter, wrist-thick becomes arm-thick, or frame with two ridgepoles from a shared high prop, and in quinzees, widen the pile rather than thinning walls, keeping the 30 centimeter forearm gauge everywhere. Assign the coldest sleepers the middle positions, which are several degrees warmer than the outside berths, and rotate the outside positions during long nights; put the strongest or most heat-generating members outside. Children lose heat faster than adults, more surface area per kilogram, and belong in the middle or against an adult, never on an outside berth or alone in an oversized shelter. Group shelters also demand entrance discipline, one person entering and exiting flushes shared warm air, so consolidate trips, and the entrance still gets sized to the broadest occupant, not the average. There is a psychological dividend worth naming: shared shelters keep the group's judgment pooled, morale up, and any deterioration, hypothermia's confusion, an injury worsening, observed by someone able to act, which no thermal calculation captures but every rescue statistic reflects. The practical ceiling is about four bodies per simple field shelter; beyond that, spans, entrances, and squabbles all grow faster than the thermal benefit, and the group should build twice.

sections.heading: The build budget: calories, daylight, and when to shrink the plan
sections.body: Shelter size is also an economics problem, because you pay for every cubic meter twice: once in the heat it leaks and once in the energy and daylight it costs to build, and in a survival situation both currencies are scarce. Put rough numbers on the costs. A debris hut built to the body-sized specification, ridgepole, ribs, lattice, and an arm-deep debris blanket, takes a practiced builder alone about 1.5 to 2 hours and a first-timer 2 to 4; the debris gathering dominates, because a meter-deep blanket over even a small wedge means moving several cubic meters of leaf litter, dozens of armload trips. A quinzee costs 2 to 4 hours including the mandatory 1 to 2 hour sintering wait; a snow trench, 30 to 60 minutes; a tarp pitch, 10 to 20 minutes; a proper insulation bed alone, 30 to 60 minutes of gathering. Physical output during building runs 300 to 500 kilocalories per hour, comparable to steady hiking, so an oversized shelter that adds two hours of work has burned most of a day's food ration you may not have, and, worse, it has soaked your base layers in sweat that will chill you all night. The planning rule that follows is the survival maxim: start shelter work early, a minimum of two hours before dark for a debris hut, three in snow, because cold fingers, invisible materials, and panic all arrive with dusk, and every task doubles in duration after it. Now the decision logic. Size the plan to the time and energy actually available, not to the shelter you would prefer: with three hours and good materials, build the full body-sized hut; with one hour, build the bed and a wind wall, a knee-high barrier of logs, snow, or packed debris on the windward side of a body-length hollow, because a thick bed plus windbreak captures a large share of a full shelter's benefit at a fraction of its cost; with twenty minutes of light, spend all of them on ground insulation and getting your body into every layer you carry, inside any natural windbreak you can find, a deadfall, a rock lee, a dense conifer's skirt. Never let the perfect shelter consume the daylight the adequate one needed. The same budget governs upgrades: a shelter is not finished or unfinished but a stack of improvements in descending value, bed thickness, windproofing, roof insulation, entrance plug, and each dawn or rest period can buy the next increment. If you expect multiple nights, invest early, an hour spent doubling the debris blanket on day one pays dividends every night after, and consider that a camp you will occupy for days justifies the sitting alcove and interior storage you rightly refused for one night. Injury, illness, and group weakness shift the calculus toward smaller and sooner: a hypothermic or exhausted person needs any shelter in thirty minutes, not a good one in three hours, and the group's strongest should build while the weakest insulate and warm. Budget honestly, shrink willingly, and remember that the shelter that exists always outperforms the one still being perfected.

sections.heading: The dry run: testing fit before dark, and reading the night's feedback
sections.body: No shelter dimension is verified until your body has tested it, and the test must happen while there is still light and energy to act on the result. Builders systematically misjudge enclosed space, interiors read 20 to 30 percent larger than they are during construction, and the errors hide until you are inside: the ridgepole that grazes your nose, the bed that ends at your calves, the entrance that pins your shoulders. The dry run, the sequenced rehearsal in the procedure below, performed fully dressed in your sleeping clothing, takes ten minutes that repay themselves at 2 a.m. Then treat the first night itself as instrumentation, because your body reports each failure channel by its own signature. Cold rising from beneath, felt at hips and shoulder blades, means the bed has compressed thin or you rolled off its edge: re-center, pull in more insulation, and double the bed in the morning, since under-bedding is the most common first-night finding. A draft along one side means a wall or plug gap; find it with a licked finger and stuff it. A cold face under a clear sky with a warm body means radiant loss through thin roof overhead: add material there. Waking damp under a tarp, or frost furring a snow ceiling, means ventilation is losing to moisture: open the vent, crack the plug, re-smooth a snow dome so melt runs to the walls. General cold despite still air usually means the volume is too large for your output, and the overnight fix is to shrink the shelter around yourself by pulling debris, gear, or snow blocks into the dead air beyond your feet and head, then rebuild smaller or thicker at first light. Spend the morning's first energy on the single highest-value fix, noted while the night is vivid. That loop, size, test, read the night, adjust, is the real skill, and it converges fast because the feedback is immediate and honest; a comfortable night is calibration too, and its dimensions, in your own fists and cubits, become field-verified numbers for your body worth deliberately remembering.
steps: 1. Fully dressed for sleeping, crawl in through the entrance; note whether shoulders bind (widen by one fist if they do).
2. Lie in your actual sleeping posture on the finished bed and hold still for two minutes; feel for ground contact under hip and shoulder.
3. Check clearances: nose and shoulder should clear the roof by a hand span; you should touch every wall without stretching.
4. Turn over completely, both directions; deliberate effort is correct, impossibility is not.
5. Probe walls and roof from inside for daylight, thin spots, and gaps; mark each and fix from outside.
6. Fit the entrance plug from inside, then remove it and exit quickly three times; the plug must work with cold, gloved hands.
7. Verify the vent: with the plug in place, a wisp of airflow should be detectable at the vent opening.
8. Lie in for ten minutes at dusk; a snug, correctly sized shelter becomes noticeably warmer around you within that time, and stillness of the air inside is the sign the envelope is closed.

guides.safetyNote: Never seal any shelter airtight: keep a fist-sized vent and a loose-fitting entrance plug, because exhaled carbon dioxide accumulates in closed spaces and any flame (candle or stove) produces lethal, odorless carbon monoxide. In snow shelters, keep walls and roofs at least 30 cm thick, carve the sleeping platform above the entrance, keep a digging tool inside, and have a partner outside while excavating — thin-walled snow shelters can collapse and bury the digger. Keep open flames at least 1.5 meters from flammable roofing, and never build in drainage channels, avalanche paths, or under dead standing timber.

guides.title: Water Proximity Versus Camp Safety
guides.summary: Why the best campsites are near water but never beside it: the flood, cold, insect, wildlife, and sanitation hazards of waterside ground, and a practical method for choosing a safe camp that still keeps water within working reach.

sections.heading: The oldest campsite decision
sections.body: Every camp needs water and every camp needs safety, and the ground that offers the most of one usually offers the least of the other. This is among the oldest trade-offs in human life outdoors: settlements, hunting camps, and armies have always gravitated to rivers, springs, and lakeshores, and rivers, springs, and lakeshores have always flooded, chilled, bitten, and occasionally drowned the people sleeping beside them. The novice instinct is almost universal and almost always wrong: arrive tired at a beautiful creek, find the flat, soft, open bench right beside the water, and pitch there, because carrying water even eighty metres feels like pointless labor at the end of a long day. The experienced instinct runs the other way: find the water, then deliberately walk away from it, uphill if possible, and accept ten minutes of daily water-hauling as the cheap premium on an insurance policy against hazards that operate mostly at night, mostly without warning, and occasionally with lethal speed. The hazards stack in a way that is easy to underestimate because each one alone seems modest. Waterside ground floods, and flash floods in particular kill campers nearly every year in arid regions, often under clear skies, from storms tens of kilometres away. Valley bottoms and drainages collect the coldest, dampest air of the night, so the streamside camp is routinely five to ten degrees Celsius colder than a bench fifty vertical metres higher, a difference that turns a marginal sleeping bag into a bad night or worse. Still and slow water breeds mosquitoes and, in much of the world, the diseases they carry. Water is also the one resource every animal in the landscape must visit, so shorelines and stream banks are wildlife highways, and a tent pitched on one is pitched in the middle of the road. Finally, dense human use of waterside ground concentrates human waste exactly where it most efficiently contaminates the water everyone else drinks, which is why land agencies converged on distance rules in the first place. None of this argues for dry camping as a virtue in itself. Water proximity is genuinely valuable: cooking, cleaning, hydration, and morale all improve when water is a short walk rather than an expedition, and in hot climates a camp too far from water creates its own dangers. The skill this guide teaches is not choosing between water and safety but pricing the trade correctly: knowing which waterside hazards are present on a given night, which are deadly and which merely uncomfortable, how far and how high is far and high enough, and how to organize a camp so that the water you walked away from is still effortless to use. The rule of thumb that anchors everything else is simple to state and worth memorizing before the mechanisms that justify it: camp at least sixty metres from water, above the highest flood evidence you can find, never in a dry watercourse, and haul what you need.

sections.heading: Why water pulls so hard
sections.body: Understanding the pull is the first step to resisting it, because the pull is real physiology and real labor, not mere laziness. A resting adult in a temperate climate needs roughly two to three litres of water a day; hard hiking in heat can triple that, and a camp of four people cooking two hot meals can easily run through fifteen to twenty litres between arrival and departure. Water is also heavy in a way nothing else in a pack is: one litre weighs one kilogram, so a single evening's supply for a small group is a ten to twenty kilogram carry, and every metre of distance and elevation between camp and source is paid for in trips with awkward, sloshing containers. Cooking multiplies the trips, because most backcountry meals are rehydrated, pots need rinsing, and spills happen. Washing multiplies them again. In cold conditions the pull strengthens further: melting snow for water burns roughly twice the stove fuel of merely boiling it, so liquid water within reach can decide whether a fuel supply lasts the trip. There is also a navigational and psychological gravity to water. Trails follow drainages, flat ground concentrates in valley bottoms, and after a long day the sound of running water reads as arrival in a way a dry bench never does; humans are simply drawn to shorelines, a preference so consistent that real-estate markets price it. All of this is legitimate, and it explains why the correct answer is almost never the far extreme, a camp so distant from water that hydration itself becomes rationed. Dehydration is not a trivial counter-hazard: a loss of two percent of body weight in water measurably degrades judgment and physical performance, and the classic error chain in hot country, too little water in camp, so less cooking, so less eating, so less energy, so worse decisions the next day, begins with a campsite chosen too far from a source. The resolution of the tension is logistical, not heroic. Sixty to one hundred metres of separation, the distance land managers ask for and the distance that clears most flood, cold, and wildlife hazards on most ground, costs a round-trip walk of three or four minutes. Done once with adequate containers, that walk supplies an entire evening and morning: collapsible bladders and folding buckets of six to ten litres exist precisely so that one trip replaces eight, and a camp that fills its containers at arrival, before boots come off, feels as water-rich as one pitched on the bank. The pull of water, in other words, is best defeated by capacity and timing rather than willpower: carry enough container to make distance cheap, fill everything on first arrival while energy remains, station the full containers at the kitchen, and the seductive streamside bench loses its only real argument while keeping every one of its dangers.

sections.heading: The 200-foot rule and where it comes from
sections.body: Most public-land agencies and the Leave No Trace program converge on the same number: camp at least 200 feet, about 60 metres or roughly 70 adult paces, from lakes, streams, springs, and wetlands. The rule has three separate justifications, which is why it has proven so durable. The first is water quality. Human waste, food scraps, soap, and trampled soil all migrate downhill and into water, and 60 metres of vegetated soil is the buffer that field studies of backcountry sanitation found gives filtration and soil microbes a reasonable chance to capture pathogens and nutrients before they reach the source everyone downstream drinks from. The same logic sets the standard cathole rule: human waste buried 15 to 20 centimetres deep, at least 60 metres from water, camp, and trails. The second justification is ecology. The strip of ground beside water, the riparian zone, is disproportionately alive: it hosts a large share of a landscape's plant diversity, nesting birds, amphibians, and the insect base of the food chain, and it is also the slowest ground to recover from trampling, because banks are soft, roots are shallow, and soils are wet. Concentrated camping on banks strips vegetation, compacts soil, collapses bank edges, and turns the most productive ground in the landscape into bare dirt; the 60 metre setback moves that wear onto tougher, drier, more recoverable ground. The third justification is access, both animal and human. Wildlife must reach water, and a shoreline ringed with tents is a fence; other people want to fish, draw water, and pass along banks, and campsites planted on the water deny the shore to everyone else while broadcasting noise across the one surface that carries sound best. The rule's limits are worth knowing as clearly as the rule. It is a minimum for impact, not a guarantee of safety: 60 metres of horizontal distance means nothing in a flash-flood canyon, where survivable ground is measured in vertical metres above the channel, and it does not by itself clear cold-air pools, insect range, or wildlife corridors, each of which has its own geometry. Regulations also vary and sometimes override it: many heavily used wilderness areas require 100 feet, some alpine lake basins prohibit camping within a quarter mile of specific lakes, designated-site areas require using established pads regardless of distance, and some desert water sources carry a much larger setback, commonly 400 metres in bighorn sheep country, expressly so that wildlife dependent on a single spring can drink at night unmolested. Where an established, legal campsite already exists close to water, most agencies prefer campers concentrate use there rather than pioneering a new compliant site, because a hardened site absorbs use without new damage. The working summary: treat 200 feet as the floor everywhere, check the local regulation, and then let flood, cold, and wildlife logic push you farther and higher as the ground demands.

sections.heading: Flash floods: the fastest way a camp kills
sections.body: Flash floods are the deadliest waterside hazard because they defeat the intuition that danger announces itself. The mechanism is rainfall concentration: a drainage basin is a funnel, and a thunderstorm dropping several centimetres of rain in an hour onto rock, sun-baked clay, burned ground, or already saturated soil sends most of that water directly into channels rather than into the ground. Narrow channels then do the arithmetic: the same volume that would spread harmlessly across a wide floodplain rises metres in minutes when squeezed between canyon walls. The killing features are speed, load, and remoteness. Speed: a flood front can move faster than a person can scramble, and the classic survivor account is of a roar heard seconds, not minutes, before the water arrived. Load: flash floods are not water but slurry, carrying boulders, logs, and in burned country a debris flow of mobilized ash and rock that behaves like wet concrete; knee-deep flow of such material knocks adults down, and about 60 centimetres of moving water floats vehicles. Remoteness: the storm that generates the flood can be 30 or more kilometres upstream, over a horizon, under a sky that is blue where the camper stands, which is why the phrase "it wasn't even raining" recurs in fatality reports. The 2015 Hildale, Utah floods killed twenty people including a canyon hiking party under exactly these conditions, and Antelope Canyon in 1997 killed eleven hikers in a slot that received no rain at all at the site. The terrain reading follows from the mechanism. Never camp in a dry wash, arroyo, or slot canyon bottom, however inviting the flat sand floor, and be suspicious of any gravel bar, island, or low bench within a channel; islands strand before they submerge, cutting off retreat first. In canyon country, evaluate the whole upstream basin, not the local sky: a large basin gathering distant mountains can flood from weather you will never see, and monsoon season in the American Southwest, roughly July through September, concentrates the risk in the afternoon and evening. Choose sleeping ground with vertical separation, not just horizontal: several metres above the channel bottom, with a scramble route higher that can be climbed in the dark, because floods arrive disproportionately at night when camps are asleep. Rising water sounds like wind or a train; treat any sudden roar, a sudden rise or muddying of a clear stream, or a line of fresh froth and sticks advancing on the current as an evacuation order, moving instantly uphill, abandoning gear, never trying to outrun water down-canyon. The asymmetry that governs all flash-flood decisions: the cost of camping high and hauling water is minutes of inconvenience every day, and the cost of the alternative, on the one night the funnel fills, is unsurvivable; a hazard that offers no second chances must be avoided categorically, not managed.

sections.heading: Slow floods: rivers that rise overnight
sections.body: Not all flooding is a wall of water; the commoner and more forgiving failure is the river that simply rises while you sleep, and forgiving is relative, because a camp flooded at 2 a.m. still means soaked insulation, lost gear, and a hypothermia problem in exactly the conditions least suited to solving one. Rivers rise on schedules that can be read in advance. Snowmelt rivers breathe daily: warm afternoons melt the snowpack, and the pulse travels downstream so that many mountain rivers peak in the evening or the middle of the night and run lowest in the morning, with daily swings of tens of centimetres in early summer, which means the reassuring water level seen at 4 p.m. is the day's minimum, not its mean. Rain floods lag their storms by hours in small basins and by a day or more in large ones, so a big river can rise steeply under a clearing sky from yesterday's rain two valleys away. Glacier-fed rivers add outburst risk and the same afternoon pulse, amplified in heat waves. And below any dam, the schedule is human: hydroelectric releases can raise a river a metre in an hour with no weather at all, on a timetable set by electricity demand, which is why camping on bars and low benches downstream of dams is its own category of mistake and why release schedules, where published, are worth checking. The reading of ground for slow flood risk is the reading of the river's own records. The floodplain announces itself: flat ground at river grade, fine silt or sand underfoot, water-sorted gravel, driftwood scattered far from the current channel, and vegetation in age-ranked bands, bare sediment nearest the water, then willows and alders, then young cottonwoods, then mature forest; each band marks how often that ground drowns, and sleeping among willows means sleeping on ground the river visits regularly. Cut banks, oxbows, and side channels that look like dry gullies are the river's alternate routes and refill first. The practical margin for an overnight camp on a healthy river in stable weather is to take the visible high-water evidence, the debris lines and silt stains, and camp above the highest of it, adding extra height in melt season, during storms anywhere in the basin, or below dams. A stick pushed into the sand at the waterline at dusk, checked at any night waking, is the oldest river gauge there is and costs nothing; a rise of more than a few centimetres against it in the evening hours is the river voting for the higher bench, and moving camp by headlamp at 10 p.m. is dramatically better than at 2 a.m. in water. On multi-day trips, note that boats, unlike sleepers, are lost to modest rises: hauling craft well above the debris line and tying them off is part of camp-making, not boat-keeping.

sections.heading: Reading flood evidence on the ground
sections.body: Rivers and creeks keep honest records of their own worst behavior, and learning to read them converts campsite selection from guesswork into evidence. The most direct record is the debris line, also called the wrack line or strandline: a ragged band of sticks, grass, pine needles, leaves, and trash deposited where floating material stranded as the last high water receded. There are usually several, and the rule is to find the highest one, not the freshest; the fresh line near the current water marks a recent ordinary rise, while a bleached, half-buried line of larger wood metres higher marks what the channel does in a serious year. Related signs extend the record. Silt stains and water marks paint rocks, bridge abutments, and tree trunks with a horizontal tide line of fine pale sediment; grass and flexible shrubs combed flat in a consistent downstream direction were laid down by moving water; small rafts of matted vegetation lodged in the upstream forks of trees and bushes, sometimes head-high, show flow depth with brutal clarity, and finding one above eye level in a streamside thicket is the strongest possible argument for the bench above. Sediment itself testifies: water-rounded gravel and cobbles far from the channel were carried there by flow strong enough to move them; sheets of fine sand or cracked, curling mud plates mark slack water where a flood paused and dropped its load; a soft, level sand floor in a desert wash is not a campsite but a flood deposit, freshly graded by the last event and awaiting the next. Vegetation gives the long-term record. Riparian species, willow, alder, sedge, cattail, and in the desert Southwest tamarisk and seep willow, grow where their roots reach water and their stems tolerate being drowned; a campsite among them is inside the flood envelope by definition. Even-aged stands of young cottonwood or sycamore date a big flood the way burn scars date a fire, since these trees germinate on fresh flood sediment. Conversely, mature upland species, sagebrush, juniper, ponderosa pine, oak, growing undisturbed with deep litter and lichen-crusted rocks, mark ground the water has not visited in the lifetime of those plants, which is the certificate a sleeping spot wants. Scour completes the picture: undercut banks, exposed root balls, rocks polished clean of lichen in a band along the channel, and log jams stacked against boulders all show the reach and force of past flow. The synthesis takes two minutes at any candidate site: walk a line from the water uphill, note the highest debris, stain, or riparian vegetation, and place the tent above the highest evidence with a margin, a metre or more of extra height in storm or melt season. Where the evidence is confusing or absent, as on freshly disturbed or heavily used ground, assume the record was erased, not that the floods never came.

sections.heading: Cold air, damp air: the streamside microclimate
sections.body: Even on a night when the water behaves perfectly, the streamside camp is punished by physics, because valley bottoms manufacture the coldest, dampest air of the night and drainages deliver it. The mechanism is cold-air drainage, called katabatic flow. After sunset, ground that radiated heat to a clear sky all evening chills the air in contact with it; cold air is denser than warm, so it slides downslope like a liquid, follows gullies and stream courses, and ponds on the lowest flat ground exactly as water would. The result, familiar to every gardener and fruit farmer who sites orchards on slopes for frost protection, is temperature inversion: on calm, clear nights, the valley floor can run five to ten degrees Celsius colder than a bench or shoulder only twenty to fifty vertical metres higher, and frost hollows show frost weeks earlier and later in the season than adjacent slopes. Meteorologists call the favored zone the thermal belt, the band on a slope above the pooled cold air and below the freely cooling ridge, and it is the classic instruction in military and mountaineering fieldcraft alike: camp neither in the bottom nor on the crest, but partway up. Water compounds the cold with moisture. Rivers and lakes feed the night air with vapor, and when the pooled cold air reaches its dew point, the water condenses, first as heavy dew on every surface, then as radiation fog, which forms preferentially over water and wet ground and can hold a valley floor near saturation until mid-morning while the slopes above sit in sun. For a camper the consequences are concrete: condensation soaks the inside of a single-wall shelter and the outside of a sleeping bag, wet down loses most of its insulating power, everything packed in the morning is heavier, and in the cold pool a marginal bag rated near the night's minimum fails, because the streamside minimum is not the forecast minimum, which is measured at a station, but several degrees below it. Wind adds a final variable: valley systems breathe, with a cool down-valley wind at night and an up-valley wind by day, so the bottom camp is not only colder but often steadily drafty in the coldest hours. The remedies are geometric and cheap. Climb: twenty to fifty vertical metres above the water is usually enough to escape the pool, and the debris-line rule already pushed the camp that way. Avoid enclosed hollows, sinks, and the inside of meander bends with high banks, which trap cold air even at elevation. Prefer a gentle slope or a bench with an open downhill exit through which cold air can drain away rather than pond. Use vegetation as a thermometer: lush, frost-tender growth and ferns mark damp cold ground, while drier grasses and upland shrubs mark the belt. In warm seasons the same logic runs in reverse and can be exploited deliberately: in a heat wave, the cold pool by the water is the coolest bedroom in the landscape, an advanced trade made knowingly, dew accepted in exchange for sleep.

sections.heading: Insects, disease, and the biology of standing water
sections.body: The insect hazard of waterside camping is not general bad luck; it is the specific biology of a few families of flies, and its geometry can be learned. Mosquitoes develop as aquatic larvae in still or barely moving water, from lake margins, marshes, and beaver ponds down to puddles, tire ruts, and snowmelt pools, and the adults of most species remain within a few hundred metres to a few kilometres of their breeding water. Females hunt from dusk through the night, guided by exhaled carbon dioxide, body heat, and odor, and they are weak fliers, grounded or at least hindered by wind above roughly ten kilometres per hour. Each fact converts directly into a camping decision: distance from marshy margins matters more than distance from clean moving water, a breezy point, spit, or open rise beats a sheltered hollow, and the hours around sunset, when a camp is being cooked in and sat in, are the hours the site choice is paid for. Blackflies invert one rule: they breed in clean running water and bite by day, so a riverside camp in blackfly season trades the mosquito's night shift for a day shift. In much of the world the stakes are higher than comfort. Malaria, dengue, and a family of encephalitis viruses travel in mosquitoes; in malarial regions the campsite rules, distance from breeding water, wind exposure, and a net over every sleeper from dusk onward, are medical measures, not comfort measures, and the net, ideally insecticide-treated, is the single most effective item carried. Ticks, though not aquatic, concentrate in the same riparian corridors, because the brushy, humid vegetation along water is both their preferred microclimate and the highway of the deer and rodents that feed them; camps set in streamside grass and willow thickets collect more of them than camps on open, dry ground. The water itself carries its own biology. Assume all backcountry surface water, however clear and cold, may carry Giardia and Cryptosporidium cysts and bacterial pathogens from wildlife and upstream users, and treat it: a rolling boil for one minute, three minutes at high altitude, kills everything of concern; filters of 0.2 micron rating remove protozoa and bacteria; chemical treatment and ultraviolet devices each work with their own time and clarity requirements. In schistosomiasis regions of Africa, Asia, and South America, the hazard extends to skin contact with slow fresh water, and wading or washing barefoot in lake margins is itself an exposure. The synthesis for site selection: scan a candidate camp for the still-water signature, marsh grass, cattails, scummy backwaters, abandoned ponds, within a few hundred metres upwind; prefer wind-exposed, well-drained ground; keep the kitchen and the sitting hours out of the dusk shade near vegetation; and let the tent's mesh, not the campfire's smoke, be the plan for the night shift.

sections.heading: Wildlife highways: everyone drinks here
sections.body: Water is the one resource no animal can skip, and that single fact organizes the movement of every species in a landscape around the same shorelines and stream banks a camper finds attractive. Deer, elk, and moose move to water at dawn and dusk along habitual trails; predators follow the prey; bears work shorelines and salmon streams as feeding grounds, not merely watering points; and in dry country the geometry sharpens brutally, because a single spring or tank may be the only water for many kilometres, making the ground around it the hub of every nocturnal schedule in the area. A tent pitched on a game trail or between a bedding area and the water does not merely risk an encounter; it schedules one. The signs are readable in minutes: worn paths converging on the water like spokes, tracks pressed into soft bank mud, droppings, browsed and rubbed vegetation, wallows, and in bear country the specific signature of torn logs, overturned rocks, claw-marked trees, and fish remains along streams. The rules that follow are mostly the standard camping rules with the geometry made explicit. Keep the sleeping site off trails and out of the funnel between cover and water; the standard 60 metre setback helps, but in heavily used corridors it pays to move farther and to one side, out of the line of travel rather than merely back from the bank. In grizzly country the practice codified in North American parks is a triangle: the tent, the kitchen, and the food storage each at least 60 to 100 metres apart, with the kitchen downwind of the tent and food hung four metres up and away from trunks or sealed in bear-resistant canisters; along salmon streams in season, the correct choice is often not to camp near the stream at all. Around African and South Asian waters the calculus changes species but not logic: hippopotamus, which kill more people in Africa than any other large mammal, graze ashore at night along habitual paths from the water, and a camp between a hippo and its river is the classic fatal siting error; crocodiles make the water's edge itself, within a few metres of any sizable tropical river or lake, ground for drawing water at speed and with a partner, not for lingering, washing, or pitching. Even harmless traffic costs sleep: raccoons, skunks, mice, and porcupines patrol shorelines for food, and the waterside camp donates its cookware and boot leather to them disproportionately. None of this makes wildlife the enemy; the point is the opposite. The 400 metre setbacks around desert springs exist because animals that must drink will forgo water rather than approach a human camp, and in drought that forbearance kills them. Camping off the water is simultaneously the safe choice and the courteous one: the animals keep their access, the camper keeps their food, and both parties keep the night uneventful.

sections.heading: The water's edge itself: banks, crossings, and drowning
sections.body: Apart from floods and animals, the edge of moving water is mechanically dangerous ground, and the statistics of backcountry fatalities put drowning near the top of every list, ahead of the hazards that get more campfire attention. Banks fail. An undercut bank, carved hollow by the current on the outside of a bend, can look like solid turf while overhanging open water, and it collapses under a person's weight precisely at the deepest, fastest part of the channel; the same bend geometry means the inside of a meander offers gravel beaches and slow water while the outside offers depth, speed, and undercut willows, so which side of a bend a camp and its water-drawing spot sit on is a real safety variable. Wet rocks, algae-slick ledges, and steep grassy banks turn a two-second water errand into a fall, and the person filling bottles at dusk in camp shoes on a slick boulder is the actual accident scenario, far more than any dramatic one. The cold multiplies everything: immersion in water below about 15 degrees Celsius triggers cold-shock gasping and rapid loss of grip strength, so even a strong swimmer who goes in beside camp in a mountain stream has a couple of minutes of useful function, and rivers fed by snow or glaciers run near five degrees all summer. Camps should therefore fix a single safe water point, chosen in daylight: low, gently shelving bank, slow current, solid footing, no undercut, and reachable by headlamp without crossing wet rock; children and non-swimmers in camp make this a rule to state out loud, since shorelines are where unsupervised wandering ends up. Crossings deserve their own respect, because a camp on the wrong side of rising water becomes a trap. Moving water knee-deep can take an adult's feet if it is fast; the standard mountaineering guidance is to treat anything above the knee as serious, unbuckle the pack's hip belt before entering so the pack can be shed, face upstream angling across and down, use a staff or paired arms for a third point of contact, and cross wide, shallow, braided reaches rather than narrow chutes, in the morning when snowmelt rivers run lowest. A rope tied to a wader, the intuitive safety measure, is a documented killer in current unless rigged by trained people at an angle with a release, because a taut rope holds a fallen swimmer under. The planning rule that ties this to campsite choice: never camp across rising water from your exit route with weather inbound, and if an evening ford was marginal, expect the morning after rain, or the evening during melt, to be worse; the safe campsite on the near side, with an extra kilometre of walking tomorrow, beats the pretty one across the channel every time the water is moving.

sections.heading: Lakeshores, coasts, and tidal ground
sections.body: Still water softens some running-water hazards and substitutes its own. On lakes, the flood mechanisms are slower, seasonal rise, storm surge pushed by wind, and on large lakes the seiche, a sloshing oscillation in which wind or pressure piles water at one end of the basin and releases it to rock back and forth for hours, capable of raising a calm shoreline by a metre or more on big waters like the Great Lakes. The practical lakeshore rules are wind and evidence: the debris line marks storm reach exactly as on rivers, waves on a long fetch, the open distance wind travels over water, can build surprisingly large and eat low beaches, and a point or exposed spit that blesses a camp with insect-clearing breeze in the evening can strand a tent in spray or worse when the weather turns. Sand and gravel beaches drain and dry quickly and make forgiving tent ground above the debris line; marshy and reedy margins offer the worst of everything, insects, cold damp air, soft ground, and awkward water access, and are better admired from the bench behind them. The seacoast adds the tide, a flood on a printed schedule, and it is astonishing how many coastal camping accidents are simply failures to consult it. Tidal range varies from under a metre in enclosed seas to over ten in funnel-shaped bays like Fundy and the Severn; the range also varies through the month, peaking at spring tides just after new and full moon, so the dry line of seaweed and shell that marks last night's high water may be metres short of tonight's. The coastal rules are mechanical. Find the highest wrack line, then camp above it with margin, adding more at spring tides and any onshore blow, because storm surge and swell run-up stack on top of the predicted tide. Never camp on a beach backed by cliffs or headlands without confirming, against the tide table and not against optimism, that the beach and your exit remain passable at high water; coastal walkers and campers are regularly trapped in coves by a rising tide with cold water doing the rest. Estuaries and tidal flats deserve double caution: the tide floods flat ground horizontally at walking pace or faster, channels behind a walker fill first and cut off retreat exactly as river islands do, and broad sand flats that invite an evening stroll from camp are the setting of recurring multiple-fatality accidents, such as Morecambe Bay's. Fresh water on coasts is its own planning problem, since streams reaching the sea are often brackish for their last stretch; drawing water above the tidal reach, marked by the last riffle or the disappearance of seaweed, and carrying it to a camp set high and dry is the standard pattern, one more argument that the good coastal camp, like the good river camp, sits back from the edge it depends on.

sections.heading: Special environments: deserts, snow country, and the tropics
sections.body: The water-versus-safety trade does not disappear in extreme environments; it changes sign and scale, and three environments deserve explicit treatment. In deserts the paradox is at its sharpest: water is the scarcest resource and the ground near it is the most dangerous in the landscape. Dry washes and arroyos are the flash-flood delivery system, smooth-floored precisely because floods regrade them, and the standing rule admits no exceptions, never a camp in the channel, however calm the sky, with sleeping ground chosen on rises, terraces above the highest debris, or open desert pavement well away from any drainage. Desert springs and tanks add the wildlife geometry at maximum intensity, since every animal for kilometres depends on the one source, hence the common 400 metre setback in bighorn country; they add human history too, because desert water has always concentrated people, and camping directly on a spring in many regions squats on an archaeological site as well as a lifeline. The desert compromise is to water up, filling every container at the source in daylight, then dry-camp deliberately on safe ground, a practice so standard it has a name, and it converts the region's worst hazard ground into a brief errand. Snow country inverts the supply problem: water is everywhere as snow and expensive as liquid, since melting snow costs roughly twice the fuel of boiling the same quantity, so winter camps prize the running creek or the lake with a maintainable hole. The hazards invert too. Streams under snowpack hide beneath snow bridges that drop a traveler into moving water at air temperatures where soaked clothing is immediately life-threatening; lake ice is trustworthy only when thick and cold, with about ten centimetres of clear new ice the usual minimum for a person on foot and much more needed for groups, and running water, inlets, and outlets thin the ice invisibly. Valley-bottom cold pooling is strongest in winter, routinely making the creekside flat the coldest ground for kilometres, and slopes above water courses carry avalanche paths whose runouts, readable as swaths of broken or missing trees, sometimes reach the valley floor; the winter camp therefore sits in the thermal belt, off runouts, drawing water at a chosen safe point or melting snow with budgeted fuel. The wet tropics soften temperature and sharpen biology and rise-rate: rain falls in volumes temperate campers underestimate, rivers respond in hours, and the still margins breed disease vectors at scale, so the tropical rules are river-camp rules amplified, generous vertical margin above the water, a hammock or raised bed rather than ground sleeping in flood-prone bottoms, nets treated and used from dusk, all water treated without exception, and in schistosomiasis and crocodile country a deliberate discipline about where skin and water are allowed to meet at all.

sections.heading: Sanitation: keeping the water clean
sections.body: Every rule pushing camps back from water has a mirror image: the camp's own wastes must be kept out of the water, because the stream beside a popular campsite is the drinking supply of every camp downstream, and the pathogens that make backcountry water untrustworthy in the first place arrive substantially from people. The core discipline is distance plus soil. Human feces carry Giardia, Cryptosporidium, E. coli, norovirus, and hepatitis A, all of which survive days to months in cool moist ground; a cathole 15 to 20 centimetres deep, dug with a trowel at least 60 metres from any water, camp, or trail, in organic soil where microbial life is densest, sited where runoff will not carry it downhill into a drainage, is the minimum standard, refilled and disguised afterward. In high-traffic corridors, on river trips, above treeline, and in slickrock and snow environments where soil is absent, the standard rises to packing waste out, and modern river regulations commonly require it outright; commercial waste-bag kits with gelling agents make this less unpleasant than it sounds. Urine is comparatively benign but attracts salt-hungry wildlife and accumulates odor at popular sites, so it goes on durable ground, rock or bare soil, away from camps and water. Washing is the sneaky pathway. Soap, including biodegradable soap, biodegrades in soil, not in water, and directly harms aquatic life in the concentrations a wash-up produces, so all washing of bodies, dishes, and clothes happens with carried water in a pot or collapsible basin at the 60 metre line, never in the stream or lake; wash water is then scattered broadly, and dishwater is first strained through a small screen or bandanna so food particles, which are bear attractants and rot in water, travel out with the trash. Toothpaste is spat into a cathole or broadcast in a fine spray away from water, not into it. Food waste follows the same logic: no scraps in the water, no burying of leftovers, which animals excavate within hours, and greasy pans wiped before washing so the grease goes to the trash rather than the ground. The kitchen itself sits at the setback line or beyond, both for wildlife separation and because spills and rinse water concentrate there. On the intake side, the camp protects itself with source choice and treatment: draw water upstream of camp, upstream of trails and stock crossings where possible, from moving rather than stagnant water, and treat everything, boiling one minute at a rolling boil, filtering at 0.2 microns, or dosing and waiting per the chemical's instructions, since clarity is no certificate. A camp run this way is almost perfectly decoupled from the water it uses: nothing of the camp reaches the stream, and nothing in the stream reaches the camp untreated, which is the entire object of the exercise.

sections.heading: Rigging the camp so distance costs nothing
sections.body: The sixty-metre camp fails in practice when it is inconvenient, because tired people revert to the water's edge the moment hauling becomes annoying; the craft is therefore logistical, making distance cheap enough that the safe camp is also the lazy one. Capacity is the whole trick. A camp that owns six to ten litres of container per person can supply an entire evening and morning in one trip; a camp limited to individual one-litre bottles is condemned to a shuttle service and will drift toward the bank. The standing kit for a small group is one or two large collapsible vessels, a ten litre folding bucket or water bladder weighs under two hundred grams empty and packs to nothing, plus each person's bottles, and, where the source is a trickle or a seep, a shallow scoop or cut-down bottle for filling. The routine matters as much as the kit: water is fetched immediately on arrival, while boots are still on and energy remains, with one person carrying the group's large vessels while others pitch shelters; full containers are stationed, one at the kitchen for cooking and dishes, one near the tents for night thirst and tooth-brushing, so that after dusk nobody has a reason to walk to the water at all, which is exactly when banks, cold water, and wildlife traffic are most dangerous. Filtration or chemical treatment is run in camp rather than at the source, both to keep bank time short and because treating from a settled bulk container clogs filters less than sucking silty water at the stream. The water point itself is chosen once, in daylight, for footing and access, low shelving bank, slow current, no undercut, and flagged in memory so a night trip, if one must happen, follows known ground with a headlamp. In the morning the routine runs in reverse: containers are topped for the day's walk before striking camp, and the site is left with no path of trampled vegetation from tents to water, which is the visible signature of a camp that did this wrong. The same logistics unlock the deliberate dry camp, one of the most useful tools in the repertoire: watering up at the last source in the afternoon, carrying three to five litres per person, and camping on safe, beautiful, empty ground far from any water at all, free of floods, cold pools, insects, and traffic, is standard practice in desert travel and steep country, and turns the entire water-versus-safety dilemma into a non-event on nights it is used. Distance, once rigged for, stops being a cost and becomes the campsite's cheapest feature.
ingredients: One large collapsible water container per two to three people, six to ten litres, folding bucket or bladder style.
Individual bottles or reservoirs totalling two to three litres per person.
A filter, chemical treatment, or stove and pot for boiling, sized to the group's daily volume.
A shallow scoop or cut-down bottle for drawing from seeps and trickles.
A small screen or bandanna for straining dishwater, and a trowel for catholes at the sixty metre line.

sections.heading: Choosing the site: a field procedure
sections.body: The full evaluation of a waterside campsite takes under ten minutes once the eye is trained, and it is worth performing as an explicit checklist until it becomes reflex, because the errors it catches are exactly the ones fatigue invites at the end of a walking day. The procedure assumes the common case: arrival near a water source with an hour or more of usable light, which is itself the first discipline, since sites chosen by headlamp skip every check that follows; arriving early enough is a navigation decision made at lunchtime. The sequence moves from the fatal hazards to the merely uncomfortable ones in strict order, because a site that fails an early check is abandoned without wasting attention on the later ones: watercourse and flood exposure first, then bank and access safety, then cold-air geometry, then biology, and only then the pleasant questions of view, morning sun, and flat ground for sleeping. Two habits complete the method. First, the two-minute walk: candidate benches twenty to fifty metres above and back from the obvious waterside flat are invisible from the water and almost always better; most campers never look. Second, the night audit: before dark, everyone should know three things, where is the safe uphill line if water rises, where is the fixed water point if something must be fetched, and where are headlamps; a camp that can answer them has converted its site choice into an executable night plan.
steps: 1. Confirm the legal frame: check area regulations for required setbacks, designated sites, or closures around the water source.
2. Identify the watercourse type: perennial river, seasonal creek, dry wash, lake, or tidal shore, and rule out categorically any channel bottom, wash, gravel bar, or island.

3. Walk uphill from the water and find the highest flood evidence: debris lines, silt stains, rafted vegetation in bushes, water-sorted sediment, and the boundary where riparian plants give way to upland species.

4. Place the sleeping area above the highest evidence with margin, at least sixty metres horizontal from the water, adding vertical margin during storms, snowmelt season, below dams, and at spring tides on coasts.
5. Check the ground overhead and upslope: dead limbs and standing dead trees within falling distance, cut banks above, avalanche runouts in winter.

6. Read the cold-air geometry: avoid hollows and enclosed bottoms, prefer a bench or gentle slope with a downhill drain for cold air, twenty to fifty vertical metres above the water where terrain allows.
7. Scan a few hundred metres upwind for still-water insect breeding ground and prefer breeze-exposed, well-drained ground; in disease regions, plan nets before dark.

8. Look for wildlife signs: converging trails, tracks, droppings, torn logs, fish remains; move out of travel corridors and separate tent, kitchen, and food storage by sixty to one hundred metres in bear country.
9. Fix the single safe water point in daylight: shelving bank, slow current, sound footing, reachable by headlamp; fill all containers immediately on arrival.
10. Brief the group on the night plan: the uphill escape line, the water point, and where lights and shoes are kept for a fast move.

sections.heading: When it goes wrong anyway
sections.body: No siting method reduces risk to zero, and the difference between an incident and a fatality at the water's edge is usually the quality of the response in the first minutes, so the failure modes deserve rehearsal in advance. Rising water at night announces itself as sound, a new roar, a change in the stream's pitch, or arrives as wet floor and floating gear; the response is immediate and unheroic, move people uphill first, along the escape line identified at dusk, with shoes and headlamps if they are at hand and without them if they are not, abandoning the tent and everything in it without hesitation, because gear is replaceable and the characteristic drowning of flood events happens during salvage attempts and vehicle or channel crossings, not in the first surprise. Nobody re-enters moving water for equipment, and a group regroups and counts heads at the high point, not at the wreck. If someone is swept away, the only useful help from shore is thrown, not swum: a line, a drybag on a strap, a branch, with rescuers braced and never tied to anything; a swimmer in current should go feet-first on their back, angling toward shore, and stand up only in slack shallow water, since a foot trapped between rocks in moving water is the mechanism that holds heads under. The aftermath of any soaking is a hypothermia problem on a schedule: wet clothing strips heat about twenty-five times faster than air, so the priorities after the count are dry layers, wind shelter, sugar and hot drink if a stove survived, and skin-to-skin warming in a bag for anyone deteriorating, with shivering treated as a warning stage and its cessation in a still-cold person treated as an emergency. Slower failures ask for judgment rather than sprinting. A camp that proves at midnight to be in a cold pool or under dripping condensation is uncomfortable, not dangerous, and moving in the dark usually costs more than it buys; the correct response is every layer on, bag drawn tight, and a note to climb higher tomorrow. A tide misjudged is the exception: water advancing on a coastal camp is moved away from immediately and uphill, before it reaches gear, because coastal ground behind a camp can cliff out and the water will not pause to negotiate. Wildlife in camp at night is managed from inside shelters with noise and light, never by a sprint to move food that should have been secured at dusk. And after any of these, the honest debrief is the mechanism by which the method improves: identify which check was skipped, arriving too late to see the debris line, trusting a clear sky over a big upstream basin, camping on the pretty bench inside the meander, and convert the night's luck into the next camp's habit. The water will keep its side of the bargain; the margin is the camper's to keep.

guides.safetyNote: Never camp in a dry wash, canyon bottom, or on a gravel bar, even under a clear sky; flash floods are generated by storms too far away to see or hear. Set camp at least 60 metres from water and above the highest debris line, and treat all backcountry water before drinking.

guides.title: Avoiding Widowmakers and Dead Standing Timber
guides.summary: How to recognise, assess and stay clear of falling limbs, snags and unstable dead trees: the biology and mechanics of tree failure, field inspection, campsite siting, weather triggers, and what to do when something comes down.

sections.heading: The hazard directly above your head
sections.body:
Almost everyone who spends time in forested country learns to watch the ground. They watch for loose rock, for river crossings, for the branch that will trip them, for the snake or the wet root. Very few learn to watch the air above their heads with the same discipline, and yet in wooded terrain the overhead hazard is the one most likely to kill outright and the one least likely to be seen coming. Falling limbs and collapsing dead trees are quiet, fast and essentially undodgeable. There is no skill that lets a person hear a branch release forty feet up and step aside in time.

The word for the hazard is old logging slang. A widowmaker is any loose or broken limb, top, or piece of a tree that is hung up or unstably attached and liable to come down without warning. In some regions the term is applied more loosely to any dangerous overhead wood; foresters and wildland firefighters use tighter language, calling a standing dead tree a snag and any tree with a structural defect a danger tree or hazard tree. All three are the same practical problem viewed from slightly different angles.

The physics explain why this hazard is disproportionate to its apparent size. A modest dead branch of ten kilograms falling fifteen metres arrives with a kinetic energy of about 1,470 joules, using energy equals mass times gravity times height. That is in the same range as a rifle bullet, delivered by a blunt object with a broken end. It hits at about seventeen metres per second, some sixty kilometres per hour, from a direction the victim is not looking. A larger limb of eighty kilograms from twenty metres carries roughly 15,700 joules, which is well past what any helmet or shelter will meaningfully absorb.

In occupational statistics the pattern is stark. Logging is consistently among the most dangerous occupations in industrialised countries, and being struck by a falling object rather than by the saw is the leading mechanism of fatal injury within it. On wildland fire assignments in North America, snags are a recurring killer during mop-up, the supposedly quiet phase after the fire front has passed, and the hazard is named explicitly in the standard safety briefings issued to crews. Recreational deaths follow the same pattern: people are killed in tents, in hammocks, in parked vehicles and around campfires, usually at night, usually in wind or after rain, and usually beneath a tree they never examined.

The encouraging half of the picture is that this is one of the most avoidable serious hazards in the outdoors. It requires no equipment, no strength and no expensive training. It requires the habit of looking up before you stop, and the willingness to walk another two hundred metres to a place with nothing dead overhead. Almost every fatality involves someone who did not look, or who looked, saw the problem, and stayed anyway because moving was inconvenient.

sections.heading: A working vocabulary of overhead wood
sections.body:
Precision in naming helps because different defects behave differently, and a term used loosely will hide the specific thing that is about to fail. Six categories cover nearly everything encountered in the field.

A snag is a standing dead tree, still rooted, with or without its top and branches. Snags are the classic overhead danger and also valuable wildlife habitat, which is why land managers leave them standing away from trails and campsites rather than clearing them wholesale. A hard snag has recently died and still has firm wood, tight bark and fine branches. A soft snag has been dead long enough that decay has advanced, bark has sloughed away and small branches have gone, leaving a grey, punky column. The soft snag is the one liable to fold rather than topple, and the direction it goes is far harder to predict.

A widowmaker in the strict sense is a detached or partly detached limb caught in the canopy, sitting on other branches or wedged in a fork, held only by friction, a strip of bark, or a splinter. Because it is already broken it has no remaining strength to lose; it comes down when the next gust, the next vibration, or the next warm afternoon that dries and shrinks the holding fibres releases it. These are the hardest hazards to see, because they are up in the leaf canopy and often look like ordinary branches from below.

A hung-up tree is one that has been cut or blown over and has fallen into a neighbouring tree instead of reaching the ground. It is under enormous stored elastic energy and is notoriously lethal. Loggers treat hung-up trees as an emergency to be resolved from a distance with a winch, never by climbing, cutting the supporting tree, or working underneath.

A hanger or chicot is a broken top or upper trunk section, still resting on the stem below, waiting to slide off. Root failure or windthrow describes the whole tree coming out of the ground with its root plate, common in saturated soils and shallow-rooted species. Finally, a leaner is a living or dead tree tipped from vertical, either recently, in which case the root plate may be actively pulling out, or long ago, in which case the tree has usually laid down reaction wood and stabilised itself.

Two further terms matter for assessment. A defect is any structural weakness: a cavity, a crack, a fungal fruiting body, a codominant fork, a lightning scar. A target is the person or object that would be struck. Formal danger tree assessment always couples the two, because a hazardous tree in a place nobody goes is only a tree. Risk is defect multiplied by exposure, and the practical lever available to a person on foot is almost always the exposure side.

sections.heading: How trees die and what happens next
sections.body:
A tree does not simply switch off. Death arrives through one of a handful of routes, and the route determines how the resulting snag will behave for the next decade, which in turn determines how dangerous it is at any given moment.

Insect attack is the most spectacular at landscape scale. Bark beetles, of which the mountain pine beetle is the best documented, tunnel between bark and sapwood, severing the tree's transport tissue and introducing blue-stain fungi that block water movement. The outbreak that ran through British Columbia and the western United States from the late 1990s into the 2010s affected on the order of eighteen million hectares of lodgepole pine, converting whole valleys into standing dead forest simultaneously. That synchronisation matters enormously: it means everything in a stand reaches the brittle, falling stage at roughly the same time, and mass fall events follow.

Fire kills by heating the cambium, the thin living layer under the bark, past about sixty degrees Celsius. Trees may look intact and remain standing for years afterward, but the roots have often burned as well, particularly where fire ran through deep duff or peat, and the anchoring is gone even though the trunk looks solid. Drought kills by cavitation, air bubbles breaking the water columns in the xylem, and drought-killed stands can cover enormous areas. Root disease, lightning, flooding, herbicide, salt, girdling by animals and simple old age account for the remainder.

Once dead, the tree begins a fairly predictable decomposition sequence. Fine twigs go first, within one to three years. Bark loosens and sheds over roughly three to eight years for most conifers, though the timing varies enormously with species and climate. Larger branches drop through the same period. The sapwood decays before the heartwood, so the tree becomes a shell around a firmer core, and this is the interval when the trunk still looks reassuringly solid while its outer strength has already gone. Roots decay from the fine ends inward, and this is the invisible process that matters most, because a snag with sound-looking timber and rotted anchor roots will simply lie down in a moderate wind.

Field observations across western North American conifers give a rough shape to the timeline. Snag fall rates are low for the first two or three years, rise sharply between years three and eight, and by fifteen to twenty years most have gone. Species differ hugely. Western redcedar, larch, black locust and other decay-resistant timbers may stand for fifty years or more. Aspen, birch, poplar and true firs collapse fast.

The practical rule that comes out of this is uncomfortable but honest. The most dangerous snag is not the obvious rotten one. It is the one that died four or five years ago, still looks like a tree, still has a solid-sounding trunk, and has quietly lost its roots.

sections.heading: Why branches let go: the mechanics of detachment
sections.body:
Understanding the mechanism behind detachment converts a vague sense of unease into a specific set of things to look for. Four distinct failure mechanics account for nearly all falling wood.
