Tick-borne illness has its own signatures. Lyme disease classically produces an expanding red rash, erythema migrans, appearing 3 to 30 days after the bite at the attachment site, often but not always with central clearing giving the bull's-eye appearance; it may be accompanied by fever, fatigue, headache and joint pain, and the rash is absent in a substantial minority of cases. Prompt antibiotic treatment, usually doxycycline, is highly effective, and delay is what produces the persistent joint, cardiac and neurological complications. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is far more acute, with fever, severe headache and a rash that typically begins on wrists and ankles and spreads inward; it carries meaningful mortality if not treated within about five days of onset, and treatment should not wait for confirmation.

Other patterns worth recognising: African trypanosomiasis after a painful tsetse bite, with a chancre, fever and later neurological change; leishmaniasis as a slowly enlarging painless skin ulcer weeks to months after sandfly exposure, or as fever with weight loss and abdominal swelling in the visceral form; and scrub typhus with fever, headache and a dark scab at the mite bite site.

The practical rule for anyone away from care is simple. Record the date and place of significant exposures. Treat any fever after exposure in an endemic area as urgent, seek assessment rather than waiting to see, and always volunteer the travel and exposure history unprompted, because the diagnosis frequently hinges on it.

sections.heading: When it goes wrong: failure modes and recovery
sections.body:
Even a carefully chosen camp can be overrun, and knowing the common failure patterns lets you fix the right thing rather than flailing. The most frequent failure is a site that was fine at dusk and intolerable at two in the morning. The cause is nearly always drainage air: the breeze that was present when you pitched was a daytime thermal circulation, it died with the sun, and cold humid air has since pooled around you. The fix is to move uphill, even 20 or 30 metres, or onto any feature the drainage flows past rather than into. If moving in darkness is unsafe, the interim measures are a smudge fire upwind, sealing the shelter and accepting the heat, and covering all skin.

The second failure is a compromised barrier. A single small tear, an unsealed zip, a net margin lying loose on the ground, or fabric pressed against a shoulder will produce dozens of bites while the rest of the arrangement works perfectly. When bites appear despite netting, look for the breach before blaming the equipment: inspect the seams and the zip, check that the margin is tucked under the mat, and check whether the bites are concentrated on the body part touching the mesh. Carry a needle and thread and repair tears the moment they appear.

The third is a breeding site you created. A camp occupied more than a week that starts benign and becomes progressively worse has almost certainly generated its own mosquitoes in a tarpaulin fold, an upturned lid, a wheel rut or a latrine sump. The cycle from egg to adult takes as little as seven days in warm weather, which matches the timing exactly. Walk the camp and empty everything.

The fourth is exhausted or degraded consumables. Permethrin loses effect after several washes, repellent runs out, netting perishes in ultraviolet light. When chemical protection fails, fall back on the free measures immediately: relocate for wind and elevation, cover all skin with layered clothing, build smudge fires, and shift activity out of the dusk and dawn windows.

If a camp becomes genuinely untenable — a driver ant column crossing it, a disturbed wasp nest, a hatch dense enough to make breathing unpleasant — the correct response is to move rather than endure. Pack quickly, move upwind and uphill, and re-pitch. Nights lost to sleeplessness compound into poor decisions, and the risk of a bad decision on difficult ground the following day usually exceeds the risk of a night move.

Finally, watch the people. Heavy bite loads cause fluid loss, secondary infection from scratching, and in extreme cases anaemia. Keep bites clean, keep fingernails short, treat itch with antihistamine so that people are not scratching open wounds, and take seriously anyone whose sleep has been destroyed for more than a night or two — their judgement is now the weakest link in the party.

guides.safetyNote: Any fever after time in a malaria-endemic area is a medical emergency until proven otherwise and needs assessment the same day; state the travel history explicitly. Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen in suspected dengue. Permethrin is for fabric only, never skin, and is highly toxic to cats and to fish until dry. Keep DEET off eyes, mouth and broken skin, and use 30 percent or less on children. Never burn a smudge fire inside an enclosed shelter — wood smoke carries carbon monoxide. Anyone with a known bee, wasp or ant venom allergy should carry two adrenaline auto-injectors on their person.
